Chapter 1 — Discrete-Time Signals and Systems: how is it examined?
column4:
8 hrs  \(\cdot\) the largest chapter, 105 questions across the 45 papers  \(\cdot\) worth about 12 of 80 marks every year  \(\cdot\) 10 syllabus sub-topics  \(\cdot\) numericals in the Ch1 companion.
Read this first:
  • Convolution is the single most-asked question in the whole subject: some form of “find \(y(n)\) given \(h(n)\) and \(x(n)\)'' appears in 34 of 45 papers TOP 34, usually for 5 or 6 marks. If you learn one thing in this chapter, learn that.
  • The chapter's other four regulars, in order:
    • energy Vs power signal \(+\) is it periodic TOP 10,
    • test a given system for linearity / time-invariance / causality / stability HOT 7,
    • find the fundamental period of a given sequence HOT 7,
    • sampling an analog signal and writing down \(x[n]\) HOT 7.
  • Counted by topic rather than by exact question, system properties come up in 16 papers and sampling in 10, so nothing here is optional.
  • The marks sit in the method, not the answer. Almost every question in this chapter is a 3-line recipe applied to new numbers. Sections 1.3, 1.4, 1.8 and 1.9 each end with the recipe written out as steps: memorise those, not the worked examples.
  • Tier chips count papers out of 45: TOP n \(\ge10\) papers, HOT n 4–9, PIN n 1–3. Bold year codes are Regular exams, plain are Back; typewriter codes are EX 753 (BEX) papers.

column1: Define and compare continuous-time and discrete-time signals; classify a given signal
column4:
By the independent variable
  • Continuous-time (analog): \(x(t)\) defined for a continuum of \(t\).
    • Eg speech voltage at a microphone, video signal.
  • Discrete-time: \(x[n]\) defined only at discrete instants, \(n\) integer.
    • Instants need not be equally spaced, but in practice \(t=nT\) is used.
    • Eg monthly sales of a corporation, daily stock-market average.
    • \(x[3.12]\) does not exist. A DT signal is a sequence, not a function sampled finely.
By the value the signal takes
  • Continuous-valued: amplitude takes any value in a range.
  • Discrete-valued: amplitude comes from a finite set.
  • Digital signal \(=\) discrete in time \(+\) discrete in value.
    • This is the only kind a processor can store, so A/D does both steps: sampling (Ch 1.10) then quantization (Ch 8).
  • Exam trap: “discrete-time'' and “digital'' are not synonyms. Sampling alone gives a discrete-time, continuous-valued signal.

column1: Define even and odd discrete-time signals; find the even and odd part of a given signal
column4:
Definitions
  • Even (symmetric): \(x[-n]=x[n]\).
  • Odd (antisymmetric): \(x[-n]=-x[n]\).
  • An odd signal must have \(x[0]=0\), since \(x[0]=-x[0]\).
  • Any signal splits into exactly one even \(+\) one odd part.
The two formulas
\[ x_e[n]=\tfrac12\big(x[n]+x[-n]\big),\qquad x_o[n]=\tfrac12\big(x[n]-x[-n]\big) \]
Derivation, if the question says “show that''
  • Start from \(x[n]=x_e[n]+x_o[n]\) (1)
  • Put \(n\to-n\): \(x[-n]=x_e[-n]+x_o[-n]\) (2)
  • Use \(x_e[-n]=x_e[n]\) and \(x_o[-n]=-x_o[n]\) in (2): \(x[-n]=x_e[n]-x_o[n]\) (3)
  • (1)\(+\)(3) \(\rightarrow\) \(x[n]+x[-n]=2x_e[n]\).
  • (1)\(-\)(3) \(\rightarrow\) \(x[n]-x[-n]=2x_o[n]\).
Method, every time
  1. Write \(x[n]\) as a sequence with the \(n=0\) sample marked.
  2. Fold it to get \(x[-n]\): same samples, index sign flipped.
  3. Half the sum, half the difference, aligning on \(n\).
  4. Check: \(x_e\) must be symmetric about \(n=0\) and \(x_o[0]=0\).

column1: Define and plot the unit step / unit impulse; explain their relation
column4:
The three building blocks and the chain that links them. BB Sir, deck 1.7
The five standard sequences
  • Unit impulse \(\delta[n]=1\) at \(n=0\), else \(0\).
  • Unit step \(u[n]=1\) for \(n\ge0\), else \(0\).
  • Unit ramp \(r[n]=n\) for \(n\ge0\), else \(0\).
  • Real exponential \(x[n]=\alpha^n\): decays for \(|\alpha|<1\), grows for \(|\alpha|>1\), alternates sign when \(\alpha<0\).
  • Complex exponential \(x[n]=r^ne^{j\theta n} =r^n(\cos\theta n+j\sin\theta n)\).
Relations worth quoting (this is the marks)
\[ \delta[n]=u[n]-u[n-1],\qquad u[n]=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{n}\delta[k] \]
  • Step is the running sum of the impulse; impulse is the first difference of the step.
  • Ramp is the running sum of the step: \(\delta\to u\to r\).
  • Sifting: \(x[n]\delta[n-k]=x[k]\delta[n-k]\), so \(x[n]=\sum_k x[k]\,\delta[n-k]\). This one line is what makes convolution work (§1.9).

column1: Define / compare energy and power signals, and classify the given signal
column4:
Over a finite interval \(n_1\le n\le n_2\)
\[ E=\sum_{n=n_1}^{n_2}|x[n]|^2,\qquad P_{av}=\frac{1}{n_2-n_1+1}\sum_{n=n_1}^{n_2}|x[n]|^2 \]
Over all time
\[ E=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{n=-N}^{N}|x[n]|^2,\qquad P=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{2N+1}\sum_{n=-N}^{N}|x[n]|^2 \]
  • Energy signal: \(0<E<\infty\), and then \(P=0\).
  • Power signal: \(0<P<\infty\), and then \(E=\infty\).
  • A signal can be neither (Eg \(x[n]=n\)), and never both.
How to decide in one line
  1. Finite-length or decaying sequence \(\rightarrow\) energy signal.
  2. Never-ending, bounded, non-decaying \(\rightarrow\) power signal.
  3. Every periodic signal is a power signal, with \(P=\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|x[n]|^2\) over one period.
  4. Every complex exponential \(e^{j(\omega_0n+\phi)}\) has \(|x[n]|=1\), so \(P=1\) and \(E=\infty\): power signal, no calculation needed. That is the whole answer to 79 Ba and 82 Bh.
Standard results to quote
  • \(x[n]=\delta[n]\): \(E=1\), \(P=0\) \(\rightarrow\) energy.
  • \(x[n]=u[n]\): \(E=\infty\), \(P=\tfrac12\) \(\rightarrow\) power. \(P=\frac12\), not 1: the sum runs over \(2N+1\) samples but only \(N+1\) are non-zero.
  • \(x[n]=A\) (constant): \(E=\infty\), \(P=A^2\) \(\rightarrow\) power.
  • \(x[n]=a^nu[n]\), \(|a|<1\): \(E=\dfrac{1}{1-a^2}\) \(\rightarrow\) energy.
Units
  • Follow the signal: a voltage signal gives energy in V\(^2\)s and power in V\(^2\).
Sums you will need in every one of these (learn this block)
\[ \sum_{n=-N}^{N}1=2N+1,\qquad \sum_{n=0}^{N}1=N+1 \] \[ \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}a^n=\begin{cases} N, & a=1\\[2pt] \dfrac{1-a^N}{1-a}, & a\ne1\end{cases} \]
\[ \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a^n=\frac{1}{1-a}\quad (|a|<1),\qquad \sum_{n=k}^{\infty}a^n=\frac{a^k}{1-a} \] \[ \cos\theta=\tfrac12(e^{j\theta}+e^{-j\theta}),\quad \sin\theta=\tfrac{1}{2j}(e^{j\theta}-e^{-j\theta}) \]

column1: Determine whether the given sequence is periodic; if it is, find the fundamental period
column4:
Definition
  • \(x[n]\) is periodic with period \(N>0\) if \(x[n]=x[n+N]\) for all \(n\).
  • Smallest such \(N\) is the fundamental period. \(N\) must be an integer: that is the whole difference from the continuous-time case.
The rule, and where it comes from
  • For \(x[n]=e^{j\omega_0n}\) to repeat: \(e^{j\omega_0(n+N)}=e^{j\omega_0n}\) \(\rightarrow\) \(e^{j\omega_0N}=1\) \(\rightarrow\) \(\omega_0N=2\pi m\).
  • So \(\dfrac{\omega_0}{2\pi}=\dfrac{m}{N}\) must be a rational number.
  • A discrete-time sinusoid is periodic only if \(\omega_0/2\pi\) is rational.
  • Then \(N=\dfrac{2\pi m}{\omega_0}\) with \(m\) the smallest integer making \(N\) an integer.
Method, every time
  1. Read off \(\omega_0\) (the coefficient of \(n\) inside \(\cos\), \(\sin\) or the exponent).
  2. Form \(\omega_0/2\pi\). Irrational \(\rightarrow\) aperiodic, stop.
  3. Rational \(=m/N\) in lowest terms \(\rightarrow\) fundamental period is \(N\).
  4. Sum of two periodic signals: \(N=\mathrm{LCM}(N_1,N_2)\), and it is periodic only if \(N_1/N_2\) is rational.
The three traps the papers actually set
  • \(x[n]=\sin(0.8n)\) or \(e^{j(7/5)n}\): \(\omega_0\) has no \(\pi\) in it, so \(\omega_0/2\pi\) is irrational \(\rightarrow\) aperiodic (66 Ma, 69 Bh).
  • \(x[n]=\cos(\pi n^2/8)\): \(n^2\), not \(n\) \(\rightarrow\) not a sinusoid, test \(x[n+N]=x[n]\) directly. It is periodic, \(N=8\) (70 Ch).
  • \(\sin(\pi n/\sqrt2+\pi/8)\): the \(\sqrt2\) makes \(\omega_0/2\pi\) irrational \(\rightarrow\) aperiodic (67 Mng).

column1: Show that a discrete-time signal is periodic in frequency with period \(2\pi\)
column4:
• Raise the frequency by \(2\pi\): \[ e^{j(\omega_0+2\pi)n}=e^{j2\pi n}e^{j\omega_0n}=e^{j\omega_0n} \] because \(e^{j2\pi n}=1\) for integer \(n\).
  • So \(\omega_0\), \(\omega_0\pm2\pi\), \(\omega_0\pm4\pi\ldots\) are the same sequence, sample for sample.
  • Consequences worth one line each:
    • All distinct DT frequencies lie in one span of \(2\pi\), usually \(-\pi\le\omega<\pi\).
    • \(\omega=\pi\) is the highest rate of oscillation (alternating \(+1,-1\)); \(\omega=0\) and \(\omega=2\pi\) are both DC.
    • In continuous time nothing like this happens: \(e^{j\Omega t}\) is distinct for every \(\Omega\).
\(\cos(\omega n)\) at \(\omega=5\), \(5+2\pi\), \(5+4\pi\), \(5+6\pi\): four different formulas, one sequence. BB Sir, deck 1.1

column1: Plot the transformed sequence, Eg \(x[-2n+3]\) or \(u[n]-u[n-3]+5\delta[n-4]+nu[n-6]\)
column4:
The three operations
  • Shift \(x[n-k]\): delay by \(k\) (move right) for \(k>0\); advance for \(k<0\).
  • Fold (time reversal) \(x[-n]\): mirror about \(n=0\).
  • Scale \(x[an]\):
    • \(|a|>1\) integer \(=\) decimation, keep every \(a\)-th sample, samples are lost.
    • \(|a|<1\) \(=\) interpolation, new samples must be filled in.
    • Not reversible like the CT case: this is why down-sampling needs its own treatment.
  • Amplitude operations: addition, multiplication, scaling act sample by sample on aligned indices.
Order of operations for \(x[an+b]\) (where marks are lost)
  1. Shift first, then scale/fold, or you will shift by the wrong amount.
  2. Safer still: work index by index. Set \(m=an+b\), then for each sample \(x[m]\) of the original, its new position is \(n=(m-b)/a\).
  3. Keep only integer \(n\); a non-integer means that sample disappears.
  4. Check one point: put \(n=0\) into \(an+b\) and confirm the value lands where you drew it.
Worked index map: \(x[-2n+3]\), \(x[n]=\{1,2,0,-1,-3,-4\}\) starting at \(n=0\)
  • \(n=0\rightarrow x[3]=-1\); \(n=1\rightarrow x[1]=2\); \(n=-1\rightarrow x[5]=-4\); \(n=2\rightarrow x[-1]=0\).
  • Only odd-indexed original samples survive: folding \(+\) decimation by 2.

column1: Explain how the Fourier series coefficients are calculated
column4:
The pair
  • A periodic \(x[n]\) of period \(N\) has fundamental frequency \(\omega_0=2\pi/N\).
\[ x[n]=\sum_{k=\langle N\rangle}a_k\,e^{jk(2\pi/N)n} \quad\text{(synthesis)} \] \[ a_k=\frac1N\sum_{n=\langle N\rangle}x[n]\,e^{-jk(2\pi/N)n} \quad\text{(analysis)} \]
  • \(\langle N\rangle\) means any \(N\) consecutive values, usually \(0\) to \(N-1\).
  • \(a_k=a_{k+N}\): only \(N\) distinct coefficients exist, because \(e^{j(k+N)\omega_0n}=e^{jk\omega_0n}\).
  • That is the one real difference from the continuous-time Fourier series, which has infinitely many distinct coefficients.
Deriving \(a_k\), if the question says “explain the process''
  1. Start from the synthesis equation.
  2. Multiply both sides by \(e^{-jr(2\pi/N)n}\) and sum over one period.
  3. Interchange the two summations.
  4. Use the orthogonality result \[ \sum_{n=\langle N\rangle}e^{j(k-r)(2\pi/N)n} =\begin{cases}N, & k-r=0,\pm N,\pm2N\ldots\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases} \]
  5. Every term dies except \(k=r\), leaving \(\sum x[n]e^{-jr(2\pi/N)n}=a_rN\).
Method for a numerical (faster than the integral)
  1. Find \(N\) first (§1.4), then \(\omega_0=2\pi/N\).
  2. Expand every \(\cos\)/\(\sin\) with Euler's formula.
  3. Force each exponent into the form \(jk(2\pi/N)n\) and read \(a_k\) off by inspection.
  4. Use \(a_k=a_{k+N}\) for anything outside \(0\le k\le N-1\).
Properties of the DTFS (x[n], y[n] both period N)
PropertySignalCoefficient
Linearity\(Ax[n]+By[n]\)\(Aa_k+Bb_k\)
Time shift\(x[n-n_0]\)\(a_k\,e^{-jk(2\pi/N)n_0}\)
Frequency shift\(e^{jM(2\pi/N)n}x[n]\)\(a_{k-M}\)
Time reversal\(x[-n]\)\(a_{-k}\)
Conjugation\(x^*[n]\)\(a^*_{-k}\)
Periodic convolution\(\sum_{r=\langle N\rangle}x[r]y[n-r]\)\(N\,a_kb_k\)
Multiplication\(x[n]y[n]\)\(\sum_{l=\langle N\rangle}a_l\,b_{k-l}\)
Parseval\(\frac1N\sum_{n=\langle N\rangle}|x[n]|^2\)\(\sum_{k=\langle N\rangle}|a_k|^2\)
Conjugate symmetry, asked as a rider: if \(x[n]\) is real then \(a_{-k}=a^*_k\). Real and even \(\rightarrow\) \(a_k\) real and even; real and odd \(\rightarrow\) \(a_k\) imaginary and odd with \(a_0=0\). Parseval reads: total average power in one period \(=\) sum of the average powers \(|a_k|^2\) of all harmonics.

column1: Explain the Fourier transform multiplication property for two sequences; write Dirichlet's conditions
column4:
The pair
\[ X(e^{j\omega})=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}x[n]e^{-j\omega n},\qquad x[n]=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{2\pi}X(e^{j\omega})e^{j\omega n}\,d\omega \]
  • Derived from the DTFS by letting \(N\to\infty\): the discrete lines \(Na_k\) merge into the continuous envelope \(X(e^{j\omega})\).
  • \(X(e^{j\omega})\) is periodic in \(\omega\) with period \(2\pi\), because \(e^{-jn(\omega+2\pi)}=e^{-j\omega n}\). So the inverse integral can be taken over any \(2\pi\) span.
  • Exists when \(x[n]\) is absolutely summable, \(\sum|x[n]|<\infty\).
Dirichlet's conditions (quote all three)
  1. \(x[n]\) is absolutely summable, \(\sum_n|x[n]|<\infty\).
  2. \(x[n]\) has a finite number of maxima and minima in any finite interval.
  3. \(x[n]\) has a finite number of finite discontinuities in any finite interval.
Sufficient, not necessary: \(u[n]\) fails condition 1 yet has a DTFT once impulses in \(\omega\) are allowed.
Multiplication property, and why it is not a plain product
  • Convolution in one domain \(=\) multiplication in the other, both ways:
\[ x[n]*h[n]\;\longleftrightarrow\;X(e^{j\omega})H(e^{j\omega}) \] \[ x_1[n]\,x_2[n]\;\longleftrightarrow\; \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{2\pi}X_1(e^{j\theta})X_2(e^{j(\omega-\theta)})\,d\theta \]
  • The second is a periodic (circular) convolution of the two spectra, scaled by \(1/2\pi\), integrated over any \(2\pi\) interval.
  • It has to be periodic: both spectra are \(2\pi\)-periodic, so an ordinary infinite convolution would diverge.
  • Proof in one move: substitute the inverse DTFT of \(x_1[n]\) into the forward DTFT of the product, then swap the sum and the integral.
  • This is the windowing property used to explain Gibbs oscillation in Ch 5: truncating \(h[n]\) with a window multiplies in time, so it convolves in frequency and smears the band edge.
Properties of the DTFT
PropertySignalTransform
Linearity\(ax_1[n]+bx_2[n]\)\(aX_1(e^{j\omega})+bX_2(e^{j\omega})\)
Time shift\(x[n-n_0]\)\(e^{-j\omega n_0}X(e^{j\omega})\)
Frequency shift\(e^{j\omega_0n}x[n]\)\(X(e^{j(\omega-\omega_0)})\)
Time reversal\(x[-n]\)\(X(e^{-j\omega})\)
Conjugation\(x^*[n]\)\(X^*(e^{-j\omega})\)
Convolution\(x[n]*h[n]\)\(X(e^{j\omega})H(e^{j\omega})\)
Multiplication\(x_1[n]x_2[n]\)periodic convolution of the spectra, \(\div2\pi\)
Parseval\(\sum_n|x[n]|^2\)\(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{2\pi}|X(e^{j\omega})|^2d\omega\)
If \(x[n]\) is real, \(X(e^{j\omega})\) is conjugate symmetric: magnitude even, phase odd. Real and even \(\rightarrow\) transform real and even; real and odd \(\rightarrow\) transform imaginary and odd. Parseval here says energy, not power: it is the DTFS version that talks about power.

column1: Test the given system for linearity, time-invariance, causality, memory and BIBO stability
column4:
The six properties, with the test that proves each
  • Static / memoryless: \(y[n]\) depends only on \(x[n]\) at the same \(n\).
    • Test: does any shifted index \(x[n-k]\), \(x[2n]\) or past output appear? If yes, dynamic.
  • Invertible: distinct inputs give distinct outputs, so an inverse system exists with \(h[n]*h_1[n]=\delta[n]\).
  • Causal: \(y[n]\) uses only present and past inputs.
    • Test: look for \(x[n+k]\), \(k>0\), or a folded index. \(y[n]=x[-n]\) is non-causal: at \(n=-2\) it needs \(x[2]\).
  • Time invariant: shift the input, the output shifts identically.
  • Linear: superposition holds.
  • BIBO stable: every bounded input gives a bounded output.
Linearity, the only reliable way to write it
  1. \(x_1[n]\rightarrow y_1[n]\) and \(x_2[n]\rightarrow y_2[n]\).
  2. Apply \(x[n]=a\,x_1[n]+b\,x_2[n]\) and compute \(y[n]\) from the system equation.
  3. Compare against \(a\,y_1[n]+b\,y_2[n]\). Equal \(\rightarrow\) linear.
Eg \(y[n]=nx[n]\): \(n(ax_1+bx_2)=a\,nx_1+b\,nx_2\) ✓linear. \(y[n]=x^2[n]\): the cross term \(2abx_1x_2\) survives ×not linear.
Time invariance, the only reliable way to write it
  1. Delayed input: put \(x_1[n]=x[n-n_0]\) into the equation, call the result \(y_1[n]\).
  2. Delayed output: write \(y[n-n_0]\) by replacing every \(n\) in \(y[n]\), including the explicit ones.
  3. Equal \(\rightarrow\) time invariant.
Eg \(y[n]=nx[n]\): \(y_1[n]=nx[n-n_0]\) but \(y[n-n_0]=(n-n_0)x[n-n_0]\) ×time varying. \(y[n]=\sin(x[n])\) ✓time invariant. An explicit \(n\) multiplying the input is the classic time-varying flag; folding \(y[n]=x[-n]\) is time varying too.
BIBO stability
  • Bounded means \(|x[n]|\le M_x<\infty\) for all \(n\).
  • To disprove: find one bounded input giving an unbounded output. A constant or \(u[n]\) almost always works.
    • Eg \(y[n]=nx[n]\) with \(x[n]=1\) gives \(y[n]=n\rightarrow\infty\) ×unstable.
    • Eg \(y[n]=\sum_{k=0}^{n}x[k]\) (accumulator) with \(x[n]=u[n]\) gives \(y[n]=n+1\) ×unstable. That is 80 Bh in one line.
  • To prove for an LTI system, use the impulse-response test in §1.9 instead: \(\sum_k|h[k]|<\infty\).
  • Recursive example, 81 Ba: \(y[n]=x[n]+e^{a}y[n-1]\) has \(h[n]=(e^a)^nu[n]\), so it is stable only if \(|e^a|<1\), i.e. \(a<0\).
Answer skeleton 5 10
  1. State the property in one line.
  2. Apply its test to this system, showing the algebra.
  3. Give the verdict with the reason attached, Eg “not time invariant, because the explicit \(n\) is not delayed''.
Marks are awarded per property, so answer all the parts asked even if one is obvious. A bare “yes/no'' with no working scores nothing.
Results worth memorising
  • \(y[n]=x[-n]\): linear ✓, time varying ×, non-causal ×, stable ✓.
  • \(y[n]=x[n^2]\) or \(x[2n]\): linear ✓, time varying ×.
  • \(y[n]=x^2[n]\), \(e^{x[n]}\), \(\log x[n]\): non-linear ×, but time invariant ✓and memoryless ✓.
  • \(y[n]=y[n-4]+x[n-4]\): linear ✓, time invariant ✓, causal ✓, dynamic and unstable.
  • \(y[n]=\cos(\frac{5\pi}{8}n+\frac{\pi}{4})\) has no input at all: not a system response, so it fails linearity trivially.

column1: What is the convolution summation? Derive its equation and explain its significance
column4:
Derivation, four steps (this is the full-mark answer)
  1. Decompose the input into impulses. By the sifting property, \[ x[n]=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}x[k]\,\delta[n-k] \] i.e. \(\ldots+x[-1]\delta[n+1]+x[0]\delta[n]+x[1]\delta[n-1]+\ldots\)
  2. Use time invariance. If \(\delta[n]\rightarrow h[n]\), then \(\delta[n-k]\rightarrow h[n-k]\).
  3. Use linearity. The input is a weighted sum of shifted impulses, so the output is the same weighted sum of shifted impulse responses.
  4. Therefore \[ y[n]=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}x[k]\,h[n-k]=x[n]*h[n] \]
Significance, if asked 2
  • \(h[n]\) alone characterises an LTI system completely. Know the impulse response, know the output for every possible input.
  • It converts a system description into an arithmetic operation, so the response can be computed rather than solved.
  • Causality and stability both become simple tests on \(h[n]\) (below).
Building \(h[a-n]\): fold \(h[n]\), then slide. Each value of \(a\) gives one output sample. BB Sir, deck 3
The graphical method, four steps
  1. Fold \(h[k]\rightarrow h[-k]\).
  2. Shift by \(n\): \(h[n-k]\).
  3. Multiply with \(x[k]\) sample by sample.
  4. Sum the products. That single number is \(y[n]\). Repeat for each \(n\).
Shortcut for two finite sequences: the output starts at \(n_x+n_h\) (sum of the starting indices) and has \(L_x+L_h-1\) samples. Use it to check your answer's length and position, every time.
Properties of LTI systems
  • Identity: \(x[n]*\delta[n]=x[n]\).
  • Shifting: \(x[n]*\delta[n-k]=x[n-k]\).
  • Commutative: \(x[n]*h[n]=h[n]*x[n]\): fold whichever sequence is shorter.
  • Distributive: \(x*(h_1+h_2)=x*h_1+x*h_2\) \(\rightarrow\) two systems in parallel add their impulse responses.
  • Associative: \(x*(h_1*h_2)=(x*h_1)*h_2\) \(\rightarrow\) two systems in cascade convolve their impulse responses, and their order does not matter.
  • Memoryless \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(h[n]=k\,\delta[n]\), giving \(y[n]=kx[n]\).
  • Invertible \(\Leftrightarrow\) there is \(h_1[n]\) with \(h[n]*h_1[n]=\delta[n]\).
  • Causal \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(h[n]=0\) for \(n<0\).
    • From \(y[n]=\sum_k h[k]x[n-k]\): terms with \(k<0\) would need future inputs.
  • BIBO stable \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(\sum_{k}|h[k]|<\infty\) (absolutely summable).
  • Step response \(s[n]=h[n]*u[n]=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{n}h[k]\), so \(h[n]=s[n]-s[n-1]\).
Proof of the stability condition, if asked to derive it
  • \(|y[n]|=\big|\sum_k h[k]x[n-k]\big|\le\sum_k|h[k]|\,|x[n-k]|\) by the triangle inequality and \(|ab|=|a||b|\).
  • Bound the input, \(|x[n-k]|\le M_x\): \(|y[n]|\le M_x\sum_k|h[k]|\).
  • So the output is bounded whenever \(\sum_k|h[k]|<\infty\).
Worked cases: \(h[n]=\delta[n-n_0]\) gives \(\sum|h|=1\), stable. \(h[n]=u[n-n_0]\) gives \(\sum|h|=\infty\), unstable. \(h[n]=a^nu[n]\) gives \(\sum|h|=1/(1-|a|)\), stable only if \(|a|<1\).

FIRIIR

The reason IIR needs a difference equation: convolution would need infinite memory, so it cannot be implemented directly.
Recursive Vs non-recursive
  • Non-recursive: output from present and past inputs only, \(y[n]=F\{x[n],\ldots,x[n-M]\}\). No feedback. A causal FIR system is non-recursive.
    • Eg moving average \(y[n]=\frac13\{x[n]+x[n-1]+x[n-2]\}\).
  • Recursive: output also uses past outputs, \(y[n]=F\{y[n-1],\ldots,y[n-N],x[n],\ldots,x[n-M]\}\). Has a feedback loop.
    • Eg \(y[n]=x[n]+a\,y[n-1]\).
    • Recursive form of the moving average (asked in 70 Ma): \(y[n]=y[n-1]+\frac1M\{x[n]-x[n-M]\}\): one add and one subtract per sample instead of \(M\) adds.
  • FIR/IIR is about the impulse response; recursive/non-recursive is about the implementation. They usually coincide but are not the same statement: a recursive structure can still realise an FIR response.

column1: State the linear constant-coefficient difference equation; find the zero-input and zero-state response
column4:
General form
\[ \sum_{k=0}^{N}a_k\,y[n-k]=\sum_{k=0}^{M}b_k\,x[n-k],\qquad a_0=1 \] \[ \text{or}\quad y[n]=-\sum_{k=1}^{N}a_k\,y[n-k]+\sum_{k=0}^{M}b_k\,x[n-k] \]
  • \(N\) is the order of the system.
  • \(N=0\) \(\rightarrow\) non-recursive (FIR); \(N\ge1\) \(\rightarrow\) recursive.
Total response \(=\) zero-input \(+\) zero-state
  • Iterating \(y[n]=a\,y[n-1]+x[n]\) from \(y[-1]\) gives \[ y[n]=\underbrace{a^{n+1}y[-1]}_{\text{zero input}} +\underbrace{\sum_{k=0}^{n}a^kx[n-k]}_{\text{zero state}} \]
  • Zero-state (forced) response: set \(y[-1]=0\). The part the input forces on the system. A system with zero initial conditions is called relaxed.
  • Zero-input (natural, free) response: set \(x[n]=0\). Depends only on the system and its initial conditions.
  • An LTI system must be relaxed. With non-zero initial conditions the system is not linear, which is why questions say “initially relaxed''.

column1: Find the frequency response of an LTI system / its response to a complex exponential
column4:
• Feed \(x[n]=e^{j\omega n}\) into the convolution sum: \[ y[n]=\sum_k h[k]e^{j\omega(n-k)} =e^{j\omega n}\underbrace{\sum_k h[k]e^{-j\omega k}}_{H(e^{j\omega})} \]
  • So \(y[n]=H(e^{j\omega})\,e^{j\omega n}\): the input comes out unchanged in shape, only scaled.
  • \(e^{j\omega n}\) is therefore an eigenfunction of every LTI system, and \(H(e^{j\omega})\), the DTFT of \(h[n]\), is the eigenvalue, called the frequency response.
  • \(|H(e^{j\omega})|\) is the magnitude response, \(\angle H(e^{j\omega})\) the phase response. Both are \(2\pi\)-periodic (§1.4).
The shortcut (do not convolve these)
  1. The question gives \(x[n]=Ae^{j\omega_0n}\) over all \(n\), so it is not a finite sequence: graphical convolution is the wrong tool.
  2. Compute \(H(e^{j\omega})\) once. For \(h[n]=a^nu[n]\): \[ H(e^{j\omega})=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a^ne^{-j\omega n}=\frac{1}{1-ae^{-j\omega}} \]
  3. Evaluate at the \(\omega_0\) the question gives.
  4. Answer: \(y[n]=A\,H(e^{j\omega_0})\,e^{j\omega_0n}\).
For a sum of sinusoids (73 Shr) do this once per frequency and add: superposition. For a real cosine, write it as two exponentials at \(\pm\omega_0\) and use conjugate symmetry.

column1: What is sampling? How is the spectrum of the sampled signal related to that of the continuous-time signal? Explain aliasing
column4:
Shifted copies, their sum, and the resulting \(X(e^{j\omega})\). The copies overlap here, so the triangle is distorted: this is aliasing. Chapterwise Ch2 p43
The relation (quote this equation)
  • Sampling means \(x[n]=x_c(nT)\), with \(T\) the sampling period and \(F_s=1/T\) the sampling rate.
  • Substituting into the inverse CTFT and regrouping gives
\[ X(e^{j\omega})=\frac1T\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} X_c\!\left(j\frac{\omega}{T}+j\frac{2\pi k}{T}\right) \]
  • In words: the spectrum of the sampled signal is the spectrum of the analog signal, scaled by \(1/T\), repeated every \(\Omega_s=2\pi/T\), with the analog frequency mapped to \(\omega=\Omega T\).
  • Three-step recipe for the diagram: (1) cut \(X_c(j\Omega)\) into bands of width \(2\pi/T\); (2) shift every band to the centre; (3) add.
Aliasing
  • If the copies are spaced closer than the signal is wide, they overlap and add. The overlapped region can no longer be separated.
  • A high frequency then reappears as, and is indistinguishable from, a lower one.
  • Cure: sample faster, or band-limit the input first.
Sampling theorem
  • Aliasing disappears when \[ \Omega_s=\frac{2\pi}{T}\ge2W \quad\text{or}\quad F_s\ge2F_{max} \]
  • \(2F_{max}\) is the Nyquist rate; \(F_s/2\) is the folding frequency.
  • Oversampling means \(F_s\) is taken well above the Nyquist rate: it pushes the copies further apart, so the anti-aliasing filter can be gentler (76 Bh asks exactly this).
  • When the criterion holds, every copy but \(k=0\) is zero in \(-\pi\le\omega<\pi\), so \(X(e^{j\omega})=\frac1T X_c(j\omega/T)\): the shape is preserved, only scaled. That is why perfect reconstruction is possible.
  • The relative width of the digital spectrum is \(\rho=2W/\Omega_s\): the faster you sample, the narrower the signal sits inside the \(2\pi\) span.
Same signal at the Nyquist rate, twice it, three times it. The copies pull apart and the gap between them grows. Chapterwise Ch2 p45

column1: Why is an anti-aliasing filter needed? Describe the effect of the sample-and-hold circuit at the input of an A/D converter
column4:
Anti-aliasing filter
  • A real signal is never perfectly band-limited: noise and harmonics run above \(F_s/2\).
  • Those components would fold down into the band of interest and cannot be removed afterwards: once aliased, the damage is permanent.
  • So an analog low pass filter is placed before the sampler, with cut-off at or below \(F_s/2\).
  • It is analog by necessity: a digital filter would come after the sampling that caused the problem.
  • Practical filters are not brickwall, which is the second reason to oversample: it widens the transition band the filter is allowed to use.
Sample-and-hold
  • An A/D converter needs a constant input during its conversion time. A signal still moving would be converted to a wrong, smeared value.
  • The S/H circuit tracks the input, then freezes it at the sampling instant and holds it flat until the conversion finishes.
  • Effects to state:
    • Holding is a zero-order hold: it multiplies the spectrum by a \(\mathrm{sinc}\)-shaped envelope, so high frequencies droop.
    • That droop is corrected later by a digital \(\times1/\mathrm{sinc}\) equaliser.
    • Real S/H adds aperture jitter, droop during hold and a small pedestal error.
  • Reconstruction at the output is the mirror image: D/A holds each sample flat, then an analog smoothing low pass filter removes the spectral images.

Convolution alone is 34 of the 45 papers. The four convolution sections below come first for that reason. Within a section the method is worked once, in full, and every other paper that ran the same method is listed under it with its data and its answer: same process, different numbers, so only the numbers change.
What you need before starting

  • Length and position check, use it every time: for two finite sequences the output starts at \(n_x+n_h\) and has \(L_x+L_h-1\) samples.

  • \(u[n+A]-u[n-B]\) is a window: it is 1 for \(-A\le n\le B-1\) and 0 elsewhere, so it has \(A+B\) taps. Getting these two limits right is most of the marks.

column1: 2  Convolution where one sequence is infinite
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2078 Bhadra · Q2 · [5]
Find the output of LTI system having impulse response \(h[n]=u[n]-u[n-4]\) and input signal \(x[n]=(1/2)^n\,u[n]\).
column4:
Method (used for every problem in this section)
  1. Turn the window into limits. \(h[n]=u[n]-u[n-4]\) is 1 for \(0\le n\le3\), so \(h[n-k]=1\) for \(0\le n-k\le3\), i.e. \(n-3\le k\le n\).
  2. Combine with the other sequence's own limits. \(x[k]=(1/2)^k\) needs \(k\ge0\). So \(k\) runs from \(\max(0,n-3)\) to \(n\).
  3. The \(\max\) is why there are two ranges. Solve \(\max(0,n-3)\):
    • \(0\le n\le3\): lower limit is \(0\) (the window hangs off the left of \(x\)),
    • \(n\ge4\): lower limit is \(n-3\) (the window is fully inside \(x\)),
    • \(n<0\): no overlap at all, \(y[n]=0\).
  4. Sum the geometric series on each range separately.
  5. Check: the two formulas must agree in value at the last sample of the first range against a direct count.
Range A, \(0\le n\le3\)
\[ y[n]=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left(\tfrac12\right)^k =\frac{1-\left(\frac12\right)^{n+1}}{1-\frac12} =2\left[1-\left(\tfrac12\right)^{n+1}\right] =\boxed{\;2-\left(\tfrac12\right)^{n}\;} \] Sample values: \(y[0]=1\), \(y[1]=1.5\), \(y[2]=1.75\), \(y[3]=1.875\).
Range B, \(n\ge4\)
\[ y[n]=\sum_{k=n-3}^{n}\left(\tfrac12\right)^k =\frac{\left(\frac12\right)^{n-3}-\left(\frac12\right)^{n+1}}{1-\frac12} =2\left(\tfrac12\right)^{n-3}\left[1-\left(\tfrac12\right)^{4}\right] =\boxed{\;15\left(\tfrac12\right)^{n}\;} \] Sample values: \(y[4]=0.9375\), \(y[5]=0.46875\), and it decays by half each step. Why the peak is at \(n=3\): that is the last \(n\) at which the whole window still sits over the large early samples of \(x\).
Final answer
\[ y[n]=\begin{cases} 0, & n<0\\[2pt] 2-\left(\frac12\right)^{n}, & 0\le n\le3\\[2pt] 15\left(\frac12\right)^{n}, & n\ge4 \end{cases} \]

  • \[ y[n]=46656\sum_{k=0}^{n-3}\left(\tfrac16\right)^k\left(\tfrac13\right)^{n-k} =46656\left(\tfrac13\right)^n\sum_{k=0}^{n-3}\left(\tfrac12\right)^k \]
  • The ratio is \(\frac{1/6}{1/3}=\frac12\): two different bases collapse to one geometric sum, which is the whole trick here.
  • \[ \boxed{\;y[n]=3456\left(\tfrac13\right)^{n-3}-1728\left(\tfrac16\right)^{n-3}, \quad n\ge3\;} \]
  • Check: \(y[3]=3456-1728=1728\), \(y[4]=1152-288=864\), \(y[6]=128-8=120\).
68 Bh 5: both sides infinite, one left-sided
  • Given \(x[n]=3^nu[-n-5]\), \(h[n]=u[n-5]\).
  • \(u[-n-5]\) is 1 for \(n\le-5\): a left-sided signal, and \(3^n\) decays as \(n\to-\infty\), so the sum converges.
  • Overlap needs \(k\le-5\) and \(n-k\ge5\) i.e. \(k\le n-5\). Upper limit is \(\min(-5,\,n-5)\), lower limit \(-\infty\).
  • \(n\le0\): upper limit \(n-5\), so \[ y[n]=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{n-5}3^k=\frac{3^{n-5}}{1-\frac13} =\boxed{\;\tfrac12\,3^{\,n-4}\;} \]
  • \(n\ge0\): upper limit is fixed at \(-5\), so \(y[n]\) stops changing: \[ y[n]=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{-5}3^k=\tfrac32\cdot3^{-5}=\boxed{\;\tfrac{1}{162}\;} \]
  • Running the series backwards is the only new idea: for a left-sided sum put \(k=-m\) and it is an ordinary \(\sum(1/3)^m\).
73 Bh 8: finite \(\times\) finite, but symbolic
  • Given \(x[n]=1\) for \(0\le n\le4\), \(h[n]=a^n\) for \(0\le n\le6\), \(a>1\).
  • Both finite, so the answer runs \(n=0\) to \(10\): but \(a\) is symbolic, so it is written as sums, not samples.
  • Overlap needs \(0\le k\le4\) and \(0\le n-k\le6\), i.e. \(\max(0,n-6)\le k\le\min(4,n)\).
  • Two \(\min/\max\) switches means three ranges, not two. With \(S(k)=\dfrac{a^{k+1}-1}{a-1}\): \[ y[n]=\begin{cases} S(n), & 0\le n\le4\\ S(n)-S(n-5), & 5\le n\le6\\ S(6)-S(n-5), & 7\le n\le10 \end{cases} \]
  • Check with \(a=2\): \(y[0]=1\), \(y[4]=31\), \(y[6]=127-31=96\), \(y[10]=127-63=64\).
76 Ash 6: the question as printed cannot be solved
  • The paper prints \(x[n]=2^n4[-n]\), \(0<a<1\) and \(h[n]=4[n]\): the sequence symbols are mangled, and it is meant to read \(x[n]=a^nu[-n]\), \(h[n]=u[n]\).
  • With \(0<a<1\) that diverges. \(a^nu[-n]\) grows without bound as \(n\to-\infty\), so \(\sum_{k\le\min(0,n)}a^k\) is infinite for every \(n\).
  • Reading A, the standard textbook problem and the one that fits the printed \(0<a<1\): \(x[n]=a^nu[n]\), \(h[n]=u[n]\). \[ y[n]=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a^k=\boxed{\;\frac{1-a^{n+1}}{1-a}\;}\quad n\ge0 \] As \(n\to\infty\) this tends to \(1/(1-a)\): a running sum that settles.
  • Reading B, keeping \(u[-n]\) literally, which needs \(a>1\) instead: \[ y[n]=\frac{a^{\,n+1}}{a-1}\ (n\le0),\qquad y[n]=\frac{a}{a-1}\ (n\ge0) \]
  • In the exam: state the inconsistency in one line, then solve reading A. verified/added

column1: 3  Response to a complex exponential
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2080 Baishakh · Q2 · [5]
Find the output of LTI system having impulse response \(h[n]=(1/2)^n*u[n]\) and input \(x[n]=5e^{j\pi n/3}\) for \(-\infty<n<\infty\).
column4:
The paper prints a stray “\(*\)'' between \((1/2)^n\) and \(u[n]\); it is a product, not a convolution.
Method (used for every problem in this section)
  1. Recognise the input: a single complex exponential running over all \(n\) is an eigenfunction, so \(y[n]=H(e^{j\omega_0})\,x[n]\) and no convolution is needed.
  2. Find the frequency response once: \[ H(e^{j\omega})=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\tfrac12\right)^ne^{-j\omega n} =\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\tfrac12 e^{-j\omega}\right)^n =\frac{1}{1-\frac12e^{-j\omega}} \] converging because \(|\frac12e^{-j\omega}|=\frac12<1\).
  3. Substitute \(\omega_0\) from the input, here \(\omega_0=\pi/3\).
  4. Put the denominator into rectangular form, then into polar form.
  5. Answer \(=\) input \(\times\) that complex number.
Step-by-step
  • \(e^{-j\pi/3}=\cos60^\circ-j\sin60^\circ=0.5-j0.866\).
  • Denominator \(=1-\frac12(0.5-j0.866)=1-0.25+j0.433=0.75+j0.433\).
  • \(|0.75+j0.433|=\sqrt{0.5625+0.1875}=\sqrt{0.75}=0.8660\),   \(\angle=\tan^{-1}\!\frac{0.433}{0.75}=30^\circ\).
  • So \(H(e^{j\pi/3})=\dfrac{1}{0.866\angle30^\circ}=1.1547\angle-30^\circ\).
\[ \boxed{\;y[n]=5\times1.1547\,e^{-j\pi/6}\,e^{j\pi n/3} =5.7735\,e^{j(\pi n/3-\pi/6)}\;} \] Read the answer: the sinusoid keeps its frequency, its amplitude is multiplied by \(1.1547\) and it is delayed in phase by \(30^\circ\). That sentence is worth a mark on its own.

column1: 5  Energy and power of a given signal
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2079 Bhadra · Q1 · [2+2]
Define energy and power signal. Determine whether the signal \(x[n]=\cos(2\pi n/5)+\sin(\pi n/3)\) is periodic or not. If periodic, find its fundamental period.
column4:
Method (used for every problem in this section)
  1. Look at \(|x[n]|\) before computing anything.
    • Bounded and never dying away \(\rightarrow\) power signal, \(E=\infty\).
    • Dying away or finite length \(\rightarrow\) energy signal, \(P=0\).
  2. Only then evaluate the one quantity that is finite. Computing both wastes time.
  3. For a periodic signal use one period: \(P=\dfrac1N\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|x[n]|^2\).
  4. For a decaying signal use \(E=\displaystyle\sum_n|x[n]|^2\) and the geometric sum.
  5. State the verdict as a sentence: “\(E=\infty\) and \(P\) is finite and non-zero, so it is a power signal.''
Worked: the 79 Bh signal
  • \(x[n]=\cos(2\pi n/5)+\sin(\pi n/3)\) is a sum of two sinusoids: bounded, never decays.
  • Both parts are periodic (§6 gives \(N=30\)), so the sum is periodic \(\rightarrow\) power signal, \(E=\infty\).
  • Power without summing: two sinusoids at different frequencies are orthogonal over the common period, so their powers add. \[ P=\frac{A_1^2}{2}+\frac{A_2^2}{2}=\frac12+\frac12=\boxed{\;1\;} \]
  • Quotable: a real sinusoid of amplitude \(A\) has \(P=A^2/2\); a complex exponential of amplitude \(A\) has \(P=A^2\) (no factor of 2, because \(|e^{j\theta}|=1\) rather than an oscillating cosine).
68 Bh 5: “find the energy and power of \(x[n]=u[n]\)''
  • Energy: \(E=\displaystyle\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}|u[n]|^2 =\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}1=\boxed{\;\infty\;}\)
  • Power: the limit runs over \(2N+1\) samples but only \(N+1\) of them are non-zero: \[ P=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{2N+1}\sum_{n=0}^{N}1 =\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{N+1}{2N+1}=\boxed{\;\tfrac12\;} \]
  • \(P=\frac12\), not 1. This is the single most common slip in the chapter, and 72 Ka asks the same thing beside \(\delta[n]\).
  • \(x[n]=\delta[n]\) (72 Ka): \(E=1\), and \(P=\lim\frac{1}{2N+1}=0\) \(\rightarrow\) energy signal.

column1: 6  Periodicity and fundamental period
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2080 Bhadra · Q1 · [5]
Determine whether the signal \(x[n]=e^{j\pi n/16}\cos(n\pi/17)\) is periodic or not. If periodic, find its fundamental period.
column4:
Method (used for every problem in this section)
  1. Read off \(\omega_0\) for each factor or term.
  2. Form \(\dfrac{\omega_0}{2\pi}\). Irrational \(\rightarrow\) aperiodic, stop there.
  3. Rational: write it as \(\dfrac{m}{N}\) in lowest terms; \(N\) is that term's period.
  4. Combine: for a sum or a product of periodic terms, the overall period is \(\mathrm{LCM}(N_1,N_2)\).
  5. Check by substitution if unsure: confirm \(x[n+N]=x[n]\) and that no smaller divisor of \(N\) works.
Worked: the 80 Bh signal
  • First factor \(e^{j\pi n/16}\): \(\omega_1=\dfrac{\pi}{16}\), so \(\dfrac{\omega_1}{2\pi}=\dfrac{1}{32}\) \(\rightarrow\) \(N_1=32\).
  • Second factor \(\cos(n\pi/17)\): \(\omega_2=\dfrac{\pi}{17}\), so \(\dfrac{\omega_2}{2\pi}=\dfrac{1}{34}\) \(\rightarrow\) \(N_2=34\).
  • Both rational, so the product is periodic.
  • \(32=2^5\), \(34=2\times17\), so \(\mathrm{LCM}=2^5\times17\).
\[ \boxed{\;N=544\;} \] Do not multiply \(32\times34=1088\). The LCM is the answer; multiplying is only right when the two are coprime.
The three traps, each a real paper
  • 70 Ch (i) \(\cos(\pi n^2/8)\): \(n^2\), so it is not a sinusoid in \(n\) and the \(\omega_0/2\pi\) rule does not apply. Test directly: \[ \cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi(n+8)^2}{8}\right) =\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi n^2}{8}+2\pi n+8\pi\right) =\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi n^2}{8}\right) \] since \(2\pi n\) and \(8\pi\) are whole multiples of \(2\pi\). \(N=4\) fails, so \(N=8\).
  • 70 Ch (ii) \(\cos(n/2)\cos(\pi n/4)\): the first factor has \(\omega=\frac12\) with no \(\pi\), so \(\omega/2\pi=1/4\pi\) is irrational \(\rightarrow\) the product is aperiodic. One irrational factor is enough.
  • 80 Ba (a) \(\sin(n\pi)+\cos(n\pi)\): \(\sin(n\pi)=0\) for every integer \(n\), so the signal is just \(\cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n\) and \(N=2\). Treating it as \(\mathrm{LCM}(2,2)\) gives the same answer, but say why the sine vanished.

Method for \(x[an+b]\) (index map, never “shift then scale'')
  1. Take \(x[n]=\{1,2,0,-1,-3,-4\}\) starting at \(n=0\), so \(x[0]=1,\ldots,x[5]=-4\).
  2. For each output index \(n\), compute the argument \(m=-2n+3\) and copy \(x[m]\).
  3. Keep only those \(n\) for which \(m\) lands on an existing sample, \(0\le m\le5\): \[ 0\le-2n+3\le5 \;\Rightarrow\; -1\le n\le1.5 \;\Rightarrow\; n=-1,0,1 \]
  4. Only three samples survive, because scaling by 2 throws away every second one.
\(n\)\(m=-2n+3\)\(x[m]\)\(y[n]\)
\(-1\)\(5\)\(-4\)\(-4\)
\(0\)\(3\)\(-1\)\(-1\)

column1: 9  Testing a system for its properties
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2068 Bhadra · Q1 · [5]
State whether or not the system \(y[n]=e^{x[2n]}\) is (a) linear (b) time invariant (c) memoryless (d) causal, where \(x[n]\) is input to system and \(y[n]\) is output of system.
column4:
Worked in full: \(y[n]=e^{x[2n]}\)
  • (a) Linear?
    • \(x_1\rightarrow e^{x_1[2n]}\), \(x_2\rightarrow e^{x_2[2n]}\).
    • Input \(ax_1+bx_2\) gives \(e^{a x_1[2n]+b x_2[2n]} =e^{ax_1[2n]}\cdot e^{bx_2[2n]}\).
    • Required: \(a\,e^{x_1[2n]}+b\,e^{x_2[2n]}\). A product is not a weighted sum.
    • Not linear ×
  • (b) Time invariant?
    • Delayed input: \(x_1[n]=x[n-n_0]\) gives \(y_1[n]=e^{x[2n-n_0]}\).
    • Delayed output: \(y[n-n_0]=e^{x[2(n-n_0)]}=e^{x[2n-2n_0]}\).
    • \(2n-n_0\ne2n-2n_0\), so not time invariant ×
    • This is the general rule: any time-scaled index \(x[2n]\), \(x[n^2]\), \(x[-n]\) makes a system time varying.
  • (c) Memoryless?
    • At \(n=3\) the output needs \(x[6]\), a different instant.
    • Not memoryless ×(it is dynamic).
  • (d) Causal?
    • For \(n>0\), \(2n>n\): the output at \(n=3\) needs \(x[6]\), a future input.
    • Not causal ×
  • Stable? (not asked here, but 66 Ma asks it)
    • \(|x[n]|\le M\) gives \(|y[n]|\le e^{M}\), finite \(\rightarrow\) BIBO stable ✓
Answer shape that scores: one line of algebra per property, then the verdict with its reason. “Not linear'' alone gets nothing.

column1: 10  Sampling an analog signal
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2081 Chaitra · Q1 · [1+3+3]
Consider the analog signal \(x_a(t)=3\cos100\pi t\).
  1. Determine the minimum sampling rate required to avoid aliasing.
  2. Suppose that signal is sampled at \(F_s=75\) Hz. What is the discrete time signal obtained after sampling?
  3. Assume now that we sample this signal using a sampling rate \(F_s=5{,}000\) samples/sec. What is discrete time signal after sampling?
column4:
Method (used for every problem in this section)
  1. Read the analog frequency off the argument: \(\cos(2\pi Ft)\), so \(2\pi F=100\pi\) gives \(F=50\) Hz. Divide by \(2\pi\), not by \(\pi\).
  2. Nyquist rate \(=2F_{max}\).
  3. Substitute \(t=nT=n/F_s\): the digital frequency is \(\omega=\dfrac{2\pi F}{F_s}\) rad/sample.
  4. Fold \(\omega\) into \(-\pi\le\omega<\pi\) by subtracting multiples of \(2\pi\). If you had to subtract anything, that term has aliased: say so.
  5. Write the answer as \(x[n]=A\cos(\omega n)\) with the folded \(\omega\).
(a) Minimum sampling rate
  • \(F=\dfrac{100\pi}{2\pi}=50\) Hz.
  • \[ F_s\ge2F=\boxed{\;100\text{ Hz}\;} \]
(b) \(F_s=75\) Hz: below Nyquist
  • \(\omega=\dfrac{2\pi\times50}{75}=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\) rad/sample.
  • \(\frac{4\pi}{3}>\pi\), so fold: \(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}-2\pi=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\).
  • Cosine is even, so \[ \boxed{\;x[n]=3\cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi n}{3}\right)\;} \]
  • Aliased: this is the same sequence a 25 Hz analog cosine would have given at 75 Hz. 75 Hz is below the 100 Hz Nyquist rate, exactly as part (a) warned.
(c) \(F_s=5000\) Hz: well above Nyquist
  • \(\omega=\dfrac{2\pi\times50}{5000}=\dfrac{\pi}{50}\), already inside \([-\pi,\pi)\).
  • \[ \boxed{\;x[n]=3\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi n}{50}\right)\;} \] no aliasing.
Every other paper that runs this same method
  • 78 Ch 2+2+3: same signal, \(F_s=200\) Hz. \(\omega=\frac{2\pi\cdot50}{200}=\frac{\pi}{2}\) \(\rightarrow\) \(x[n]=3\cos(\pi n/2)\), no aliasing.
  • 80 Ch 3+4: \(x(t)=\sin2000\pi t-5\cos12000\pi t+10\sin6000\pi t\), \(F_s=5000\).
    • \(F=1000,\,6000,\,3000\) Hz \(\rightarrow\) \(\omega=0.4\pi,\;2.4\pi,\;1.2\pi\).
    • Fold: \(2.4\pi-2\pi=0.4\pi\) and \(1.2\pi-2\pi=-0.8\pi\).
    • \[ x[n]=\sin(0.4\pi n)-5\cos(0.4\pi n)-10\sin(0.8\pi n) \]
    • Two of the three aliased, and the 6000 Hz term landed on top of the 1000 Hz term: they are now indistinguishable. The sign of the last term flips because \(\sin\) is odd.
    • For \(0\le n\le3\): \(x[n]=\{-5,\;-6.472,\;14.143,\;-6.053\}\) to 3 dp.
  • 73 Bh 3+4: identical but with \(+5\cos12000\pi t\), so the middle term keeps its \(+\) sign.
  • 73 Ma 4: \(x(t)=\cos1000\pi t+3\sin3000\pi t+5\cos5000\pi t\), \(F_s=6000\).
    • \(F=500,\,1500,\,2500\) \(\rightarrow\) \(\omega=\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{5\pi}{6}\): all already inside \([-\pi,\pi)\), no aliasing, because \(F_s=6000>2\times2500\).
  • 76 Bh 2+1+1+2+2: \(x(t)=3\cos50\pi t+10\sin300\pi t-0.7\cos100\pi t\), \(F_s=5000\).
    • \(F=25,\,150,\,50\) \(\rightarrow\) \(F_{max}=150\), Nyquist \(=300\) Hz.
    • \(\omega=\frac{\pi}{100},\;\frac{3\pi}{50},\;\frac{\pi}{50}\), no aliasing.
    • Reconstruction: since \(F_s\) is above Nyquist the original \(x(t)\) comes back exactly, \(x_r(t)=x(t)\). That is the whole answer to part (c): the sampling theorem guarantees it.

column1: 11  Difference equation: zero-input and zero-state response
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2078 Bhadra · Q4 · [4]
Determine the zero-input response for a second order system given by: \(y[n]-3y[n-1]-4y[n-2]=x[n]\)
column4:
Method
  1. Zero input means set \(x[n]=0\), leaving the homogeneous equation \(y[n]-3y[n-1]-4y[n-2]=0\).
  2. Try \(y[n]=\lambda^n\) and divide through by \(\lambda^{n-2}\) to get the characteristic equation.
  3. Solve for the roots.
  4. The response is a weighted sum of \(\lambda_i^{\,n}\); fix the weights from the initial conditions.
Step-by-step
  • \(\lambda^n-3\lambda^{n-1}-4\lambda^{n-2}=0 \;\Rightarrow\;\lambda^2-3\lambda-4=0\)
  • \((\lambda-4)(\lambda+1)=0\;\Rightarrow\;\lambda_1=4,\;\lambda_2=-1\)
  • \[ \boxed{\;y_{zi}[n]=C_1(4)^n+C_2(-1)^n\;} \]
Fixing the constants
  • The paper gives no initial conditions, so the boxed form above is the full answer. If \(y[-1]\) and \(y[-2]\) are supplied, solve \[ \tfrac{C_1}{4}-C_2=y[-1],\qquad \tfrac{C_1}{16}+C_2=y[-2] \]
  • \[ C_1=\frac{16\,(y[-1]+y[-2])}{5},\qquad C_2=\frac{4y[-2]-y[-1]}{5} \] verified/added
  • Read the roots: \(|\lambda_1|=4>1\), so the natural response grows without bound and the system is unstable. Saying that earns the last mark.
The other half, if asked
  • Zero-state response: set the initial conditions to zero and convolve, \(y_{zs}[n]=x[n]*h[n]\), or use \(H(z)\) (Ch 2).
  • Total \(=y_{zi}+y_{zs}\). An LTI system must be relaxed, so a question that gives non-zero initial conditions is not asking about an LTI system.

column4:
4 hrs  \(\cdot\) 61 questions across the 45 papers  \(\cdot\) worth about 7 of 80 marks  \(\cdot\) 3 syllabus sub-topics  \(\cdot\) the shortest chapter, and the best marks-per-hour in the subject.
Read this first:
  • Only two things are ever asked, and they are asked together:
    • state the properties of the ROC TOP 14: a 1 to 5 mark bookwork question, same answer every year,
    • find the inverse Z-transform of a given \(X(z)\) with a given ROC TOP 32, for 5 or 6 marks.
  • Those two appear as one question, Q3, in almost every paper. Learn §2.2 and §2.5 and the chapter is finished.
  • The ROC is not decoration. The same \(X(z)\) has a different \(x[n]\) for every ROC, and papers exploit that: 81 Ba, 82 Ba and 71 Ch each ask for three answers from one \(X(z)\).
  • Properties with proofs (convolution HOT 5, time shift, scaling) are worth 3 to 6 marks and come from §2.3.
  • Use one method for every inverse: divide by \(z\), partial-fraction \(X(z)/z\), multiply back so every term reads \(z/(z-a)\). §2.5 explains why.

column1: Define the Z-transform. How is it related to the DTFT? Explain the scaling property
column4:
Bilateral (two-sided) Z-transform
\[ X(z)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}x[n]\,z^{-n},\qquad z=re^{j\omega} \]
  • \(z\) is a complex variable, so \(X(z)\) is defined on a plane, not a line.
  • The sum exists only where it converges: that region is the ROC, and \(X(z)\) without its ROC is only half an answer.
  • Splitting the sum shows where the two halves live: \[ X(z)=\underbrace{\sum_{n=-\infty}^{-1}x[n]z^{-n}}_{\text{left-sided part}} +\underbrace{\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x[n]z^{-n}}_{\text{right-sided part}} \] The right half needs \(|z|\) large, the left half needs \(|z|\) small; an ROC is where both hold at once.
Relation to the DTFT (quote this)
\[ X(e^{j\omega})=X(z)\Big|_{z=e^{j\omega}} \]
  • Put \(r=1\): the Z-transform evaluated on the unit circle is the DTFT.
  • So the DTFT exists if and only if the ROC contains the unit circle. That one sentence answers half the theory questions in this chapter.
  • In reverse: \(X(z)\) is the DTFT of the exponentially weighted sequence \(x[n]r^{-n}\). The \(r^{-n}\) is what lets the Z-transform handle growing sequences the DTFT cannot.
  • Going round the unit circle once is \(\omega\) advancing by \(2\pi\): the same \(2\pi\)-periodicity as §1.4.
Unilateral (one-sided) Z-transform
\[ X^{+}(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x[n]\,z^{-n} \]
  • Ignores \(n<0\) entirely, so its ROC is always the outside of a circle and need not be stated.
  • Importance: it is the only version that can carry initial conditions, so it is what solves a difference equation for a system that is not relaxed.
  • Time delay property of the one-sided transform (73 Ma asks this): \[ Z^{+}\{x[n-k]\}=z^{-k}X^{+}(z)+\sum_{m=1}^{k}x[-m]\,z^{-(k-m)} \]
  • The extra sum is the initial conditions; the bilateral version has no such term, which is exactly why the one-sided transform is the one that solves a difference equation with given \(y[-1]\), \(y[-2]\).
Standard pairs (memorise these five)
\(x[n]\)\(X(z)\)ROCNote
\(\delta[n]\)\(1\)all \(z\)finite duration
\(u[n]\)\(\dfrac{1}{1-z^{-1}}=\dfrac{z}{z-1}\)\(|z|>1\)pole on the unit circle, so not stable
\(a^nu[n]\)\(\dfrac{1}{1-az^{-1}}=\dfrac{z}{z-a}\)\(|z|>|a|\)right-sided, causal
\(-a^nu[-n-1]\)\(\dfrac{1}{1-az^{-1}}=\dfrac{z}{z-a}\)\(|z|<|a|\)left-sided, anticausal
\(n\,a^nu[n]\)\(\dfrac{az^{-1}}{(1-az^{-1})^2}\)\(|z|>|a|\)repeated pole; also \(\dfrac{az}{(z-a)^2}\)
Rows 3 and 4 have the identical \(X(z)\) and differ only in the ROC. That is the whole reason the ROC must be given, and the reason an inverse cannot be started until you have read it.

column1: Define the ROC. State and explain the properties of the region of convergence
column4:
Definition
  • The ROC is the set of values of \(z\) for which \(\sum_n|x[n]||z|^{-n}\) converges, i.e. where \(X(z)\) actually exists.
  • It depends only on \(|z|=r\), never on the angle, which is why it is always drawn as circles.
The eight properties (this is the answer, in this order)
  1. The ROC is a ring or a disc in the \(z\)-plane, centred on the origin.
  2. The DTFT of \(x[n]\) converges absolutely if and only if the ROC includes the unit circle.
  3. The ROC cannot contain any pole. \(X(z)\) is infinite at a pole, so the sum cannot converge there.
  4. If \(x[n]\) is finite duration, the ROC is the entire \(z\)-plane, possibly except \(z=0\) and/or \(z=\infty\).
  5. If \(x[n]\) is right-sided (\(x[n]=0\) for \(n<N_1\)), the ROC extends outward from the outermost finite pole, possibly including \(z=\infty\).
  6. If \(x[n]\) is left-sided (\(x[n]=0\) for \(n>N_2\)), the ROC extends inward from the innermost non-zero pole, possibly including \(z=0\).
  7. If \(x[n]\) is two-sided, the ROC is a ring bounded inside and outside by a pole, containing none.
  8. The ROC must be a connected region.
For a 4 or 5 mark answer add one line of why to properties 3, 5 and 6, and sketch the three cases. For 1 or 2 marks, the definition plus properties 1, 3 and 5 is enough.
Right-sided \(x[n]=a^nu[n]\): the series \(\sum(az^{-1})^n\) converges for \(|az^{-1}|<1\), i.e. \(|z|>|a|\): everything outside the pole circle. BB Sir, deck 2.1
Left-sided \(x[n]=-a^nu[-n-1]\): same \(X(z)=z/(z-a)\), but the ROC is \(|z|<|a|\), the disc inside the pole circle. BB Sir, deck 2.1
Two-sided: the ROC is the ring between two poles. It contains the unit circle here, so this signal has a DTFT. Chapterwise Ch3
Stability and causality from the ROC (asked with the properties)
  • Causal \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(h[n]=0\) for \(n<0\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) the ROC is the outside of the outermost pole, and includes \(z=\infty\).
  • BIBO stable \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(\sum|h[n]|<\infty\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) the ROC contains the unit circle.
  • Causal and stable together \(\Leftrightarrow\) every pole lies strictly inside the unit circle. This is the single most quoted line in Chapters 2, 3 and 6.
  • A stable but non-causal system is possible: the ROC is a ring that contains the unit circle but does not reach \(z=\infty\).
Reading the ROC off a question (the skill the numericals need)
  1. Find the poles.
  2. Mark their radii on a line.
  3. The given ROC lies in one of the gaps. Any pole with radius below that gap is right-sided; any pole above it is left-sided.
A given ROC that contains a pole is impossible: two papers print exactly that, see Ch2-num §4.

PropertyTransformROC
Linearity\(a\,x_1[n]+b\,x_2[n]\;\rightarrow\;aX_1(z)+bX_2(z)\)at least \(R_{x_1}\cap R_{x_2}\)

Scaling in \(z\) (multiply by \(a^n\))\(a^n x[n]\;\rightarrow\;X(a^{-1}z)\)\(|a|r_1<|z|<|a|r_2\)
Differentiation\(n\,x[n]\;\rightarrow\;-z\dfrac{dX(z)}{dz}\)\(R_x\)
Time reversal\(x[-n]\;\rightarrow\;X(z^{-1})\)\(\dfrac{1}{r_2}<|z|<\dfrac{1}{r_1}\)
Convolution\(x_1[n]*x_2[n]\;\rightarrow\;X_1(z)X_2(z)\)at least \(R_{x_1}\cap R_{x_2}\)

Convolution, proved (the 3 to 6 mark answer)
  • Start from the definition of the convolution sum: \(x[n]=\sum_{k}x_1[k]\,x_2[n-k]\).
  • Transform both sides: \[ X(z)=\sum_{n}\Big[\sum_{k}x_1[k]x_2[n-k]\Big]z^{-n} \]
  • Interchange the order of summation (the step that earns the mark): \[ X(z)=\sum_{k}x_1[k]\sum_{n}x_2[n-k]z^{-n} \]
  • The inner sum is the time-shift property: \(\sum_n x_2[n-k]z^{-n} =z^{-k}X_2(z)\). \[ X(z)=X_2(z)\sum_{k}x_1[k]z^{-k}=X_1(z)\,X_2(z) \]
  • “At least'' the intersection: a pole of one can be cancelled by a zero of the other, which makes the ROC larger than the intersection. Say this: it is the part most answers miss.
Time shift, proved 3 69 Ch
  • Let \(y[n]=x[n-k]\), so \(Y(z)=\sum_n x[n-k]z^{-n}\).
  • Substitute \(m=n-k\), so \(n=m+k\): \[ Y(z)=\sum_m x[m]z^{-(m+k)}=z^{-k}\sum_m x[m]z^{-m}=z^{-k}X(z) \]
  • Why the ROC can change: \(z^{-k}\) adds poles at \(z=0\) (for \(k>0\)) or at \(z=\infty\) (for \(k<0\)), so those two points may drop out.
Scaling, proved 3 74 Bh
  • \[ Z\{a^nx[n]\}=\sum_n a^nx[n]z^{-n}=\sum_n x[n](a^{-1}z)^{-n}=X(a^{-1}z) \]
  • The ROC \(r_1<|z|<r_2\) becomes \(r_1<|a^{-1}z|<r_2\), i.e. \(|a|r_1<|z|<|a|r_2\): every pole is scaled by \(a\).
  • Example: \(u[n]\rightarrow\frac{1}{1-z^{-1}}\), so \(a^nu[n]\rightarrow\frac{1}{1-az^{-1}}\), pole moved from 1 to \(a\).
Differentiation, used in every \(na^n\) question
  • Differentiate \(X(z)=\sum x[n]z^{-n}\) term by term and multiply by \(-z\): \[ Z\{n\,x[n]\}=-z\frac{dX(z)}{dz} \]
  • Applied to \(a^nu[n]\) it gives \(Z\{na^nu[n]\}=\dfrac{az^{-1}}{(1-az^{-1})^2}\), \(|z|>|a|\): the answer 78 Ch and 70 Ma both ask for.

column1: Find the Z-transform of the given signal and locate its ROC
column4:
Method
  1. Split \(x[n]\) into its terms.
  2. Transform each with a standard pair, writing its own ROC beside it.
    • \(a^nu[n]\rightarrow\frac{1}{1-az^{-1}}\), ROC \(|z|>|a|\) (outside).
    • \(-b^nu[-n-1]\rightarrow\frac{1}{1-bz^{-1}}\), ROC \(|z|<|b|\) (inside).
    • Watch the sign: a \(+b^nu[-n-1]\) term transforms to \(-\frac{1}{1-bz^{-1}}\).
  3. The ROC of the sum is the intersection of the individual ROCs.
  4. If the intersection is empty, the Z-transform does not exist: and that is the full answer. 70 Ch prints exactly such a signal (Ch2-num §6).
Why the intersection can be empty
  • A right-sided term needs \(|z|>R_1\); a left-sided term needs \(|z|<R_2\).
  • The ring \(R_1<|z|<R_2\) exists only if \(R_1<R_2\): the right-sided pole must be the inner one.
  • \(R_1=R_2\) or \(R_1>R_2\) leaves nothing, so \(X(z)\) does not exist even though each term separately transforms perfectly well.
Two standard transforms the papers ask for by name
  • \(x[n]=na^nu[n]\) (78 Ch, 70 Ma): use differentiation: \[ X(z)=\frac{az^{-1}}{(1-az^{-1})^2},\qquad |z|>|a| \]
  • Derivation in one line: \(-z\dfrac{d}{dz}\dfrac{z}{z-a} =-z\cdot\dfrac{(z-a)-z}{(z-a)^2}=\dfrac{az}{(z-a)^2}\).
  • \(x[n]=\cos\omega n\) for \(n\ge0\) (74 Ma): write the cosine as two exponentials and add two geometric series: \[ X(z)=\frac{1-z^{-1}\cos\omega}{1-2z^{-1}\cos\omega+z^{-2}},\qquad |z|>1 \] Its two poles are \(e^{\pm j\omega}\), on the unit circle, which is why the ROC excludes it and why a pure sinusoid is not BIBO stable.

column1: Determine the inverse Z-transform of the given \(X(z)\) for the stated ROC
column4:
Which method, and when
  1. Partial fractions: the default. Use unless the question names another method. Gives a closed form for every \(n\).
  2. Long division (power series): use when the question says so (77 Ch, 76 Bh, 73 Bh, 72 Ma, 70 Ma). Gives numbers, not a closed form, so give 4 or 5 terms and the recurrence.
  3. By inspection: when \(X(z)\) is already a finite polynomial, read the coefficients straight off as impulses (74 Ash, 78 Ch).
  4. The contour-integral / residue method is never asked in these 45 papers.
Why divide by \(z\) first
  • The standard pairs are \(\dfrac{z}{z-a}\leftrightarrow a^nu[n]\), with a \(z\) on top.
  • Expanding \(X(z)\) directly gives terms \(\dfrac{A}{z-a}\) with no \(z\) on top, and each then needs an extra time shift. Expanding \(X(z)/z\) puts the \(z\) back for free.
  • Use it every single time, including the repeated-pole cases. One idiom, no decisions.
The partial-fraction method, in one fixed order
  1. Is \(X(z)\) proper? If the numerator's degree is \(\ge\) the denominator's, long-divide first and keep the polynomial part aside: it becomes impulses.
  2. Divide by \(z\) and expand \(X(z)/z\) in partial fractions.
  3. Multiply back by \(z\), so every term reads \(\dfrac{A\,z}{z-a}\).
  4. Assign each pole a side from the ROC (§2.2).
  5. Write the answer term by term with the pairs opposite.
The pair table, both sides
TermROC \(|z|>|a|\)ROC \(|z|<|a|\)
\(\dfrac{z}{z-a}\)\(a^n u[n]\)\(-a^n u[-n-1]\)
\(\dfrac{z}{(z-a)^2}\)\(n\,a^{n-1}u[n]\)\(-n\,a^{n-1}u[-n-1]\)
constant \(C\)\(C\delta[n]\)\(C\delta[n]\)
\(z^k\)\(\delta[n+k]\), an advance
The right-hand column is just the left with a minus sign and \(u[-n-1]\) instead of \(u[n]\). That is the only thing the ROC changes.
Long division: which way to divide (where the marks are lost)
  • Right-sided (ROC outside, causal): arrange both polynomials in ascending powers of \(z^{-1}\) and divide. The quotient \(x[0]+x[1]z^{-1}+x[2]z^{-2}+\ldots\) is read off directly.
  • Left-sided (ROC inside, anticausal): arrange in ascending powers of \(z\) instead. The quotient gives \(x[-1]z,\,x[-2]z^2,\ldots\)
  • Dividing the wrong way round gives the other sequence, which is a valid series for a different ROC: and scores zero.
  • Faster than dividing: read the recurrence straight off the denominator. For \(X(z)=\dfrac{1}{1-a_1z^{-1}-a_2z^{-2}}\), \[ x[n]=a_1x[n-1]+a_2x[n-2],\quad x[0]=1 \] and then just iterate. This is the same difference equation the filter implements (Ch 4).
  • Always give the recurrence as well as the terms: it shows the pattern continues and it is what a 6-mark answer wants.

  3. Assign each pole a side from the ROC: pole radius below the ROC \(\rightarrow\) right-sided; above \(\rightarrow\) left-sided.

column1: 1  Partial fractions, and how the ROC picks the answer
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2082 Baishakh · Q3 · [1+5]
Define the ROC. Find the inverse z-transform of \(X(z)=\dfrac{1}{1-1.5z^{-1}+0.5z^{-2}}\) using partial fraction method for (a) \(|z|>1\)  (b) \(|z|<0.5\)  (c) \(0.5<|z|<1\).
column4:
Step 1: factor the denominator and mark the poles
  • \(1-1.5z^{-1}+0.5z^{-2}=(1-z^{-1})(1-0.5z^{-1})\), so the poles are at \(z=1\) and \(z=0.5\).
  • Numerator degree 0 \(<\) denominator degree 2, so it is already proper: no division.
  • Three ROCs are possible, and the question asks for all three: \(|z|<0.5\), \(0.5<|z|<1\), \(|z|>1\).
Step 2: partial fractions, once, for all three parts
\[ \frac{1}{(1-z^{-1})(1-0.5z^{-1})}=\frac{A}{1-z^{-1}}+\frac{B}{1-0.5z^{-1}} \]
  • Put \(w=z^{-1}\): \(1=A(1-0.5w)+B(1-w)\).
  • \(w=1\) kills \(B\): \(1=A(1-0.5)\Rightarrow \boxed{A=2}\).
  • \(w=2\) kills \(A\): \(1=B(1-2)\Rightarrow \boxed{B=-1}\).
  • Check: \(A+B=1\), the numerator's constant term ✓
\[ X(z)=\frac{2}{1-z^{-1}}-\frac{1}{1-0.5z^{-1}} \]
Step 3: the ROC decides each term's side, and nothing else changes
Partpole \(z=1\)pole \(z=0.5\)\(x[n]\)
(a) \(|z|>1\)outside both \(\rightarrow\) rightright\(\big[2-(0.5)^n\big]u[n]\)
(b) \(|z|<0.5\)inside both \(\rightarrow\) leftleft\(\big[-2+(0.5)^n\big]u[-n-1]\)
(c) \(0.5<|z|<1\)ROC is inside it \(\rightarrow\) leftROC is outside it \(\rightarrow\) right\(-2u[-n-1]-(0.5)^nu[n]\)
Reading the three answers
  • (a) is causal: \(x[0]=1\), \(x[1]=1.5\), \(x[2]=1.75\ldots\) climbing to 2. Contains the unit circle? No: so this one is not stable.
  • (b) is anticausal: \(x[-1]=0\), \(x[-2]=2\), \(x[-3]=6\), growing as \(n\to-\infty\).
  • (c) is two-sided and is the only one whose ROC contains \(|z|=1\), so (c) is the stable one: \(x[0]=-1\), \(x[1]=-0.5\), and \(x[n]=-2\) for every \(n\le-1\).
  • All three come from the same two fractions. Only the choice of pair changes. That is the whole examinable idea.
  • If the question gives one ROC, do steps 1 and 2 identically and read one row of the table.
  • If it says “causal'' instead of giving an ROC, that means the outermost row: every pole right-sided.

column1: 2  Improper in \(z^{-1}\): divide first, the quotient becomes impulses
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2080 Bhadra · Q3 · [1+6]
Define ROC. Find the inverse z-transform of \(H(z)=\dfrac{1+2z^{-1}+z^{-2}}{1-0.75z^{-1}+0.125z^{-2}}\), ROC: \(0.25<|z|<0.5\).
column4:
Step 1: spot that it is improper, and divide
  • Both numerator and denominator have degree 2 in \(z^{-1}\), so a constant must come out first. Divide the highest powers: \(z^{-2}\div0.125z^{-2}=8\).
  • \[ N-8D=(1-8)+(2+6)z^{-1}+(1-1)z^{-2}=-7+8z^{-1} \]
  • \[ H(z)=8+\frac{-7+8z^{-1}}{1-0.75z^{-1}+0.125z^{-2}} \]
  • The 8 is already an answer: a constant is \(8\delta[n]\).
Step 2: factor, then partial fractions on the remainder
  • \(1-0.75z^{-1}+0.125z^{-2}=(1-0.5z^{-1})(1-0.25z^{-1})\): poles \(0.5\) and \(0.25\).
  • With \(w=z^{-1}\): \(-7+8w=A(1-0.25w)+B(1-0.5w)\).
  • \(w=2\): \(-7+16=9=A(0.5)\Rightarrow A=18\).    \(w=4\): \(-7+32=25=B(-1)\Rightarrow B=-25\).
  • Check \(A+B=-7\) ✓
\[ H(z)=8+\frac{18}{1-0.5z^{-1}}-\frac{25}{1-0.25z^{-1}} \]
Step 3: the ROC \(0.25<|z|<0.5\) splits the two poles
  • Pole \(0.5\): the ROC lies inside it \(\rightarrow\) left-sided \(\rightarrow\) \(-18(0.5)^nu[-n-1]\).
  • Pole \(0.25\): the ROC lies outside it \(\rightarrow\) right-sided \(\rightarrow\) \(-25(0.25)^nu[n]\).
  • \[ \boxed{\;h[n]=8\delta[n]-18(0.5)^nu[-n-1]-25(0.25)^nu[n]\;} \]
  • Check: \(h[0]=8+0-25=-17\); \(h[1]=-25(0.25)=-6.25\); \(h[-1]=-18(2)=-36\); \(h[-2]=-18(4)=-72\).
  • The ROC is a ring not containing \(|z|=1\), so this system is neither causal nor stable: worth one line if the question asks.

QUESTION AS PRINTED 2079 Bhadra · Q3 · [6]
Find the inverse z-transform of \(X(z)=\dfrac{2z^4+2z^3-3z+2}{z^2-1.5z-1}\), ROC: \(|z|<0.5\), using partial fraction expansion.

Step 1: poles, and what the ROC means
  • \(z^2-1.5z-1=(z-2)(z+0.5)\): poles at \(z=2\) and \(z=-0.5\), radii 2 and 0.5.
  • ROC \(|z|<0.5\) is inside both, so both poles are left-sided and the whole answer carries \(u[-n-1]\).
Step 2: long division in \(z\), because the numerator is degree 4
Written as ordinary polynomial division, highest power first. The missing \(z^2\) term is carried as \(0z^2\).
Quotient termsubtractnew remainder

\(5z\)\(5z(z^2-1.5z-1)=5z^3-7.5z^2-5z\)\(9.5z^2+2z+2\)
\(9.5\)\(9.5(z^2-1.5z-1)=9.5z^2-14.25z-9.5\)\(16.25z+11.5\)

  • \(C=\dfrac{11.5}{(-2)(0.5)}=-11.5\)

  • \(2z^2\rightarrow2\delta[n+2]\), \(5z\rightarrow5\delta[n+1]\), \(9.5\rightarrow9.5\delta[n]\) (powers of \(z\) are advances).

column1: 5  Repeated poles: the \(X(z)/z\) method earning its keep
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2076 Ashwin · Q3 · [3+6]
State Convolution property of Z-transform. Find inverse Z-transform of \(X(z)=\dfrac{z}{(z-0.6)(z+0.5)^2}\), ROC: \(|z|>0.6\).
column4:
Step 1: divide by \(z\), which removes the numerator entirely
\[ \frac{X(z)}{z}=\frac{1}{(z-0.6)(z+0.5)^2} =\frac{A}{z-0.6}+\frac{B}{z+0.5}+\frac{C}{(z+0.5)^2} \]
  • \(A\): cover \((z-0.6)\) and put \(z=0.6\): \(A=\dfrac{1}{(0.6+0.5)^2}=\dfrac{1}{1.21}=0.8264\).
  • \(C\): cover \((z+0.5)^2\) and put \(z=-0.5\): \(C=\dfrac{1}{-0.5-0.6}=\dfrac{1}{-1.1}=-0.9091\).
  • \(B\): clear denominators, \(1=A(z+0.5)^2+B(z-0.6)(z+0.5)+C(z-0.6)\), and match the \(z^2\) coefficient: \(0=A+B\), so \(B=-A=-0.8264\).
  • Matching one coefficient is faster than differentiating, and it is the step to use for every repeated pole.
Step 2: multiply back by \(z\) and apply the pairs
\[ X(z)=\frac{0.8264\,z}{z-0.6}-\frac{0.8264\,z}{z+0.5}-\frac{0.9091\,z}{(z+0.5)^2} \]
  • ROC \(|z|>0.6\) is outside both poles, so every term is right-sided.
  • \(\dfrac{z}{z-a}\rightarrow a^nu[n]\) and \(\dfrac{z}{(z-a)^2}\rightarrow n\,a^{n-1}u[n]\), here with \(a=-0.5\).
\[ x[n]=\Big[0.8264(0.6)^n-0.8264(-0.5)^n -0.9091\,n(-0.5)^{n-1}\Big]u[n] \]
  • Tidier, using \((-0.5)^{n-1}=-2(-0.5)^n\):
\[ \boxed{\;x[n]=\Big[0.8264(0.6)^n+(1.8182n-0.8264)(-0.5)^n\Big]u[n]\;} \]
Check
\(n\)substitution\(x[n]\)
0\(0.8264-0.8264\)\(0\)
1\(0.4959+(1.8182-0.8264)(-0.5)\)\(0\)
2\(0.2975+(3.6364-0.8264)(0.25)\)\(1\)
3\(0.1785+(5.4545-0.8264)(-0.125)\)\(-0.4\)
\(x[0]=x[1]=0\) is correct, not a slip. \(X(z)\) has one \(z\) on top and a cubic underneath, so the first non-zero sample cannot appear before \(n=2\): a quick sanity check before any arithmetic.

column1: 6  Finding \(X(z)\) and locating the ROC
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2075 Chaitra · Q3 · [4+6]
State the properties of ROC. Find the Z-transform and locate the ROC of the signal \(x[n]=(0.1)^n u[n]+(0.3)^n u[-n-1]\).
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2070 Chaitra · Q3 · [2+4]
List out the properties of Region of Convergence. Find the Z-transform and locate the ROC of the signal. \(x[n]=\left(-\tfrac13\right)^n u[n]-\left(\tfrac13\right)^n u[-n-1]\)
column4:
Method
  1. Transform each term with its own ROC.
  2. Mind the sign on the left-sided term: the standard pair is \(-b^nu[-n-1]\leftrightarrow\frac{1}{1-bz^{-1}}\), so a \(+b^nu[-n-1]\) in the question picks up a minus.
  3. Intersect the two ROCs.
Worked
  • \((0.1)^nu[n]\rightarrow\dfrac{1}{1-0.1z^{-1}}\), ROC \(|z|>0.1\).
  • \((0.3)^nu[-n-1]\rightarrow-\dfrac{1}{1-0.3z^{-1}}\), ROC \(|z|<0.3\).
  • \[ \boxed{\;X(z)=\frac{1}{1-0.1z^{-1}}-\frac{1}{1-0.3z^{-1}}, \qquad 0.1<|z|<0.3\;} \]
  • The ring is non-empty because the right-sided pole (0.1) is the inner one. It does not contain \(|z|=1\), so this signal has no DTFT.
The siblings
  • 75 Ash 3+6: \(x[n]=(0.6)^nu[n]+(0.25)^nu[n]\): both right-sided, so both ROCs are “outside'' and the intersection is the larger one: \[ X(z)=\frac{1}{1-0.6z^{-1}}+\frac{1}{1-0.25z^{-1}},\qquad |z|>0.6 \]
  • 75 Bh 4+6: \(x[n]=(0.25)^nu[n]+(0.6)^nu[-n-1]\): the mirror of 75 Ch: \[ X(z)=\frac{1}{1-0.25z^{-1}}-\frac{1}{1-0.6z^{-1}},\qquad 0.25<|z|<0.6 \]
  • 73 Ma 1+4: \(x[n]=(0.5+j0.2)^nu[n]+(-j)^nu[-n-1]\).
    • Radii are \(|0.5+j0.2|=\sqrt{0.29}=0.5385\) and \(|-j|=1\), so ROC \(0.5385<|z|<1\).
    • \(z=0.4\) is outside the ROC, so \(X(0.4)\) does not converge: that is the answer, not a number.
    • \(z=0.7\) is inside: \(X(0.7)=\dfrac{1}{1-\frac{0.5+j0.2}{0.7}} -\dfrac{1}{1+\frac{j}{0.7}}=1.4211+j2.2198\).
70 Ch and 70 Asa 2+4: the ROC comes out empty
  • First term: \(\dfrac{1}{1+\frac13z^{-1}}\), ROC \(\left|z\right|>\frac13\).
  • Second term is already in the \(-b^nu[-n-1]\) form, so \(\dfrac{1}{1-\frac13z^{-1}}\), ROC \(\left|z\right|<\frac13\).
  • Both radii are \(\frac13\). The intersection of \(|z|>\frac13\) and \(|z|<\frac13\) is empty.
  • \[ \boxed{\;\text{The Z-transform of this } x[n] \text{ does not exist.}\;} \]
  • That is a complete, correct answer, and it is the point property 8 of §2.2 is making: an ROC must be a connected, non-empty region.
The intended question verified/added
  • This is BB Sir's worked example with one digit changed: his version is \(x[n]=\left(-\frac13\right)^nu[n]-\left(\frac12\right)^nu[-n-1]\).
  • Then the radii are \(\frac13\) and \(\frac12\), the right-sided pole is the inner one, and \[ X(z)=\frac{1}{1+\frac13z^{-1}}+\frac{1}{1-\frac12z^{-1}} =\frac{2z\left(z-\frac{1}{12}\right)} {\left(z+\frac13\right)\left(z-\frac12\right)} \] with ROC \(\frac13<|z|<\frac12\).
  • In the exam: give the empty-ROC answer for the signal as printed, in two lines, then solve the \(\frac12\) version. Both halves earn marks; neither alone is the full answer.

column1: 7  Inverse by inspection: \(X(z)\) is already a polynomial
column4:
74 Ash 3+3
  • \(X(z)=z^2\left[1-\tfrac32z^{-1}\right](1+z^{-1})(1-z^{-1})\).
  • \((1+z^{-1})(1-z^{-1})=1-z^{-2}\), so \[ X(z)=z^2\left(1-\tfrac32z^{-1}\right)\left(1-z^{-2}\right) \]
  • Expand: \(z^2\left(1-\tfrac32z^{-1}-z^{-2}+\tfrac32z^{-3}\right) =z^2-1.5z-1+1.5z^{-1}\).
  • Read the coefficients as impulses, a power of \(z\) is an advance: \[ \boxed{\;x[n]=\delta[n{+}2]-1.5\delta[n{+}1]-\delta[n]+1.5\delta[n{-}1]\;} \]
  • As a sequence: \(x[n]=\{1,\,-1.5,\,\underline{-1},\,1.5\}\) for \(n=-2\ldots1\).
78 Ch 4
  • \(X(z)=z^2(1-1.5z^{-1})(1-z^{-1})(1+z^{-2})\).
  • \((1-1.5z^{-1})(1-z^{-1})=1-2.5z^{-1}+1.5z^{-2}\).
  • Times \((1+z^{-2})\): \(1-2.5z^{-1}+2.5z^{-2}-2.5z^{-3}+1.5z^{-4}\).
  • Times \(z^2\): \(z^2-2.5z+2.5-2.5z^{-1}+1.5z^{-2}\).
  • \[ \boxed{\;x[n]=\{1,\,-2.5,\,\underline{2.5},\,-2.5,\,1.5\},\quad n=-2\ldots2\;} \]
Why there is no ROC to worry about: a finite-length sequence converges everywhere except possibly \(z=0\) and \(z=\infty\) (§2.2, property 4). Both of these have positive and negative powers, so their ROC is \(0<|z|<\infty\).

column4:
6 hrs  \(\cdot\) 56 questions across the 45 papers  \(\cdot\) worth about 8.4 of 80 marks  \(\cdot\) 2 syllabus sub-topics  \(\cdot\) 6th of the 8 chapters by weight: only Ch 2 and the EX 753 extras are lighter.
Read this first:
  • 35 of the 56 questions are one question, asked again and again with the numbers changed: plot the poles and zeros in the \(z\)-plane, then sketch the magnitude response, not to scale TOP 35. It is worth 6 to 10 marks and it is the single most valuable thing in this chapter.
  • It arrives in two disguises. Either a difference equation is given and you must find \(H(z)\) first, or the poles and zeros are handed to you directly, sometimes in polar form. The second half of the work is identical.
  • The remaining 21 questions are short bookwork worth 2 to 4 marks each: causality and stability from the impulse response and the ROC HOT 7, the LCCDE and its system function HOT 6, FIR against IIR PIN 3, linear phase PIN 3, zero-input and zero-state response PIN 2.
  • Sketching does not mean guessing. Three numbers, \(|H|\) at \(\omega=0\), \(\pi/2\) and \(\pi\), plus the pole and zero angles, fix the shape completely. §3.3 gives the recipe.
  • The cheapest check in the chapter: \(H(e^{j0})=H(1)\) is the sum of all coefficients and \(H(e^{j\pi})=H(-1)\) is their alternating sum. Both are one line of arithmetic, and both are marks.

column1: Derive the expression for the frequency response of an LTI system. Show that a complex exponential is an eigenfunction of an LTI system
column4:
The eigenfunction property
Feed a complex exponential into an LTI system with impulse response \(h[n]\) and convolve: \[ y[n]=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}h[k]\,e^{j\omega(n-k)} =e^{j\omega n}\underbrace{\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}h[k]e^{-j\omega k}}_{H(e^{j\omega})} \]
  • The input comes out unchanged in shape, scaled by a complex number. So \(e^{j\omega n}\) is an eigenfunction of every LTI system and \(H(e^{j\omega})\) is the eigenvalue.
  • \(H(e^{j\omega})\) is the frequency response: the DTFT of \(h[n]\), and equally \(H(z)\) evaluated on the unit circle.
  • \[ H(e^{j\omega})=H(z)\Big|_{z=e^{j\omega}} \]
  • This substitution is legal only if the ROC contains the unit circle. If it does not, the system has no frequency response at all, however neatly \(H(z)\) factors. See §3.4.
Response to a real sinusoid
For \(x[n]=A\cos(\omega_0 n+\phi)\) and a real \(h[n]\), superposing the two exponentials gives \[ y[n]=A\,|H(e^{j\omega_0})|\cos\!\big(\omega_0 n+\phi+\angle H(e^{j\omega_0})\big) \]
  • The system can only do two things to a sinusoid: scale it by \(|H|\) and shift it by \(\angle H\). It can never change its frequency.
  • That is the whole reason the magnitude and phase responses are worth plotting.
Three properties that halve the work
  • \(H(e^{j\omega})\) is periodic in \(\omega\) with period \(2\pi\), because \(e^{j\omega n}\) is.
  • For real \(h[n]\), \(|H|\) is even and \(\angle H\) is odd in \(\omega\).
  • So everything is known from \(0\le\omega\le\pi\), and that is the only range any paper asks you to draw.
Magnitude, phase and group delay
  • Writing \(H(e^{j\omega})=|H(e^{j\omega})|\,e^{j\arg H(e^{j\omega})}\), the three standard plots are the magnitude response \(|H|\), the phase response \(\arg H\), and the group delay
  • \[ \operatorname{grd}H(e^{j\omega})=-\frac{d}{d\omega}\arg H(e^{j\omega}) \]
  • Group delay is the delay the system applies to the envelope of a narrow band of frequencies. Constant group delay means linear phase means no phase distortion: see §3.6.
  • Log magnitude is quoted in dB as \(20\log_{10}|H(e^{j\omega})|\).

column1: State the linear constant coefficient difference equation and the corresponding system function. Why do we need a difference equation?
column4:
The equation
An \(N\)th-order linear constant-coefficient difference equation relates the output samples to the input samples with coefficients that do not change with \(n\): \[ \sum_{k=0}^{N}a_k\,y[n-k]=\sum_{k=0}^{M}b_k\,x[n-k] \]
  • Linear: no products or powers of \(x\) or \(y\), no \(\sin y[n]\).
  • Constant coefficient: \(a_k\) and \(b_k\) are numbers, not functions of \(n\). This is what makes the system time-invariant.
  • Order \(N\): how many past outputs are fed back.
  • Normalising \(a_0=1\) gives the recursive computing form, which is how it is actually run on hardware:
  • \[ y[n]=\sum_{k=0}^{M}b_k x[n-k]-\sum_{k=1}^{N}a_k y[n-k] \]
The system function
Z-transform both sides, using linearity and the time-shift property \(y[n-k]\leftrightarrow z^{-k}Y(z)\): \[ Y(z)\sum_{k=0}^{N}a_k z^{-k}=X(z)\sum_{k=0}^{M}b_k z^{-k} \] \[ H(z)=\frac{Y(z)}{X(z)} =\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{M}b_k z^{-k}}{\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{N}a_k z^{-k}} =\frac{B(z)}{A(z)} \]
  • An LCCDE always gives a rational \(H(z)\), and every rational \(H(z)\) comes from some LCCDE. The two descriptions are the same object.
  • Zeros come from the \(x\) side (feedforward), poles from the \(y\) side (feedback). Read them straight off the two coefficient lists.
  • Multiply top and bottom by \(z^{N}\) to clear the negative powers before factoring.
Why we need a difference equation (a 2 mark question, asked five times)
  • It is a complete description of an LTI system in the time domain, finite and exact, whereas \(h[n]\) may be an infinitely long list.
  • It is recursive: each output uses a handful of stored past values, so an IIR response of infinite length costs finite memory and finite arithmetic.
  • It maps directly onto hardware: every term is one delay, one multiplier and one adder, which is exactly what a realisation structure draws (Ch 4).
  • It gives \(H(z)\) by inspection, so the frequency response, the poles, the zeros and the stability all follow from the same few coefficients.
  • It carries initial conditions, which is what separates the zero-input from the zero-state response.
A degree count worth remembering: if \(M<N\), then \(B(z)\) written in positive powers is short by \(N-M\), so \(H(z)\) has \(N-M\) zeros at the origin. They are real zeros and they belong on the plot, but being at \(z=0\) they are equidistant from every point of the unit circle and so contribute nothing to the magnitude shape.

column1: Plot the poles and zeros in the \(z\)-plane and sketch the magnitude response (not to scale) of the system described by the given difference equation
column4:
The geometric idea, which is the whole method
Factor \(H(z)\) into its zeros \(z_k\) and poles \(p_k\): \[ H(z)=K\,\frac{\prod_{k=1}^{M}(z-z_k)}{\prod_{k=1}^{N}(z-p_k)} \] Now put \(z=e^{j\omega}\), a point walking round the unit circle. Taking magnitudes turns the product into distances: \[ |H(e^{j\omega})|=|K|\, \frac{\prod_k\,\big|e^{j\omega}-z_k\big|}{\prod_k\,\big|e^{j\omega}-p_k\big|} \]
  • Every factor is the length of the vector drawn from a zero or a pole to the point \(e^{j\omega}\).
  • Zero distances multiply on top, pole distances divide underneath.
  • So as \(\omega\) sweeps \(0\) to \(\pi\): passing near a pole makes a denominator distance small, and \(|H|\) peaks; passing near a zero makes a numerator distance small, and \(|H|\) dips.
  • A zero exactly on the unit circle gives a distance of zero, so \(|H|\) is exactly zero there: a perfect null.
  • The closer a pole sits to the circle, the taller and narrower its peak.
The exam recipe
  1. From the LCCDE write \(H(z)=B(z)/A(z)\) in \(z^{-1}\), then multiply top and bottom by \(z^{N}\) so both are polynomials in \(z\).
  2. Factor. Roots of the numerator are zeros, roots of the denominator are poles. Use the quadratic formula: these are almost always second order and the roots almost always come out complex conjugate.
  3. Plot the unit circle, mark each zero \(\circ\) and each pole \(\times\), and do not forget the zeros at the origin.
  4. Evaluate three points, which is all a not-to-scale sketch needs:
  5. \[ |H(e^{j0})|=\left|\frac{B(1)}{A(1)}\right|,\quad \left|H(e^{j\pi/2})\right|=\left|\frac{B(j)}{A(j)}\right|,\quad |H(e^{j\pi})|=\left|\frac{B(-1)}{A(-1)}\right| \]
  6. Locate the peak at the angle of the pole, and the dip at the angle of the zero. Join the points smoothly.
  7. State the character in words: low-pass, high-pass, band-pass or notch.
\(B(1)/A(1)\) is just the sum of the coefficients, and \(B(-1)/A(-1)\) the alternating sum. Two lines of arithmetic for two anchor points of the sketch.
The algebraic form, for when a paper wants the expression and not only the picture
Each first-order factor, written with the pole or zero at radius \(r\) and angle \(\theta\), contributes \[ \big|1-re^{j\theta}e^{-j\omega}\big|^{2}=1+r^{2}-2r\cos(\omega-\theta) \]
  • In dB: \(\;20\log_{10}\big|1-re^{j\theta}e^{-j\omega}\big| =10\log_{10}\!\big(1+r^{2}-2r\cos(\omega-\theta)\big)\), added for a zero factor and subtracted for a pole factor.
  • Phase: \(\;\arg\big(1-re^{j\theta}e^{-j\omega}\big) =\arctan\dfrac{r\sin(\omega-\theta)}{1-r\cos(\omega-\theta)}\), again \(+\) for a zero and \(-\) for a pole.
  • Group delay of the same factor: \(\;\dfrac{r^{2}-r\cos(\omega-\theta)}{1+r^{2}-2r\cos(\omega-\theta)}\).
  • The minimum of \(1+r^2-2r\cos(\omega-\theta)\) is at \(\omega=\theta\), where it equals \((1-r)^2\). That is why a pole at angle \(\theta\) puts the peak of \(|H|\) at \(\omega=\theta\), and why \(r\to1\) makes it sharp.
Poles and zeros given in polar form
Several papers, and the local worked example the family is copied from, specify a radius and an angle instead of a complex number. Convert first: \[ z=re^{j\theta}=r\cos\theta+jr\sin\theta \] For example radius \(0.9\) at angle \(1.0376\) rad gives \(0.45+j0.77\), and radius \(0.892\) at \(2.5158\) rad gives \(-0.728+j0.522\). Those are the exact numbers the papers reuse, so recognising them saves a conversion.
