column1: Describe the stability and causality characteristics of an LTI system in terms of its impulse response and the ROC of its transfer function, with suitable examples
column4:
In terms of the impulse response
PropertyCondition on \(h[n]\)
Causal\(h[n]=0\) for all \(n<0\)
Stable (BIBO)\(\displaystyle\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}|h[n]|<\infty\)
  • Causality says the output cannot anticipate the input: it is a statement about when \(h[n]\) is allowed to be non-zero.
  • Stability says a bounded input always gives a bounded output, and the necessary and sufficient test is that \(h[n]\) be absolutely summable.
  • The two are independent. A system can be either, both or neither.
In terms of the ROC
PropertyCondition on the ROC
Causalexterior of the outermost pole, and includes \(z=\infty\)
Stablethe ROC contains the unit circle
Bothall poles strictly inside \(|z|=1\)
  • The last line is the one to quote: a causal system is stable if and only if every pole has \(|p|<1\).
  • A pole exactly on the circle is marginally stable, which is not BIBO stable: the frequency response blows up there.
  • Stability is also why the frequency response may not exist. If the ROC misses the unit circle, \(H(e^{j\omega})\) is undefined, so no magnitude response can be drawn at all.
One \(H(z)\), three systems (the standard worked example, and a favourite trap)
Take \(H(z)\) with poles at \(z=\tfrac12\) and \(z=3\). The algebra is identical in all three cases; only the ROC differs, and the ROC is a separate piece of information the question must supply.
ROC\(h[n]\)Causal?Stable?
\(\tfrac12<|z|<3\)\((\tfrac12)^nu[n]-2(3)^nu[-n-1]\)noyes
\(|z|>3\)\((\tfrac12)^nu[n]+2(3)^nu[n]\)yesno
\(|z|<\tfrac12\)\((\tfrac12)^nu[-n-1]+2(3)^nu[-n-1]\)nono
The middle row is the point: a causal system with a pole outside the unit circle is unstable, no matter how ordinary \(H(z)\) looks. The top row is the only stable reading, and it is not causal.

column1: Differentiate between an FIR system and an IIR system
column4:
FIRIIR
Impulse responsefinite length, \(h[n]=0\) outside \(0\le n\le M-1\)infinite length, decays but never ends
Difference equationnon-recursive, output from inputs onlyrecursive, past outputs fed back
\(H(z)\)all zeros, poles only at the originhas poles away from the origin
Stabilityalways stable, a finite sum is always boundedstable only if every pole is inside \(|z|=1\)
Linear phaseeasy, exact, by making \(h[n]\) symmetricnot achievable exactly
Order neededhigh, for a sharp responselow, for the same sharpness
Memory, arithmeticmoreless
  • The two rows examiners look for are FIR is always stable and FIR can have exactly linear phase. Those are the reasons to pay for its higher order.
  • An FIR system's \(H(z)=b_0+b_1z^{-1}+\dots+b_{M-1}z^{-(M-1)}\) written over \(z^{M-1}\) has all its poles at \(z=0\), which is inside the unit circle: the stability claim needs no further argument.

column1: What is the condition satisfied by a linear phase FIR filter? Derive the frequency response of a symmetric linear phase filter of length \(M\), \(M\) odd
column4:
What linear phase means, and why it is wanted
  • Phase is linear when \(\arg H(e^{j\omega})=-\alpha\omega\), a straight line through the origin.
  • Then the group delay \(-\dfrac{d}{d\omega}\arg H=\alpha\) is constant: every frequency is held up by the same \(\alpha\) samples.
  • A common delay shifts the signal but does not deform it. Linear phase means no phase distortion, which matters wherever shape carries the information: speech, ECG, data pulses, images.
  • If the phase were curved, different frequency components would arrive with different delays and a pulse would spread out, even with a perfectly flat \(|H|\).
  • Generalized linear phase allows a constant offset, \(\arg H=\beta-\alpha\omega\). The group delay is still constant, so it still does not distort; \(\beta=\pm\pi/2\) is what an antisymmetric \(h[n]\) produces.
The condition
An FIR filter of length \(M\) has linear phase if its impulse response is symmetric or antisymmetric about its midpoint: \[ h[n]=\pm\,h[M-1-n],\qquad 0\le n\le M-1 \]
  • \(+\) gives symmetric \(h[n]\) and phase \(-\alpha\omega\) with \(\alpha=\dfrac{M-1}{2}\).
  • \(-\) gives antisymmetric \(h[n]\) and phase \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\alpha\omega\), with the same \(\alpha\).
  • \(\alpha=(M-1)/2\) is the centre of the sequence, and it is the delay in samples. For odd \(M\) it is an integer; for even \(M\) it is a half-integer, so the filter delays by half a sample.
  • In the \(z\)-plane the condition forces zeros to occur in conjugate reciprocal groups: if \(z_0\) is a zero, so are \(z_0^{*}\), \(1/z_0\) and \(1/z_0^{*}\).
Derivation for symmetric \(h[n]\) with \(M\) odd (the 6 mark answer)
  • Start from the definition and pull out the centre term at \(n=\alpha=(M-1)/2\):
  • \[ H(e^{j\omega})=\sum_{n=0}^{M-1}h[n]e^{-j\omega n} \]
  • Substitute \(n\to M-1-n\) in the sum and use \(h[n]=h[M-1-n]\) to pair each term with its mirror image. Each pair contributes
  • \[ h[n]\big(e^{-j\omega n}+e^{-j\omega(M-1-n)}\big) =2h[n]\,e^{-j\omega\alpha}\cos\!\big(\omega(\alpha-n)\big) \]
  • Summing the \(\alpha\) pairs and the lone centre term factors the whole response:
  • \[ H(e^{j\omega})=e^{-j\omega\alpha} \underbrace{\left[h[\alpha]+2\sum_{n=0}^{\alpha-1}h[n] \cos\!\big(\omega(\alpha-n)\big)\right]}_{\text{real, call it }H_r(\omega)} \]
  • The bracket is purely real, so the entire phase is the exponential in front:
  • \[ |H(e^{j\omega})|=|H_r(\omega)|,\qquad \arg H(e^{j\omega})=-\alpha\omega\ \ (\text{plus }\pi\text{ wherever }H_r<0) \]
  • That is the proof: the phase is a straight line of slope \(-\alpha\), so the group delay is \(\alpha\) samples at every frequency.
The antisymmetric case runs identically but the mirror pair subtracts, giving \(2jh[n]\sin(\omega(\alpha-n))\) and hence \(H=je^{-j\omega\alpha}H_i(\omega)\). The extra \(j\) is the constant \(\pi/2\) in the phase, which is why an antisymmetric filter has generalized linear phase rather than the plain kind. See §5 of the numerical companion for \(h[n]=\{-1,0,1\}\), which is this case.

column1: Chapter 3 numericals — which formulas does everything come from?
column4:
35 of the 56 questions in this chapter are the same question: plot the poles and zeros, then sketch the magnitude response. All of them are below. They split into two shapes, according to whether the paper gives you a difference equation or the pole and zero locations themselves, and the second half of the work is identical in both.
The one procedure, used in §1 and §2
  1. Get \(H(z)\). From an LCCDE, Z-transform both sides and divide. Multiply top and bottom by \(z^{N}\) so both are polynomials in \(z\), not in \(z^{-1}\).
  2. Factor. Numerator roots are zeros, denominator roots are poles. These are almost always quadratics, so the quadratic formula finishes it, and complex roots always arrive in conjugate pairs.
  3. Plot: unit circle, \(\circ\) for each zero, \(\times\) for each pole, and the zeros at the origin if the numerator is the shorter polynomial.
  4. Three anchor values, which is all a not-to-scale sketch needs: \(|H(1)|\) at \(\omega=0\), \(|H(j)|\) at \(\omega=\pi/2\), \(|H(-1)|\) at \(\omega=\pi\).
  5. Peak at the pole angle, dip at the zero angle. Join smoothly, then say in words whether it is low-pass, high-pass, band-pass or a notch.
The geometry, in one line
\[ |H(e^{j\omega})|=|K|\, \frac{\prod_k|e^{j\omega}-z_k|}{\prod_k|e^{j\omega}-p_k|} \]
  • Distances from the zeros multiply on top, distances from the poles divide underneath.
  • A pole at radius \(r\) and angle \(\theta\) makes \(|H|\) peak at \(\omega=\theta\), and the peak is sharper the closer \(r\) is to 1.
  • A zero on the circle forces \(|H|\) to exactly zero at its angle.
The checks that cost nothing
  1. \(|H(1)|\) is the sum of the coefficients over the sum of the denominator coefficients; \(|H(-1)|\) is the same with alternating signs. Two lines.
  2. Complex roots must be conjugate pairs. A lone complex pole is an arithmetic slip, every time.
  3. Product of the roots of \(z^2+\alpha z+\beta\) is \(\beta\), sum is \(-\alpha\). Check your factorisation against the coefficients before plotting.
  4. If any pole has \(|p|\ge1\) and the system is stated causal, stop: the ROC excludes the unit circle and there is no frequency response to draw.

column1: 1  Difference equation given: find \(H(z)\), plot, sketch \(|H|\)
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2080 Chaitra · 2072 Ashwin · [8/7]
Plot the pole-zero in the z-plane and draw the magnitude response (not to scale) of the system described by the difference equation \(y[n]-0.4y[n-1]+0.25y[n-2]=x[n]+0.5x[n-1]\) (magnitude response only).
column4:
Step 1: transform and divide
  • Z-transform term by term, using \(y[n-k]\leftrightarrow z^{-k}Y(z)\):
  • \[ Y(z)\big(1-0.4z^{-1}+0.25z^{-2}\big)=X(z)\big(1+0.5z^{-1}\big) \]
  • \[ H(z)=\frac{1+0.5z^{-1}}{1-0.4z^{-1}+0.25z^{-2}} =\frac{z(z+0.5)}{z^{2}-0.4z+0.25} \]
  • Multiplying by \(z^{2}/z^{2}\) is what exposes the zero at the origin. Do it before factoring, every time.
Step 2: factor
  • Zeros, from the numerator \(z(z+0.5)\):
  • \[ z=0 \quad\text{and}\quad z=-0.5 \]
  • Poles, from \(z^{2}-0.4z+0.25=0\):
  • \[ z=\frac{0.4\pm\sqrt{0.16-1}}{2}=0.2\pm j0.4583 \]
  • Check: product of the poles is \(0.04+0.21=0.25\), the constant term. Sum is \(0.4\). Both agree.
  • In polar form the pole pair is
  • \[ |p|=\sqrt{0.2^{2}+0.4583^{2}}=\mathbf{0.5},\qquad \theta=\arctan\frac{0.4583}{0.2}=66.4^{\circ}=1.159\ \text{rad} \]
  • \(|p|=0.5<1\), so the causal system is stable and the frequency response exists.
  • \(|p|=0.5\) exactly, because the constant term of a monic quadratic is the product of the roots, and here that product is \(|p|^2=0.25\).
Step 3: the three anchor values
  • At \(\omega=0\), put \(z=1\): \(\;|H|=\left|\dfrac{1+0.5}{1-0.4+0.25}\right|=\dfrac{1.5}{0.85}=\mathbf{1.765}\)
  • At \(\omega=\pi/2\), put \(z=j\): \(\;|H|=\left|\dfrac{1-0.5j}{1+0.4j-0.25}\right| =\dfrac{1.118}{0.850}=\mathbf{1.315}\)
  • At \(\omega=\pi\), put \(z=-1\): \(\;|H|=\left|\dfrac{1-0.5}{1+0.4+0.25}\right|=\dfrac{0.5}{1.65}=\mathbf{0.303}\)
Step 4: read the shape off the plot
  • The pole pair sits at \(66.4^{\circ}\), so \(|H|\) peaks near there. The true peak is \(\mathbf{1.96}\) at \(\mathbf{50.9^{\circ}}\), pulled back towards \(\omega=0\) by the zero at \(z=-0.5\) sitting on the far side.
  • The zero at \(z=-0.5\) lies at angle \(180^{\circ}\), so \(|H|\) is smallest at \(\omega=\pi\), and \(0.303\) is the minimum.
  • The zero at the origin is equidistant from every point of the circle and does not shape the response at all. It still belongs on the plot.
  • Verdict: a low-pass response, rising a little to a broad hump around \(50^{\circ}\) before falling to \(0.303\) at \(\omega=\pi\).
The same poles with the zero moved: 78 Bh and 81 Bh
Two more papers ask the identical question with \(x[n]-0.4x[n-1]\) on the right instead of \(x[n]+0.5x[n-1]\). The denominator is unchanged, so the poles are the same \(0.2\pm j0.4583\); only the zero moves, from \(-0.5\) to \(+0.4\), that is from angle \(180^{\circ}\) to angle \(0^{\circ}\).
  • The zero now sits nearest \(\omega=0\), so it pulls DC down instead of \(\omega=\pi\): \(|H(1)|=0.6/0.85=\mathbf{0.706}\), \(|H(j)|=\mathbf{1.267}\), \(|H(-1)|=1.4/1.65=\mathbf{0.849}\).
  • Peak \(\mathbf{1.34}\) at \(\mathbf{73.9^{\circ}}\), and the response is now high-pass in character.
  • One sign in the numerator flips the filter from low-pass to high-pass, with the poles untouched. That is the lesson of the whole section.

75 Ch prints \(2x(n-2)+0.7x(n-1)+4x(n)\) in that order Read the delays, not the position on the page. The constant term is \(4\), so \(H(z)=(4+0.7z^{-1}+2z^{-2})/(1-0.3z^{-1})\) and \(|H(1)|=6.7/0.7=9.57\). Writing it as \(2+0.7z^{-1}+4z^{-2}\) instead gives \(9.57\) as well, because the coefficients still sum to \(6.7\), but every other value is wrong and the zeros move from \(-0.0875\pm j0.702\) to \(-0.0875\pm j0.351\).
70 Asa and 70 Ma also ask whether the system is causal and stable Yes to both, and the reason is one line: \(y(n)=x(n)+x(n-2)\) uses only present and past inputs, so it is causal; its impulse response is \(h=\{1,0,1\}\), a finite sum, so \(\sum|h[n]|=2<\infty\) and it is stable. Every FIR system is stable, which is why the question is worth only 2 marks.
81 Ba and 76 Ash: the pole is at \(z=2.75\) \(y(n)=0.67x(n)-0.3x(n-1)+2.75y(n-1)\) rearranges to \(y(n)-2.75y(n-1)=0.67x(n)-0.3x(n-1)\), so \(H(z)=(0.67z-0.3)/(z-2.75)\): one zero at \(z=0.448\) and one pole at \(z=2.75\), far outside the unit circle. If the system is causal its ROC is \(|z|>2.75\), which does not contain the unit circle, so the frequency response does not exist and neither the magnitude (81 Ba) nor the phase (76 Ash) can be drawn. Only the anticausal reading, ROC \(|z|<2.75\), is stable; on that reading \(|H|\) climbs gently from \(0.211\) at \(\omega=0\) to \(0.259\) at \(\omega=\pi\). State which reading you are using. A pole at \(0.275\) rather than \(2.75\) would make the causal system stable, and is the likeliest intended value.

column1: 2  Poles and zeros given directly
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2080 Baishakh · 2082 Bhadra · [4+6]
A filter has poles at \(0.45\pm j1.6\) and zeros at \(0.58\pm j2.06\). Map them in the \(z\)-plane and plot the magnitude response (not to scale).
column4:
Step 1: radii and angles, which is all the geometry needs
  • Poles \(0.45\pm j1.6\):
  • \[ |p|=\sqrt{0.45^{2}+1.6^{2}}=\mathbf{1.662},\qquad \theta_p=\arctan\frac{1.6}{0.45}=74.3^{\circ} \]
  • Zeros \(0.58\pm j2.06\):
  • \[ |z|=\sqrt{0.58^{2}+2.06^{2}}=\mathbf{2.140},\qquad \theta_z=\arctan\frac{2.06}{0.58}=74.3^{\circ} \]
  • Poles and zeros share the same angle, \(74.3^{\circ}\), and the zeros sit further out. So they partly cancel: the peak the poles want to make is flattened by the dip the zeros want to make.
  • Both lie outside the unit circle, so nothing is close to the circle and the response is gentle, with no sharp feature anywhere.
  • That is the answer the 6 marks are for. The sketch is nearly flat.
Step 2: the three anchor values
  • Build \(H(z)=\dfrac{(z-0.58-j2.06)(z-0.58+j2.06)}{(z-0.45-j1.6)(z-0.45+j1.6)} =\dfrac{z^{2}-1.16z+4.578}{z^{2}-0.9z+2.763}\), using (sum, product) of each conjugate pair.
  • \(|H(1)|=\left|\dfrac{1-1.16+4.578}{1-0.9+2.763}\right| =\dfrac{4.418}{2.863}=\mathbf{1.544}\)
  • \(|H(j)|=\mathbf{1.902}\),   \(|H(-1)|=\left|\dfrac{1+1.16+4.578}{1+0.9+2.763}\right| =\dfrac{6.738}{4.663}=\mathbf{1.446}\)
  • Peak \(\mathbf{2.04}\) at \(\mathbf{74^{\circ}}\), exactly the pole angle. Range \(1.45\) to \(2.04\): a shallow bump, not a resonance.
Step 3: the phase, when asked
82 Ba asks for the phase as well. Add the angle of each vector from a zero and subtract the angle of each vector from a pole: \(\arg H=\sum_k\arg(e^{j\omega}-z_k)-\sum_k\arg(e^{j\omega}-p_k)\). With conjugate pairs the imaginary parts cancel at \(\omega=0\) and \(\omega=\pi\), so the phase is zero at both ends and odd in between.

column1: 3  All-pole systems, and the steady-state response to a sinusoid
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2068 Bhadra · [7]
For the system \(y[n]-\tfrac{10}{24}y[n-1]+\tfrac{1}{24}y[n-2]=x[n]\), find the frequency response, then determine \(y[n]\) for the input \(x[n]=\sin\!\big(\tfrac{\pi}{3}n\big)+\sin\!\big(\tfrac{\pi}{5}n\big)\).
column4:
Step 1: the frequency response
  • There is no \(x\) delay, so the numerator is \(1\): the system is all-pole.
  • \[ H(z)=\frac{1}{1-\tfrac{10}{24}z^{-1}+\tfrac{1}{24}z^{-2}} =\frac{z^{2}}{z^{2}-\tfrac{5}{12}z+\tfrac{1}{24}} \]
  • Factor: \(z^{2}-\tfrac{5}{12}z+\tfrac{1}{24}=(z-\tfrac14)(z-\tfrac16)\), so the poles are \(\tfrac14\) and \(\tfrac16\), both real, both well inside the circle. Two zeros sit at the origin.
  • \[ H(e^{j\omega})=\frac{1}{\big(1-\tfrac14e^{-j\omega}\big) \big(1-\tfrac16e^{-j\omega}\big)} \]
  • \(|H|\) falls from \(1.60\) at \(\omega=0\) to \(0.686\) at \(\omega=\pi\): a gentle low-pass, with no peak because both poles are far from the circle.
Step 2: use the eigenfunction result, do not convolve
  • A sinusoid in gives the same sinusoid out, scaled by \(|H|\) and shifted by \(\angle H\) at that frequency. Evaluate \(H\) twice and stop.
  • At \(\omega=\pi/3\): \(\;|H|=\mathbf{1.1955}\), \(\;\angle H=\mathbf{-0.3987}\) rad \(=-22.85^{\circ}\).
  • At \(\omega=\pi/5\): \(\;|H|=\mathbf{1.4159}\), \(\;\angle H=\mathbf{-0.2949}\) rad \(=-16.90^{\circ}\).
  • \[ y[n]=1.1955\sin\!\Big(\frac{\pi}{3}n-0.3987\Big) +1.4159\sin\!\Big(\frac{\pi}{5}n-0.2949\Big) \]
  • The lower frequency is amplified more, which is the low-pass character showing up in the answer.
69 Bh: the same method, one line shorter
  • \(y[n]-0.8y[n-1]+0.15y[n-2]=x[n]\) gives \(z^{2}-0.8z+0.15=(z-0.5)(z-0.3)\), so the poles are \(0.5\) and \(0.3\) with a double zero at the origin.
  • \(|H|\): \(\mathbf{2.857}\) at \(\omega=0\), \(0.857\) at \(\pi/2\), \(\mathbf{0.513}\) at \(\pi\). Monotonically falling, so low-pass, peak at DC.
67 Mng as printed has a pole exactly on the unit circle The paper writes \(y[n]-\tfrac56y[n-1]-\tfrac16y[n-2]-x[n]=0\). That denominator factors as \(z^{2}-\tfrac56z-\tfrac16=(z-1)(z+\tfrac16)\), putting a pole at \(z=1\). A pole on the circle means \(|H(e^{j0})|\) is infinite, the system is only marginally stable and it is not BIBO stable, so strictly there is no frequency response to plot. Change the one sign, \(-\tfrac16\to+\tfrac16\), and the poles become \(\tfrac12\) and \(\tfrac13\), giving an ordinary low-pass with \(|H(1)|=1/[(1-\tfrac12)(1-\tfrac13)]=3\). 68 Bh asks the identical question with the \(+\) sign and poles \(\tfrac14\), \(\tfrac16\), which is strong evidence that the minus is a misprint. Answer the \(+\) version and note the printed one in a line.

column1: 4  Zero-input, zero-state and total response
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2066 Magh · [10]
A system is characterized by \(y(n)-0.5y(n-1)-0.25y(n-2)-x(n)=0\), the input is \(x(n)=0.2^{n}u(n)\) and the initial conditions are \(y(-1)=2\), \(y(-2)=4\). Find (a) the zero input response, (b) the zero state response, (c) the total response, (d) the system function \(H(z)\), (e) the poles of \(H(z)\).
column4:
(d) and (e) first, because everything else uses them
  • \[ H(z)=\frac{1}{1-0.5z^{-1}-0.25z^{-2}} =\frac{z^{2}}{z^{2}-0.5z-0.25} \]
  • Roots: \(z=\dfrac{0.5\pm\sqrt{0.25+1}}{2}=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt5}{4}\), that is \[ p_1=\mathbf{0.8090},\qquad p_2=\mathbf{-0.3090} \]
  • Both have \(|p|<1\), so the causal system is stable.
(a) Zero-input response: the input is switched off, the initial conditions drive it
  • The form is fixed by the poles: \(\;y_{zi}[n]=C_1(0.8090)^{n}+C_2(-0.3090)^{n}\).
  • Impose \(y(-1)=2\) and \(y(-2)=4\) on that form and solve the pair:
  • \[ C_1=1+\frac{2}{\sqrt5}=\mathbf{1.8944},\qquad C_2=1-\frac{2}{\sqrt5}=\mathbf{0.1056} \]
  • \[ y_{zi}[n]=1.8944\,(0.8090)^{n}+0.1056\,(-0.3090)^{n},\quad n\ge0 \]
  • Quick check by running the recurrence \(y[n]=0.5y[n-1]+0.25y[n-2]\) with no input: \(y[0]=0.5(2)+0.25(4)=2\), \(y[1]=1.5\), \(y[2]=1.25\), \(y[3]=1\). The closed form gives the same four numbers.
(b) Zero-state response: the initial conditions are zero, the input drives it
  • \(X(z)=\dfrac{1}{1-0.2z^{-1}}\), so \(Y_{zs}(z)=H(z)X(z)\) has three poles: \(0.8090\), \(-0.3090\) and \(0.2\).
  • Partial-fraction \(Y_{zs}(z)/z\) and multiply back:
  • \[ y_{zs}[n]=0.9612\,(0.8090)^{n}+0.1678\,(-0.3090)^{n} -0.1290\,(0.2)^{n},\quad n\ge0 \]
  • The three residues sum to \(1\), which must happen because \(y_{zs}[0]=1\). That is the free check. The last residue is exactly \(-\tfrac{4}{31}\).
(c) Total response
  • \[ y[n]=y_{zi}[n]+y_{zs}[n] =2.8557\,(0.8090)^{n}+0.2734\,(-0.3090)^{n}-0.1290\,(0.2)^{n} \]
  • First few values: \(3\), \(2.2\), \(1.89\), \(1.503\), \(1.2256\). Running the original recurrence with \(y(-1)=2\), \(y(-2)=4\) and \(x(n)=0.2^{n}\) gives the same sequence.
  • Natural against forced is a different split from zero-input against zero-state. The natural part is everything in \((0.8090)^n\) and \((-0.3090)^n\), which draws from both; the forced part is only the \((0.2)^n\) term.
78 Bh gives no initial conditions \(y[n]-3y[n-1]-4y[n-2]=x[n]\) has \(z^{2}-3z-4=(z-4)(z+1)\), so the zero-input response is \(y_{zi}[n]=C_1(4)^{n}+C_2(-1)^{n}\) and that form is the whole answer, since no \(y(-1)\) or \(y(-2)\) is printed to pin \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) down. Worth adding: \(|4|>1\) and \(|-1|=1\), so the zero-input response never decays and the system is unstable. Say it, because the 4 marks are for recognising the form and its behaviour.

column1: 5  Linear phase
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2070 Ashad · [2+4]
What is the condition satisfied by a linear phase FIR filter? Show that the filter with \(h(n)=\{-1,0,1\}\) is a linear phase filter.
column4:
The condition, for the 2 marks
\[ h[n]=\pm h[M-1-n],\qquad 0\le n\le M-1 \]
  • The impulse response must be symmetric (\(+\)) or antisymmetric (\(-\)) about its midpoint \(\alpha=\dfrac{M-1}{2}\).
  • That \(\alpha\) is then the constant group delay in samples.
Check the given \(h(n)\)
  • \(M=3\), so \(M-1-n\) maps \(0\leftrightarrow2\) and fixes \(1\).
  • \(h[0]=-1\) and \(h[2]=+1\), so \(h[0]=-h[2]\); and \(h[1]=0=-h[1]\).
  • So \(h[n]=-h[2-n]\): the sequence is antisymmetric, and the condition is met with the minus sign.
Now show the phase really is linear
  • \[ H(e^{j\omega})=\sum_{n=0}^{2}h[n]e^{-j\omega n}=-1+e^{-2j\omega} \]
  • Factor out the midpoint delay \(e^{-j\omega}\), which is the standard trick:
  • \[ H(e^{j\omega})=e^{-j\omega}\big(e^{-j\omega}-e^{+j\omega}\big) =e^{-j\omega}\big(-2j\sin\omega\big) =2\sin\omega\;e^{-j(\omega+\pi/2)} \]
  • \[ \big|H(e^{j\omega})\big|=2|\sin\omega|,\qquad \arg H(e^{j\omega})=-\omega-\frac{\pi}{2} \]
  • The phase is a straight line in \(\omega\) with slope \(-1\), so \[ \operatorname{grd}H=-\frac{d}{d\omega}\Big(-\omega-\frac{\pi}{2}\Big)=1 \ \text{sample}=\alpha=\frac{M-1}{2}=1 \ \checkmark \]
  • The constant \(-\pi/2\) is why this is generalized linear phase. It comes from the \(j\) in \(-2j\sin\omega\), that is from the antisymmetry, and it does not affect the group delay, so it causes no distortion.
  • The magnitude \(2|\sin\omega|\) is zero at \(\omega=0\): an antisymmetric filter always kills DC, which is why this one is a differencer.
67 Mng: show that \(h[n]=h[N-1-n]\), \(0\le n\le N-1\), is linear phase This is the general case of the same argument and it is worked in full in §3.6: pair each term with its mirror, factor out \(e^{-j\omega\alpha}\) with \(\alpha=(N-1)/2\), and what is left is a real cosine sum. Real bracket, so the whole phase is the exponential, giving \(\arg H=-\alpha\omega\). 69 Bh asks for the same derivation restricted to odd \(M\), which is the easier case because the midpoint sample \(h[\alpha]\) stands alone instead of pairing.

column1: Chapter 4 — Discrete Filter Structures: how is it examined?
column4:
8 hrs  \(\cdot\) 68 questions across the 45 papers  \(\cdot\) worth about 10 of 80 marks  \(\cdot\) 3 syllabus sub-topics  \(\cdot\) 5th of the 8 chapters by weight, and tied with Ch 1 as the longest at 8 hours.
Read this first:
  • 42 of the 68 questions are the lattice TOP 42, worth 314 of the chapter's 449 marks. It is one calculation, the step-down recursion, run on whatever polynomial the paper prints. Learn it once and two thirds of the chapter is finished.
  • The other two topics are realization structures TOP 16 (direct form I and II, cascade, parallel) and quantization TOP 10 (number formats, round-off, limit cycles).
  • Nothing in this chapter changes what the filter does. Every structure here realizes the same \(H(z)\). They differ in how much memory they need, how many multiplies, and how badly finite word length hurts them. That sentence is the answer to "why do we need different structures".
  • The lattice is stable exactly when every \(|k_m|<1\). That single line answers the "check stability" half of a dozen questions, and it needs no root finding at all.
  • A trap worth knowing before you start: a symmetric polynomial gives \(|k_N|=1\), and the recursion divides by \(1-k_N^2\). A linear-phase FIR filter has no lattice realization. Five papers ask for one anyway; see §4.4.
column9: ch4 opener

column1: Why do we need different realization structures for the same system?
column4:
What is the same
  • Every structure in this chapter realizes the same \(H(z)\), so it has the same impulse response, the same poles and zeros, and the same frequency response. With infinite precision they are indistinguishable.
  • So a question that asks you to "realize" a system is asking for a block diagram or signal flow graph, not for new mathematics.
What differs, and why it matters
  • Memory: how many delay elements. Direct Form II uses the minimum possible, \(\max(M,N)\).
  • Arithmetic: how many multiplies and adds per output sample.
  • Finite word length: how far the poles move when the coefficients are rounded to \(b\) bits, and how much round-off noise accumulates. This is the real reason cascade and parallel forms are preferred in practice: a direct form of high order is extremely sensitive, because every pole depends on every coefficient.
  • Modularity: cascade and lattice are built from identical sections.
The three building blocks, and the two ways to draw them
  • Every structure is made of unit delays \(z^{-1}\), multipliers (a constant on an arrow) and adders.
  • A block diagram draws adders as circles with \(+\); a signal flow graph draws nodes and directed branches, with the gain written on the branch. They carry the same information, and papers ask for either.
  • Transposition: reverse every arrow, swap adders with branch nodes, and exchange input with output. The transposed structure has the same \(H(z)\). No paper in the 45 asks for a transposed form, and no source in the subject covers it, but it is worth one line because it explains how two diagrams that look nothing alike can be the same filter.

column9: ch4 theory

column1: Obtain the Direct Form I and Direct Form II realization of the given system
column4:
Direct Form I: the difference equation, drawn
Start from \[ y[n]=\sum_{k=0}^{M}b_k x[n-k]-\sum_{k=1}^{N}a_k y[n-k] \]
  • Draw the feedforward part first: a chain of \(M\) delays down the input, each tapped by \(b_k\) into a summing node.
  • Then the feedback part: a chain of \(N\) delays down the output, each tapped by \(-a_k\) into the same node.
  • It is the equation copied onto paper, which is why it is the easy 2 marks.
  • Cost: \(M+N\) delays, \(M+N+1\) multiplies.
  • Read it as \(H(z)=B(z)\cdot\dfrac{1}{A(z)}\): all-zero section first, all-pole section second.
Direct Form II: swap the halves and share the delays
Because the two sections are LTI, they commute: \[ H(z)=\frac{1}{A(z)}\cdot B(z) \]
  • Put the all-pole section first. Its output is an intermediate signal \(w[n]\):
  • \[ w[n]=x[n]-\sum_{k=1}^{N}a_k w[n-k],\qquad y[n]=\sum_{k=0}^{M}b_k w[n-k] \]
  • Now both chains delay the same signal \(w[n]\), so one chain of delays serves both.
  • Cost: \(\max(M,N)\) delays, which is the fewest any structure can use. A structure with the minimum number of delays is called canonic.
  • This is the only reason Direct Form II exists: same arithmetic, half the memory.
Drawing it, in four steps
  1. Write the equation with \(y[n]\) alone on the left and watch the signs: every \(a_k\) crosses over and becomes \(-a_k\).
  2. Count \(N\) (highest \(y\) delay) and \(M\) (highest \(x\) delay). The chain has \(\max(M,N)\) delays.
  3. Down the left of the chain put \(-a_1,-a_2,\dots\) feeding back into the top adder. Down the right put \(b_0,b_1,\dots\) feeding forward into the output adder.
  4. Label \(w[n]\) at the top of the chain. A missing coefficient is a missing branch, not a zero multiplier: if the paper's equation skips \(x[n-1]\), leave that tap out.
If \(a_0\ne1\), divide the whole equation by \(a_0\) first. 74 Ch prints \(3y[n]+y[n-1]+2y[n-4]=2x[n]+x[n-3]\), and every coefficient must be divided by 3 before drawing. Forgetting this is the most common lost mark in §4.2.

column1: Realize the given \(H(z)\) in cascade form of second-order sections, and in parallel form
column4:
Cascade: multiply the sections
\[ H(z)=b_0\prod_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1+b_{1k}z^{-1}+b_{2k}z^{-2}} {1+a_{1k}z^{-1}+a_{2k}z^{-2}} \]
  • Group the poles and zeros into second-order sections, each realized in Direct Form II, and chain them output to input.
  • A complex pole must be paired with its conjugate in the same section. That is the whole point: the section then has real coefficients, \(a_{1k}=-2\mathrm{Re}(p)\) and \(a_{2k}=|p|^2\).
Parallel: add the sections
\[ H(z)=C+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\gamma_{0k}+\gamma_{1k}z^{-1}} {1+a_{1k}z^{-1}+a_{2k}z^{-2}} \]
  • Get here by partial fractions, exactly as in Chapter 2, then recombine each conjugate pair into one real second-order section.
  • \(C\) is the constant from the division when \(H(z)\) is improper; it is a direct path from input to output.
  • Real poles pair with real poles, or sit alone as a first-order section.
  • An odd number of real poles leaves one first-order section; that is normal, not an error.
  • Cascade needs factors, parallel needs partial fractions. That is the only difference in the work.
  • Parallel has the best round-off behaviour of the three: an error in one section cannot propagate into the others, because they do not feed each other.
Turning a conjugate pair into real coefficients
  • A pair of poles at \(re^{\pm j\theta}\) multiplies out to
  • \[ (1-re^{j\theta}z^{-1})(1-re^{-j\theta}z^{-1}) =1-2r\cos\theta\,z^{-1}+r^{2}z^{-2} \]
  • So a section written \(1-2r\cos\theta\,z^{-1}+r^{2}z^{-2}\) needs only \(r\) and \(\theta\), both of which the papers usually hand you directly.
  • For a pair given in rectangular form \(\sigma\pm j\omega\), it is \(1-2\sigma z^{-1}+(\sigma^{2}+\omega^{2})z^{-2}\).
  • Check every section has real coefficients before drawing. A surviving \(j\) means a pole was left unpaired.

column1: Compute the lattice coefficients and draw the structure for the given \(H(z)\); check stability
column4:
What the structure is
An \(M\)-stage lattice chains identical two-input two-output sections. Stage \(m\) takes a forward signal \(f_{m-1}\) and a backward signal \(g_{m-1}\) and produces \[ f_m[n]=f_{m-1}[n]+k_m\,g_{m-1}[n-1] \] \[ g_m[n]=k_m\,f_{m-1}[n]+g_{m-1}[n-1] \] with \(f_0[n]=g_0[n]=x[n]\) and \(y[n]=f_M[n]\).
  • The \(k_m\) are the reflection coefficients, one per stage.
  • The forward path realizes \(A_M(z)\); the backward path realizes its reverse \(z^{-M}A_M(z^{-1})\), which is what makes the all-pass of §4.5 so tidy.
  • Only one multiplier value per stage, used twice. That symmetry is why the lattice is far less sensitive to coefficient quantization than a direct form, and why it is used for speech.
The step-down recursion (direct form \(\rightarrow\) lattice)
Given \(A_M(z)=1+a_M(1)z^{-1}+\dots+a_M(M)z^{-M}\): \[ k_m=a_m(m) \] \[ a_{m-1}(i)=\frac{a_m(i)-k_m\,a_m(m-i)}{1-k_m^{2}},\quad i=1,\dots,m-1 \]
  1. Read off \(k_M\): it is the last coefficient, free.
  2. Fold \(A_M\) against its own reverse, divide by \(1-k_M^{2}\), and you have \(A_{M-1}\), one degree lower.
  3. Repeat down to \(A_1\), whose single coefficient is \(k_1\).
The step-up recursion (lattice \(\rightarrow\) direct form)
\[ a_m(i)=a_{m-1}(i)+k_m\,a_{m-1}(m-i),\qquad a_m(m)=k_m \] Same relation, rearranged. Papers ask in both directions: 79 Bh and 71 Shr give \(k=\{\tfrac14,\tfrac12,\tfrac13\}\) and want the FIR coefficients.
Stability, in one line
  • The system is stable if and only if \(|k_m|<1\) for every \(m\).
  • No root finding, no Jury table. The step-down is the Schur-Cohn test: it is testing whether every root of \(A(z)\) lies inside the unit circle.
  • A question that says "check stability" after asking for the lattice is asking you to look at the numbers you already computed. It is a free mark.
The symmetric trap: why five papers ask for an impossible lattice If \(A(z)\) is symmetric, meaning its coefficient list reads the same backwards, then \(a_M(M)=a_M(0)=1\), so \(k_M=1\) and the step-down divides by \(1-k_M^{2}=0\). A symmetric polynomial has no lattice realization. And symmetry is exactly the linear-phase condition \(h[n]=h[M-n]\) from Chapter 3, so a linear-phase FIR filter can never be put in lattice form. The papers that hit this are 72 Ch (\(1+2z^{-1}+z^{-2}\)), 73 Bh (\(1+2z^{-1}+2z^{-2}+z^{-3}\)), 75 Ch and 73 Ch (both with \(1+\tfrac23z^{-1}+\tfrac58z^{-2} +\tfrac23z^{-3}+z^{-4}\)), and 74 Ash, whose last coefficient is \(-1\). Say so, show the division by zero, and note that the zeros sit on the unit circle. It is a better answer than a page of arithmetic that cannot finish.

The papers that hit this are 72 Ch (\(1+2z^{-1}+z^{-2}\)), 73 Bh (\(1+2z^{-1}+2z^{-2}+z^{-3}\)), 75 Ch and 73 Ch (both with \(1+\tfrac23z^{-1}+\tfrac58z^{-2} +\tfrac23z^{-3}+z^{-4}\)), and 74 Ash, whose last coefficient is \(-1\). Say so, show the division by zero, and note that the zeros sit on the unit circle. It is a better answer than a page of arithmetic that cannot finish.

column1: The all-pass result, and why it is worth remembering
column2: 70 Bh gives \(H(z)=\dfrac{1+0.4z^{-1}-1.2z^{-2}+2z^{-3}}{2-1.2z^{-1}+0.4z^{-2}+z^{-3}}\) and asks how a lattice implements it. Look at the coefficients: the numerator is the denominator reversed. That is the definition of an all-pass, \(H(z)=z^{-N}A(z^{-1})/A(z)\), and the backward path of a lattice already computes exactly \(z^{-N}A(z^{-1})\). So the ladder collapses: every \(C_m\) is zero except \(C_N=1\). An all-pass filter is just a lattice with the output taken from the last backward node, no ladder taps at all. The reflection coefficients are \(k=\{-0.56,\ \tfrac23,\ \tfrac12\}\), all less than 1 in magnitude, so it is stable.

column1: Write about the sign magnitude and 2's complement representation of a binary fractional number. Write about truncation error and rounding error
column4:
The three fixed-point codes
A fraction in \([-1,1)\) with \(b\) bits after the binary point. Positive numbers look the same in all three; only negatives differ.
CodeHow a negative is formed
Sign magnitudesign bit \(1\), magnitude bits unchanged
1's complementinvert every magnitude bit
2's complementinvert every bit, add \(1\) in the last place
  • Worked, for \(\pm5/8\) in 3 bits, \(5/8=0.101_2\):
  • \(+5/8=\mathtt{0.101}\) in all three.
  • \(-5/8=\mathtt{1.101}\) (SM), \(\mathtt{1.010}\) (1's), \(\mathtt{1.011}\) (2's).
  • 2's complement is used in practice because addition needs no special case and overflows in a partial sum cancel out.
Rounding against truncation
With step \(q=2^{-b}\) and error \(e=Q(x)-x\):
SchemeError range
Rounding, any code\(-q/2\le e\le q/2\)
Truncation, sign mag.\(-(q-q_u)\le e\le(q-q_u)\)
Truncation, 2's comp.\(-(q-q_u)\le e\le0\)
  • Rounding is better, and this table is why: its error is centred on zero, so it has no bias, and its range is half as wide.
  • Truncating a sign magnitude number always shrinks the magnitude, so the error is symmetric about zero but takes the sign of \(x\).
  • Truncating a 2's complement number always moves the value down, never up, so the error is one-sided and negative: a systematic bias, a DC offset that accumulates through a filter.
  • \(q_u=2^{-b_u}\) is the step before quantization, with \(b_u>b\).
The three places quantization bites
  • Input (A/D) quantization: modelled as additive white noise of variance \(q^{2}/12\) for rounding.
  • Coefficient quantization: the \(a_k\) and \(b_k\) are stored in \(b\) bits, so the poles move. A high-order direct form is the worst case, because every pole depends on every coefficient; cascade and parallel forms confine the damage to one section, which is the practical argument for §4.3.
  • Product round-off: each multiply doubles the word length and must be shortened again. In a recursive filter this feeds back, which is §4.7.

column1: What is the limit cycle effect in a recursive system? Describe it with an example. Define dead band
column4:
What a limit cycle is
  • In a recursive filter the rounded product is fed back and rounded again. Once the signal is small enough, rounding can return the same magnitude it started from.
  • The filter then never decays: after the input stops it sits in a self-sustaining oscillation of fixed amplitude. That is a zero-input limit cycle.
  • It happens only with quantization. The ideal infinite-precision filter is perfectly stable; the limit cycle is created by the arithmetic, not by the poles.
The dead band
For the first-order \(y[n]=Q\{a\,y[n-1]\}+x[n]\) with rounding, the filter cannot escape once \[ |y[n]|\le\frac{q}{2\,(1-|a|)} \]
  • That interval is the dead band: inside it, quantization exactly undoes the decay that \(a\) should have produced.
  • The oscillation amplitude is bounded by the dead band, so a longer word (smaller \(q\)) makes it smaller but never removes it.
  • FIR filters cannot have them: no feedback, nothing to sustain.
  • If \(a>0\) the trapped value holds constant, period 1. If \(a<0\) it alternates in sign, period 2.
The worked example, 66 Ma (and the shape of every limit-cycle answer)
\(y[n]=Q\{-0.5\,y[n-1]\}+x[n]\), rounded to 3 bits so \(q=\tfrac18\), with \(y[-1]=0\) and \(x[n]=0.875\,\delta[n]\):

4\(0.0625\)\(\mathbf{0.125}\)\(\mathbf{0.125}\)rounding put it back up

  • From \(n=3\) on it alternates \(\pm\tfrac18\) for ever: a limit cycle of amplitude \(\tfrac18\) and period 2, the period coming from \(a<0\).
  • Dead band: \(\dfrac{q}{2(1-|a|)}=\dfrac{1/8}{2(1-0.5)}=\dfrac18\), which is exactly the amplitude observed. Quote the formula and the table agrees with it.
  • Step 4 is the whole mechanism in one line: \(-0.5\times(-0.125)=0.0625\), which is half a step, and rounding carries it up to a full \(0.125\) instead of down to \(0\).

column1: Chapter 4 numericals — which formulas does everything come from?
column4:
42 of the 68 questions are the lattice, and they are all one recursion. Every paper is below, grouped by what the recursion is run on. Sections 3 to 5 share a single calculation; learn it once.
The step-down, which is §3, §4 and §5
  1. Take the polynomial \(A_M(z)=1+a_M(1)z^{-1}+\dots+a_M(M)z^{-M}\). For an FIR \(H(z)=B(z)\) it is the numerator; for an all-pole or pole-zero \(H(z)\) it is always the denominator.
  2. \(k_M=a_M(M)\), read straight off the last coefficient.
  3. \[ a_{m-1}(i)=\frac{a_m(i)-k_m\,a_m(m-i)}{1-k_m^{2}},\qquad i=1,\dots,m-1 \] which folds the polynomial against its reverse and drops the degree by one.
  4. Repeat until \(A_1\), whose one coefficient is \(k_1\).
  5. Stable if and only if every \(|k_m|<1\). Nothing else to compute.
Two shortcuts worth having
  • The last step is always \(k_1=\dfrac{a_2(1)}{1+k_2}\), because \(a_2(2-1)=a_2(1)\) makes the numerator \(a_2(1)(1-k_2)\) and \(1-k_2^2=(1-k_2)(1+k_2)\).
  • Keep fractions. \(1-k^2\) breeds denominators, and a decimal answer is visibly wrong by the third stage.
The two checks
  1. Step back up: \(a_m(i)=a_{m-1}(i)+k_m a_{m-1}(m-i)\) must return the polynomial you started from. Two lines, and it catches every arithmetic slip.
  2. If any \(|k_m|=1\) exactly, stop: the polynomial is symmetric and no lattice exists. See the box in §3.

column1: 1  Direct Form I and Direct Form II
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2079 Bhadra · [2+2]
Obtain the Direct Form I and Direct Form II realization of the system \(y[n]-0.25y[n-2]=x[n]+0.4x[n-1]+0.5x[n-2]\).
column4:
Step 1: put it in computing form and read off the taps
  • \[ y[n]=x[n]+0.4x[n-1]+0.5x[n-2]+0.25y[n-2] \]
  • Feedforward \(b=\{1,\ 0.4,\ 0.5\}\), feedback \(a=\{1,\ 0,\ -0.25\}\), so the taps are \(-a_1=0\) and \(-a_2=+0.25\).
  • \(a_1=0\), so there is no \(y[n-1]\) branch at all. Leave the tap out; do not draw a multiplier by zero.
  • \(M=N=2\), so Direct Form I needs \(2+2=4\) delays and Direct Form II needs \(\max(2,2)=2\).
Step 2: Direct Form I
  • Input into a chain of two delays, tapped \(1\), \(0.4\), \(0.5\) into an adder.
  • That adder's output goes into a second chain of two delays, tapped \(0\) and \(0.25\) back into the same adder.
  • Reading left to right it is \(B(z)\) then \(1/A(z)\).
Step 3: Direct Form II
  • Swap the two halves and share one chain of two delays carrying \(w[n]\):
  • \[ w[n]=x[n]+0.25w[n-2],\qquad y[n]=w[n]+0.4w[n-1]+0.5w[n-2] \]
  • Left of the chain: one branch, \(0.25\) from \(w[n-2]\) back to the top adder. Right of the chain: three branches, \(1\), \(0.4\), \(0.5\) into the output adder.
  • Two delays instead of four, same arithmetic. That is the entire answer to "why Direct Form II".

column1: 2  Cascade and parallel realizations
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2081 Baishakh · [5]
Realize the following system in cascade form of second-order sections (signal flow graph): \(H(z)=\dfrac{10(1-0.25z^{-1})(1-0.667z^{-1})(1+2z^{-1})} {(1-0.75z^{-1})(1-0.125z^{-1})\{1-(0.5+j0.5)z^{-1}\}\{1-(0.5-j0.5)z^{-1}\}}\).
column4:
Step 1: pair the poles, then pair the zeros to match
  • The conjugate pair must stay together. With \(\sigma=0.5\) and \(\omega=0.5\):
  • \[ \{1-(0.5+j0.5)z^{-1}\}\{1-(0.5-j0.5)z^{-1}\} =1-z^{-1}+0.5z^{-2} \] using \(-2\sigma=-1\) and \(\sigma^{2}+\omega^{2}=0.5\).
  • The two real poles pair with each other: \((1-0.75z^{-1})(1-0.125z^{-1})=1-0.875z^{-1}+0.09375z^{-2}\).
  • Three zeros over four poles, so one section's numerator is first order. Pair the two "small" zeros and leave \((1+2z^{-1})\) to ride with the real-pole section: \((1-0.25z^{-1})(1-0.667z^{-1})=1-0.917z^{-1}+0.167z^{-2}\).
Step 2: write the two sections and place the gain
  • \[ H(z)=10\cdot \underbrace{\frac{1-0.917z^{-1}+0.167z^{-2}}{1-0.875z^{-1}+0.09375z^{-2}}} _{\text{section 1}}\cdot \underbrace{\frac{1+2z^{-1}}{1-z^{-1}+0.5z^{-2}}}_{\text{section 2}} \]
  • Draw each section in Direct Form II and chain them. The gain \(10\) goes on the input branch, or is split between sections to keep the internal signals from overflowing.
  • Every coefficient is real. If a \(j\) survives, a pair was split.

QUESTION AS PRINTED 2081 Baishakh · 2078 Bhadra · [5]
Determine the lattice coefficients corresponding to the FIR filter with system function \(H(z)=A_3(z)=1+\tfrac{13}{24}z^{-1}+\tfrac58 z^{-2}+\tfrac13 z^{-3}\), and check its stability.
column4:
Stage 3
  • \(k_3=a_3(3)=\mathbf{\tfrac13}\), free.
  • \(1-k_3^{2}=1-\tfrac19=\tfrac89\).
  • \[ a_2(1)=\frac{a_3(1)-k_3a_3(2)}{8/9} =\frac{\tfrac{13}{24}-\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac58}{8/9} =\frac{\tfrac{13}{24}-\tfrac5{24}}{8/9} =\frac{\tfrac13}{8/9}=\frac38 \]

Stage 2, then stage 1
  • \(k_2=a_2(2)=\mathbf{\tfrac12}\).
  • Use the shortcut \(k_1=\dfrac{a_2(1)}{1+k_2}=\dfrac{3/8}{3/2}=\mathbf{\tfrac14}\).
  • \[ \boxed{k=\left\{\tfrac14,\ \tfrac12,\ \tfrac13\right\}} \]

column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2079 Bhadra · [6]
Given a 3-stage lattice filter with coefficients \(K_1=\tfrac14\), \(K_2=\tfrac12\), \(K_3=\tfrac13\), obtain the system function and the FIR filter coefficients.
column4:
• Step up, one stage at a time, with \(a_m(i)=a_{m-1}(i)+k_m\,a_{m-1}(m-i)\) and \(a_m(m)=k_m\).
  • \(A_1(z)=1+\tfrac14z^{-1}\).
  • \(a_2(1)=a_1(1)+k_2a_1(1)=\tfrac14+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac38\), and \(a_2(2)=k_2=\tfrac12\), so \(A_2(z)=1+\tfrac38z^{-1}+\tfrac12z^{-2}\).
  • \(a_3(1)=a_2(1)+k_3a_2(2)=\tfrac38+\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac{13}{24}\); \(a_3(2)=a_2(2)+k_3a_2(1)=\tfrac12+\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac38=\tfrac58\); \(a_3(3)=k_3=\tfrac13\).
  • \[ \boxed{H(z)=A_3(z)=1+\tfrac{13}{24}z^{-1}+\tfrac58z^{-2}+\tfrac13z^{-3}} \]
  • So \(h[n]=\{1,\ \tfrac{13}{24},\ \tfrac58,\ \tfrac13\}\).
  • This is §3 run backwards, on the same numbers. 71 Shr asks it identically.
80 Ch and 74 Ma change one coefficient They give \(K_1=\tfrac14\), \(K_2=\tfrac14\), \(K_3=\tfrac13\). The same recursion gives \(a_2(1)=\tfrac14+\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac5{16}\), \(a_2(2)=\tfrac14\), then \(a_3(1)=\tfrac5{16}+\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac14=\mathbf{\tfrac{19}{48}}\), \(a_3(2)=\tfrac14+\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac5{16}=\mathbf{\tfrac{17}{48}}\), \(a_3(3)=\tfrac13\). So \(h[n]=\{1,\ \tfrac{19}{48},\ \tfrac{17}{48},\ \tfrac13\}\). The two thirds in the answer look alike but are not: \(\tfrac{19}{48}\) and \(\tfrac{17}{48}\) differ, and writing both as \(\tfrac{18}{48}=\tfrac38\) is the easy mistake.

  • Confirm with the dead band: \(\dfrac{q}{2(1-|a|)}=\dfrac{1/8}{2(1-0.5)}=\dfrac18\), exactly the amplitude observed. Quote the formula and the table together.
  • The mechanism is row 4 alone: \(-0.5\times(-0.125)=0.0625\) is half a step, and rounding lifts it back to a whole one instead of letting it fall to zero.
75 Ash: \(\pm\tfrac58\) in the three fixed-point codes
  • \(\tfrac58=0.101_2\), so with a sign bit and 3 fraction bits:
  • \(+\tfrac58=\mathtt{0.101}\) in sign magnitude, 1's complement and 2's complement alike.
  • \(-\tfrac58\): sign magnitude \(\mathtt{1.101}\) (flip the sign bit only), 1's complement \(\mathtt{1.010}\) (invert the fraction bits), 2's complement \(\mathtt{1.011}\) (invert and add \(1\) in the last place).
  • Check: 1's complement plus 1 ulp is 2's complement. \(\mathtt{1.010}+\mathtt{0.001}=\mathtt{1.011}\) ✓.
69 Bh asks for \(-192/220\) in 8-bit form, which cannot be done \(192/220=0.87273\), and \(220\) is not a power of two, so the number has no exact binary fraction in 8 bits or any other number of bits. Rounded to 8 bits it is \(-\tfrac{223}{256}=-0.871094\), giving sign magnitude \(\mathtt{1.11011111}\), 1's complement \(\mathtt{1.00100000}\) and 2's complement \(\mathtt{1.00100001}\). Almost certainly \(220\) is a misprint for \(256\), the natural 8-bit scale: \(-192/256=-0.75\) exactly, sign magnitude \(\mathtt{1.11000000}\), 1's complement \(\mathtt{1.00111111}\), 2's complement \(\mathtt{1.01000000}\). Give the clean version and note the other in a line.
67 Mng: show the two truncation error ranges by example Take \(b_u=6\) bits truncated to \(b=3\), so \(q=\tfrac18\) and \(q_u=\tfrac1{64}\), and \(q-q_u=\tfrac7{64}\). Sweeping every 6-bit fraction confirms both bounds exactly. Sign magnitude: truncating shortens the magnitude, so a positive number falls and a negative number rises, and \(e\) runs from \(-\tfrac7{64}\) to \(+\tfrac7{64}\), symmetric. 2's complement: truncating always drops the value towards \(-\infty\) whatever the sign, so \(e\) runs from \(-\tfrac7{64}\) to \(0\) and never exceeds zero. One example each way is enough: \(+0.828125\to0.75\) (error \(-\tfrac7{64}\) in both codes) and \(-0.828125\to-0.75\) in sign magnitude (error \(+\tfrac7{64}\)) but \(\to-0.875\) in 2's complement (error \(-\tfrac{3}{64}\)). That asymmetry is why 2's complement truncation adds a DC bias and rounding is preferred.

column1: Chapter 5 — FIR Filter Design: how is it examined?
column4:
6 hrs  \(\cdot\) 70 questions across the 45 papers  \(\cdot\) worth about 12 of 80 marks  \(\cdot\) 3 syllabus sub-topics  \(\cdot\) 4th of the 8 chapters by weight.
Read this first:
  • Three topics, and they divide cleanly by what you have to do:
    • Window method TOP 28: a design calculation. Pick a window, get a length, truncate the ideal response.
    • Kaiser window TOP 19: the same calculation with two formulas bolted on, for \(\beta\) and for the length.
    • Remez exchange TOP 23: pure bookwork. 23 questions, almost always the same flowchart and the same three sentences, and not one of them asks you to run the algorithm.
  • So a third of this chapter's marks are free if you memorise one flowchart. Do §5.6 first.
  • The whole design method is two lines: the ideal filter has an infinite, non-causal impulse response, so truncate it and taper the truncation so the edges do not ring.
  • The window is chosen by stopband attenuation and the length by transition width. Those are two independent lookups and they are the only two numbers a fixed-window question turns on.
  • Gibbs ripple does not shrink when you lengthen the filter. That single fact is worth 3 to 6 marks in eight papers, and it is the reason Kaiser exists.

column1: Describe how a digital FIR filter is designed by the window method, and discuss the characteristics of the different window functions
column4:
Where the ideal response comes from
An ideal low-pass filter is a brick wall in frequency. Inverse DTFT it: \[ h_d[n]=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\omega_c}^{\omega_c}e^{j\omega n}\,d\omega =\frac{\sin\omega_c n}{\pi n} \]
  • This is a \(\operatorname{sinc}\): infinitely long and non-causal, so it cannot be built.
  • Delay it by \(\alpha=\dfrac{N-1}{2}\) samples to make it causal, which is also exactly what gives linear phase:
  • \[ h_d[n]=\frac{\sin\big(\omega_c(n-\alpha)\big)}{\pi(n-\alpha)},\qquad h_d[\alpha]=\frac{\omega_c}{\pi} \]
  • The centre tap is a \(0/0\) limit, so evaluate it separately as \(\omega_c/\pi\). Forgetting that is the most common slip in the chapter.
The four steps, which are the whole method
  1. Write \(h_d[n]\) for the ideal filter, delayed by \(\alpha=(N-1)/2\).
  2. Choose the window from the required stopband attenuation.
  3. Choose \(N\) from the required transition width.
  4. Multiply: \(\;h[n]=h_d[n]\,w[n]\) for \(0\le n\le N-1\), zero elsewhere.
Other ideal responses
  • High pass: \(\delta[n-\alpha]-h_{d,\mathrm{LP}}[n]\), an all-pass minus the low pass.
  • Band pass: \(h_{d}(\omega_2)-h_{d}(\omega_1)\), the wider low pass minus the narrower.
  • Every one of them is symmetric about \(\alpha\), so every windowed FIR filter here has linear phase automatically.
Why multiplying by a window is convolving in frequency
  • \(h[n]=h_d[n]w[n]\) becomes, in frequency,
  • \[ H(e^{j\omega})=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} H_d(e^{j\theta})\,W(e^{j(\omega-\theta)})\,d\theta \]
  • So the brick wall is smeared by the window's spectrum. The result is the sharp edge replaced by a transition, plus ripple from the window's sidelobes.
  • Main lobe width sets the transition; sidelobe height sets the ripple. That one sentence explains the entire comparison table in §5.2.

column1: Explain the Gibbs phenomenon: how it arises when the rectangular window is used, and how it can be minimized
column4:
What the Gibbs phenomenon is
  • Truncating the sinc with a rectangular window convolves \(H_d\) with the Dirichlet kernel, whose sidelobes are only 13 dB below its main lobe.
  • The result overshoots the band edge by about 9 % of the discontinuity height, with ringing either side.
  • Increasing \(N\) does not help. The ripples get narrower and more numerous, but the overshoot stays at 9 %. The series converges in the mean-square sense, not uniformly.
  • That is the whole phenomenon, and the fact examiners want stated.
How to minimize it
  • Use a tapered window. Hann, Hamming and Blackman fall smoothly to zero at the ends instead of being cut off, so their sidelobes are far lower and the ripple is far smaller.
  • The price is a wider main lobe, hence a wider transition band, hence a longer filter for the same sharpness.
  • Every window is a trade of ripple against transition width.
The comparison table (learn this: it answers half the chapter)

Rectangular\(\frac{4\pi}{M+1}\)\(-13\) dB\(21\) dB\(1.8\pi/M\)
Bartlett\(8\pi/M\)\(-25\) dB\(25\) dB\(6.1\pi/M\)
Hann\(8\pi/M\)\(-31\) dB\(44\) dB\(6.2\pi/M\)
Hamming\(8\pi/M\)\(-41\) dB\(53\) dB\(6.6\pi/M\)

  • Stopband attenuation is a property of the window alone. It does not depend on \(N\) at all, which is exactly why Gibbs ripple cannot be lengthened away.
  • \(M=N-1\) throughout. Papers sometimes call \(M\) the length; read which.
  • The two columns you actually use are Stop band (to choose the window) and Transition (to choose \(N\)).
The window formulas, for \(0\le n\le M\) with \(M=N-1\)
  • \[ w_{\text{rect}}[n]=1,\qquad w_{\text{Bart}}[n]=1-\frac{|2n-M|}{M} \]
  • \[ w_{\text{Hann}}[n]=0.5-0.5\cos\frac{2\pi n}{M},\qquad w_{\text{Hamm}}[n]=0.54-0.46\cos\frac{2\pi n}{M} \]
  • \[ w_{\text{Black}}[n]=0.42-0.5\cos\frac{2\pi n}{M} +0.08\cos\frac{4\pi n}{M} \]
  • Hann ends at exactly 0; Hamming ends at 0.08. That is the only difference between them and it buys 9 dB of stopband.
  • All five are symmetric, which is what keeps the phase linear.

column1: Why is the Kaiser window better than other fixed windows? Explain the steps to design an FIR filter using it
column4:
Why it is better (the whole answer)
  • Every fixed window offers one stopband attenuation, take it or leave it. Hann gives 44 dB whether you want 30 or 43.
  • Kaiser has a shape parameter \(\beta\), so the attenuation is continuously adjustable.
  • So the two specifications decouple: \(\beta\) buys attenuation, \(N\) buys transition width, and neither is wasted on the other.
  • The result is the shortest filter that meets a given spec among all the window methods, because nothing is over-designed.
  • It is also very nearly optimal in the energy sense: it maximises the fraction of the window's energy in the main lobe.
The design equations
\[ w[n]=\frac{I_0\!\left(\beta\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{2n}{M}-1\right)^{2}}\right)} {I_0(\beta)},\qquad 0\le n\le M \]
  1. \(\delta=\min(\delta_p,\delta_s)\), then \(A=-20\log_{10}\delta\) dB.
  2. \[ \beta=\begin{cases} 0 & A\le21\\ 0.5842(A-21)^{0.4}+0.07886(A-21) & 21<A\le50\\ 0.1102(A-8.7) & A>50\end{cases} \]
  3. \[ M=\frac{A-8}{2.285\,\Delta\omega},\qquad \text{length}=M+1 \]
  4. \(I_0\) is the modified Bessel function of the first kind, order zero: \(I_0(x)=\sum_{k\ge0}\left[\frac{(x/2)^k}{k!}\right]^{2}\), and \(I_0(0)=1\).
\(\beta=0\) makes the Kaiser window rectangular, and larger \(\beta\) tapers it harder. The same \(\delta\) gives the same \(\beta\), so most papers in §2 of the companion share one value.

column1: What is an optimum filter? Explain the Remez exchange algorithm for FIR filter design, with its flowchart. Why is it superior to windowing?
column4:
What "optimum" means
  • The window method accepts whatever error the window happens to give, and that error is largest at the band edges and small in the middle. Most of the allowed tolerance goes unused.
  • An optimum (equiripple, minimax, Parks-McClellan) filter instead spreads the error evenly, so the worst case is as small as possible:
  • \[ \min_{h}\ \max_{\omega\in S}\ |E(\omega)|,\qquad E(\omega)=W(\omega)\big[H_d(\omega)-H(\omega)\big] \]
  • \(W(\omega)\) is a weight, which is how passband and stopband ripple can be traded: set \(W=\delta_s/\delta_p\) in the passband and \(1\) in the stopband.
  • \(S\) is the bands of interest only, so the transition band is simply left out rather than being forced to behave.
The alternation theorem, which is why it works
  • \(H\) is the unique best approximation if and only if \(E(\omega)\) has at least \(\mathbf{r+2}\) alternations: extrema of equal magnitude and alternating sign, where \(r\) is the number of free coefficients.
  • So the answer is recognisable when you see it: count the alternations.
  • That is what makes the filter equiripple: every ripple in a band reaches exactly the same height.
Why it beats windowing
  • Shorter filter for the same specification. The local worked comparison is worth quoting: for \(\omega_p=0.4\pi\), \(\omega_s=0.6\pi\) and \(\delta=0.0116\), the equiripple design needs \(M=26\) while a Kaiser window at the same \(\delta\) needs \(M=38\). A third fewer taps.
  • Independent control of passband and stopband ripple through \(W\).
  • Handles arbitrary multi-band shapes, not just the standard four.
The Remez exchange algorithm, as a flowchart (this is the marks)
  1. Input the band edges, the desired response \(H_d\), the weights \(W\), and the order.
  2. Guess an initial set of \(r+2\) extremal frequencies, usually spaced evenly over the bands.
  3. Solve for the deviation \(\delta\) on that set. It comes out in closed form, with no matrix inversion:
  4. \[ \delta=\frac{\sum_{k}\gamma_k H_d(\omega_k)} {\sum_{k}(-1)^{k}\gamma_k/W(\omega_k)} \]
  5. Interpolate the trial response \(H\) through the points using Lagrange interpolation, and evaluate \(E(\omega)\) on a dense grid.
  6. Exchange: find the new local extrema of \(|E|\) and make them the new extremal set.
  7. Test: if the largest \(|E|\) on the grid no longer exceeds \(|\delta|\), the alternation theorem is satisfied, so stop. Otherwise go back to step 3.
  8. Output the impulse response from the converged frequency response.
Each pass can only increase \(|\delta|\) towards its optimum, so the iteration always converges. Draw it as a loop with the test at the bottom, label the exchange step, and the flowchart marks are safe. No paper in the 45 asks for a numerical iteration.

column1: Chapter 5 numericals — which formulas does everything come from?
column4:
47 of the 70 questions are one design calculation. The other 23 are the Remez algorithm, which asks for a flowchart and never for a number: that is §5.5 of the theory, not here. Every design paper is below.
The recipe, used in §1, §2 and §3
  1. Convert the spec to \(\omega\) in radians per sample if it is given in Hz (\(\omega=2\pi f/f_s\)) or rad/s (\(\omega=\Omega/f_s\)).
  2. Window from the stopband attenuation \(A_s\), taking the cheapest that clears it. If the paper gives \(\delta_s\), first \(A_s=-20\log_{10}\delta_s\).
  3. Length \(M=c\pi/\Delta\omega\) with \(c\) from the same table, then round up to the next odd \(N\).
  4. Cut-off \(\omega_c=\dfrac{\omega_p+\omega_s}{2}\), the middle of the transition band.
  5. Coefficients \(h[n]=h_d[n]\,w[n]\), with \(h_d[n]=\dfrac{\sin(\omega_c(n-\alpha))}{\pi(n-\alpha)}\), \(\alpha=\dfrac{N-1}{2}\), and the centre tap \(h_d[\alpha]=\omega_c/\pi\) done separately.
The table, again, because everything turns on it
WindowStop bandTransition
Rectangular\(21\) dB\(1.8\pi/M\)
Bartlett\(25\) dB\(6.1\pi/M\)
Hann\(44\) dB\(6.2\pi/M\)
Hamming\(53\) dB\(6.6\pi/M\)
Blackman\(74\) dB\(11\pi/M\)
Checks that cost nothing
  1. The centre tap is always \(\omega_c/\pi\) exactly. If it is not, \(\omega_c\) is wrong.
  2. \(h[n]\) must be symmetric about \(\alpha\): compute one half and mirror it.
  3. A Hann-windowed filter has \(h[0]=h[N-1]=0\) exactly, because the window is zero there. So "the first three coefficients" begins with a zero.
  4. \(N\) odd, always, so \(\alpha\) is an integer.

QUESTION AS PRINTED 2079 Chaitra · 2075 Bhadra · [8] [6]
Design a low pass FIR filter using a suitable window for \(\omega_p=0.24\pi\), \(\omega_s=0.54\pi\) and stopband attenuation \(\alpha_s=42.2\) dB. Find the first three coefficients of the impulse response.
column4:
Step 1: the two lookups
  • \(A_s=42.2\) dB. Hann gives 44 dB, which clears it; Bartlett's 25 dB does not. So Hann, and Hamming would be over-design.
  • \(\Delta\omega=0.54\pi-0.24\pi=0.30\pi\).
  • \[ M=\frac{6.2\pi}{\Delta\omega}=\frac{6.2\pi}{0.30\pi}=20.67 \ \Rightarrow\ M=21,\quad \boxed{N=23} \] rounding up, then up again to odd.
  • \(\alpha=\dfrac{N-1}{2}=\mathbf{11}\).
Step 2: the cut-off, in the middle
  • \[ \omega_c=\frac{0.24\pi+0.54\pi}{2}=\mathbf{0.39\pi}=1.2252 \ \text{rad/sample} \]
  • \[ h_d[n]=\frac{\sin\big(0.39\pi(n-11)\big)}{\pi(n-11)},\qquad h_d[11]=\frac{\omega_c}{\pi}=\mathbf{0.39} \]
Step 3: the first three coefficients
  • Hann window, \(w[n]=0.5-0.5\cos\dfrac{2\pi n}{22}\):
  • \[ w[0]=0,\qquad w[1]=0.020254,\qquad w[2]=0.079373 \]
  • \[ h_d[0]=0.022865,\qquad h_d[1]=-0.009836,\qquad h_d[2]=-0.035350 \]
  • \[ \boxed{h[0]=0,\quad h[1]=-0.000199,\quad h[2]=-0.002806} \]
  • \(h[0]=0\) is not a mistake: the Hann window is exactly zero at both ends, so the first and last taps of the filter vanish. Say so, because it looks like an error otherwise.
  • The rest follows by symmetry, \(h[22-n]=h[n]\), with the centre tap \(h[11]=0.39\).

QUESTION AS PRINTED 2081 Baishakh · [10]
Design a linear phase FIR filter using the Kaiser window for \(0.99\le|H(e^{j\omega})|\le1.01\) for \(0\le|\omega|\le0.3\pi\) and \(|H(e^{j\omega})|\le0.01\) for \(0.35\pi\le|\omega|\le\pi\).

Step 1: read the ripples off the inequalities
  • Passband \(1\pm0.01\), so \(\delta_p=0.01\). Stopband \(\le0.01\), so \(\delta_s=0.01\).
  • \[ \delta=\min(\delta_p,\delta_s)=0.01,\qquad A=-20\log_{10}(0.01)=\mathbf{40\ \text{dB}} \]
Step 2: the shape parameter
  • \(21<A\le50\), so the middle branch applies:
  • \[ \beta=0.5842(40-21)^{0.4}+0.07886(40-21) =0.5842(3.2474)+1.4983=\mathbf{3.3953} \]
Step 3: the length, and the window
  • \(\Delta\omega=0.35\pi-0.3\pi=0.05\pi=0.15708\).
  • \[ M=\frac{A-8}{2.285\,\Delta\omega}=\frac{32}{2.285(0.15708)}=89.15 \ \Rightarrow\ M=90,\quad \boxed{N=91} \]
  • \(\omega_c=\dfrac{0.3\pi+0.35\pi}{2}=0.325\pi\), and \(\alpha=45\).
  • \[ w[n]=\frac{I_0\!\left(3.3953\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{2n}{90}-1\right)^{2}}\right)} {I_0(3.3953)},\qquad h[n]=h_d[n]w[n] \]

column1: Chapter 6 — IIR Filter Design: how is it examined?
column4:
6 hrs  \(\cdot\) 50 questions across the 45 papers  \(\cdot\) worth about 13 of 80 marks  \(\cdot\) 4 syllabus sub-topics  \(\cdot\) 2nd of the 8 chapters by weight, behind only the DFT.
Read this first:
  • 36 of the 50 questions are one calculation: design an analog Butterworth low-pass filter, then map it to digital. Learn that one procedure and the chapter is mostly done.
  • The whole subject of IIR design is two sentences. There is no good direct method in the \(z\) domain, but analog filter design is a solved, closed-form art. So design in \(s\), then map \(s\to z\).
  • Only two maps exist in this syllabus, and they split the chapter:
    • Bilinear TOP 36: \(s=\dfrac{2}{T}\dfrac{1-z^{-1}}{1+z^{-1}}\). One to one, so no aliasing, but the frequency axis is warped, so the edges must be pre-warped first.
    • Impulse invariance TOP 11: \(h[n]=h_a(nT)\). The frequency axis is linear, so no warping, but sampling an unbandlimited analog response aliases.
  • Everything else is the analog half: which prototype (Butterworth or Chebyshev), what order, what cut-off. That part is identical for both maps.
  • The sampling period cancels. When the spec is given in rad/sample, pre-warp by \(\Omega=\frac{2}{T}\tan\frac{\omega}{2}\) and map back by \(s=\frac{2}{T}\frac{1-z^{-1}}{1+z^{-1}}\), and every \(2/T\) divides out: \(H(z)\) is the same for \(T=1\), \(T=2\) or \(T=0.1\). Nine papers give a sampling frequency purely as a distraction. Set \(T=1\) and write one line saying why (§6.5).
  • The other 14 questions are bookwork: why transform at all, the two methods compared, pre-warping, and spectral transformation. All short, all below.

column1: Why do we use transformation of continuous time filter design methods to design discrete time IIR filters?
column4:
The three reasons
  1. The analog art is mature. Continuous-time IIR design is a century old and its results are tabulated. Reusing it is free.
  2. Closed-form formulas exist. Butterworth, Chebyshev and elliptic prototypes all have closed-form order, cut-off and pole expressions, so the design is arithmetic, not search.
  3. No such formulas exist in the \(z\) domain. The same approximation methods applied directly to a discrete-time filter do not give closed forms, because a digital frequency response is periodic and an analog one is not.
The three steps that follow from it
  1. Translate the spec from digital \(\omega\) to analog \(\Omega\), by the rule that belongs to the map being used.
  2. Design \(H_a(s)\): choose the prototype family, find \(N\) and \(\Omega_c\), place the poles, write \(H_a(s)\).
  3. Map back to \(H(z)\) with the same rule.
What the map must preserve
  • The \(j\Omega\) axis of the \(s\) plane must land on the unit circle of the \(z\) plane, or the frequency response is not preserved.
  • The left half plane must land inside the unit circle, or a stable analog filter becomes an unstable digital one.
  • Both maps below satisfy both conditions. That is the whole reason there are only two of them.

column1: Compare the Butterworth approximation with the Chebyshev approximation
column4:
Butterworth: maximally flat
\[ |H_a(j\Omega)|^2=\frac{1}{1+\left(\dfrac{\Omega}{\Omega_c}\right)^{2N}} \]
  • All pole. Every zero is at \(\Omega\to\infty\).
  • \(|H_a(j0)|=1\) for every \(N\), and \(|H_a(j\Omega_c)|=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\), i.e. \(\Omega_c\) is the 3 dB point whatever the order.
  • Monotonic in both bands: no ripple anywhere.
  • Poles lie on a circle of radius \(\Omega_c\), equally spaced, none on the \(j\Omega\) axis.
Chebyshev type I: equiripple passband
\[ |H_a(j\Omega)|^2=\frac{1}{1+\varepsilon^2V_N^2(\Omega/\Omega_c)} \]
  • \(V_N(x)=\cos(N\cos^{-1}x)\) for \(|x|\le1\), which oscillates between \(\pm1\), and \(\cosh(N\cosh^{-1}x)\) for \(x>1\), which climbs fast.
  • So the passband ripples between \(1\) and \(1/\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}\), and the stopband falls monotonically and steeply.
  • Type II puts the ripple in the stopband instead, by using \(V_N^{-1}\); elliptic ripples in both and is steeper still.
  • \(|H_a(j0)|=1\) for \(N\) odd but \(1/\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}\) for \(N\) even. An even-order Chebyshev filter does not have unity DC gain.
The comparison, as the answer
ButterworthChebyshev I
Passbandmonotonic, maximally flatequiripple between \(1\) and \(1/\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}\)
Stopbandmonotonicmonotonic
Transitionwidest of the three familiesnarrower for the same order
Order for a given spechighestlower, typically by a third
Poles lie ona circle, radius \(\Omega_c\)an ellipse, semi-axes \(a\Omega_c\) and \(b\Omega_c\)
Phasemost nearly linear of the threeworse, and worst near the band edge
Use whenflatness matters more than sharpnessa short filter matters more than flatness
The number to quote comes from the 45 papers' own recurring spec (\(\omega_p=0.2\pi\), \(\omega_s=0.3\pi\), 1 dB, 15 dB), asked by 73 Shr, 77 Ch and 76 Bh: Butterworth needs \(N=6\), Chebyshev only \(N=4\). That single sentence answers "compare" better than a paragraph. verified/added The local notes offer a second example, \(\Omega_p=1\), \(\Omega_s=3.33\), \(\alpha_p=0.3\) dB, \(\alpha_s=22\) dB, and print "\(n=5\) for butterworth, \(n=3\) for chebyshev". The Butterworth figure is wrong: the ratio is \(157.489/0.071519=2202.05\), its log is \(3.3429\), and \(2\log(3.33)=1.0449\), so \(N=3.1992\) and the answer is 4, not 5. The Chebyshev 3 is right. Use the paper-derived example above and this one only with the correction.

column1: The design formulas, in the form every paper's specification uses
column4:
The tolerance scheme that every paper states in words. \(\delta_1\) is the passband deviation, \(\delta_2\) the stopband gain, and only the magnitude is ever specified: an IIR filter's phase is whatever the poles give.
Attenuation is always positive dB
\[ \alpha=-20\log_{10}|H| \]
  • "maximum deviation \(1\) dB below 0 dB gain" \(\Rightarrow\alpha_p=1\).
  • "maximum gain \(-15\) dB in the stopband" \(\Rightarrow\alpha_s=15\).
  • a gain \(0.89125\) given directly \(\Rightarrow\alpha_p=-20\log_{10}0.89125=1\) dB.
  • a ripple \(\delta_p=\delta_1=0.11\) \(\Rightarrow\) the edge gain is \(1-\delta_p=0.89\), so \(\alpha_p=1.0122\) dB; but \(\delta_s=\delta_2=0.21\) is a gain already, so \(\alpha_s=13.5556\) dB.
  • Those four phrasings are the same spec four ways. Converting first, before anything else, is what makes the rest mechanical.
Order and cut-off
\[ N\ \ge\ \frac{\log_{10}\!\left[\dfrac{10^{0.1\alpha_s}-1} {10^{0.1\alpha_p}-1}\right]} {2\log_{10}(\Omega_s/\Omega_p)} \qquad\text{(Butterworth)} \] \[ N\ \ge\ \frac{\cosh^{-1}\!\sqrt{\dfrac{10^{0.1\alpha_s}-1} {10^{0.1\alpha_p}-1}}} {\cosh^{-1}(\Omega_s/\Omega_p)} \qquad\text{(Chebyshev)} \] \[ \Omega_c=\frac{\Omega_p}{\left(10^{0.1\alpha_p}-1\right)^{1/2N}},\qquad \varepsilon=\sqrt{10^{0.1\alpha_p}-1} \]
  • Always round \(N\) UP. The fractional \(N\) meets the spec exactly and is not realisable.
  • That \(\Omega_c\) makes the passband exact and leaves the stopband over-satisfied. Using \(\Omega_s\) and \(\alpha_s\) instead makes the stopband exact. Both are legal; state which you used.
  • Chebyshev needs no separate \(\Omega_c\): the passband is equiripple right up to \(\Omega_p\), so \(\Omega_c=\Omega_p\).
Butterworth poles
\[ s_k=\Omega_c\,e^{\,j\pi\frac{N+2k+1}{2N}},\qquad k=0,1,\dots,N-1 \]
  • These are the \(N\) left-half-plane roots of \(1+(s/j\Omega_c)^{2N}=0\); the other \(N\) belong to \(H_a(-s)\) and are discarded.
  • Equally spaced by \(\pi/N\) on the circle of radius \(\Omega_c\), symmetric about the real axis, never on the \(j\Omega\) axis.
  • A real pole at \(-\Omega_c\) appears only for odd \(N\).
  • \[ H_a(s)=\frac{\Omega_c^{\,N}}{\prod_{k}(s-s_k)} \]
  • The numerator \(\Omega_c^N\) is fixed by \(H_a(0)=1\), not chosen.
Chebyshev poles
\[ \alpha=\frac1\varepsilon+\sqrt{1+\frac1{\varepsilon^2}},\quad a=\frac{\alpha^{1/N}-\alpha^{-1/N}}{2},\quad b=\frac{\alpha^{1/N}+\alpha^{-1/N}}{2} \] \[ s_k=-a\Omega_c\sin\theta_k+j\,b\Omega_c\cos\theta_k,\quad \theta_k=\frac{(2k+1)\pi}{2N} \]
  • The poles sit on the ellipse \(\dfrac{\sigma^2}{a^2\Omega_c^2} +\dfrac{\Omega^2}{b^2\Omega_c^2}=1\), at the same angles a Butterworth filter would use, squashed towards the \(j\Omega\) axis.
  • \(b>1>a\) always, so the ellipse is taller than wide: the poles crowd the imaginary axis, which is what sharpens the cut-off.
Chebyshev gain, and the even-order trap
  • \(H_a(s)=\dfrac{K}{\prod_k(s-s_k)}\) with \(K=\prod_k(-s_k)\) for odd \(N\), which makes \(H_a(0)=1\).
  • For even \(N\) the equiripple passband starts at its lower edge, so \(H_a(0)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}}\) and \(K\) is divided by \(\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}\).
  • Worked instance: 72 Ma has \(\varepsilon=1\), so its \(N=2\) filter has a DC gain of \(1/\sqrt2=0.707\), not 1. It looks like an arithmetic error and is not.
  • \(\varepsilon\) and \(\Omega_c\) come entirely from the passband. Only \(N\) uses the stopband at all.

column1: Describe digital Butterworth filter design using the impulse invariance technique. What are the limitations of the impulse invariance technique?
column4:
In one line: make the digital impulse response the sampled analog one, \(h[n]=h_a(nT)\). Everything below follows from that single sentence, and so does everything wrong with the method.
The idea, and the whole derivation
  • Sample the analog impulse response: \(h[n]=h_a(nT)\). Nothing else is assumed.
  • Expand \(H_a(s)\) in partial fractions over its \(N\) simple poles \(p_k\):
  • \[ H_a(s)=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\frac{A_k}{s-p_k} \ \Longrightarrow\ h_a(t)=\sum_k A_k e^{p_kt}u(t) \]
  • Sample it and take the \(z\) transform, which is just a geometric series in \(e^{p_kT}z^{-1}\):
  • \[ H(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\!\Big(\sum_k A_ke^{p_knT}\Big)z^{-n} =\boxed{\sum_{k=1}^{N}\frac{A_k}{1-e^{p_kT}z^{-1}}} \]
  • So the rule is term by term: \(\dfrac{1}{s-p_k}\longrightarrow\dfrac{1}{1-e^{p_kT}z^{-1}}\). That is the only thing to remember.
  • Spec translation is linear: \(\Omega=\omega/T\). No pre-warping.
  • The \(T\) convention. Some texts set \(h[n]=T\,h_a(nT)\) instead, which multiplies every \(A_k\) by \(T\). Without it the filter's gain comes out near \(1/T\), so with \(T\ne1\) you must say which you used. With \(T=1\) s the two are identical, and 8 of these 11 papers set \(T=1\).
What the map does to the planes
  • Each pole moves as \(\;p_k\to e^{p_kT}\), so \(|z|=e^{\sigma_kT}\) and \(\angle z=\Omega_kT\).
  • \(\sigma_k<0\Rightarrow|z|<1\): a stable analog filter always gives a stable digital one.
  • But \(z=e^{sT}\) is many to one: every horizontal strip of width \(2\pi/T\) in the \(s\) plane maps onto the whole \(z\) plane.
  • This applies to the POLES only, not to \(H\). \(H(z)\ne H_a(s)|_{s}\) under any substitution; only the pole positions transform that simply.
The limitations (say all four)
  1. Aliasing. Sampling gives \(H(e^{j\omega})=\frac1T\sum_{k}H_a\!\left(j\frac{\omega+2\pi k}{T}\right)\). No practical analog prototype is band-limited, so the tails fold back and the response is never exactly the analog one.
  2. Low pass and band pass only. A high-pass or band-stop prototype has an infinite high-frequency tail, so it aliases catastrophically. Impulse invariance cannot make a high-pass filter.
  3. Needs a partial fraction expansion of \(H_a(s)\), and it assumes the poles are simple. Repeated poles need a separate rule.
  4. Gain depends on \(T\), so the result must be rescaled.
The spec translation, which is all of step 1
  • Take the tolerance scheme of §6.2 and divide every frequency edge by \(T\). Nothing else changes: the bands \(1-\delta_1\) and \(\delta_2\) are untouched.
  • The prototype is then specified only up to \(\pi/T\), above which it is assumed negligible. That assumption is exactly what aliasing violates, which is why the design is checked at the end rather than trusted.
  • Contrast §6.4, where the axis is bent rather than merely rescaled.
  • Practical consequence: over-design the stopband. Extra attenuation there is what buys back the margin that the folded tails eat.

column1: Explain briefly the bilinear transformation method of IIR filter design, with its advantages and disadvantages
column4:
Where the formula comes from
  • Take the simplest analog filter, \(H_a(s)=\dfrac{b}{s+a}\), i.e. \(\dfrac{dy}{dt}+ay(t)=bx(t)\).
  • Integrate over one sample interval and apply the trapezoidal rule:
  • \[ y(nT)-y(nT-T)=\frac{T}{2}\big[g(nT)+g(nT-T)\big],\quad g=bx-ay \]
  • Take \(z\) transforms and solve. The result is \(H_a(s)\) with
  • \[ \boxed{\;s=\frac{2}{T}\,\frac{1-z^{-1}}{1+z^{-1}}\;} \]
  • So the bilinear transformation IS trapezoidal integration, which is why it is stable and one to one. That sentence is worth stating: it is the only derivation in the chapter and papers ask for it.
  • Inverting, \(\;z=\dfrac{1+sT/2}{1-sT/2}\).
What it does to the planes
  • Put \(s=\sigma+j\Omega\). Then
  • \[ |z|^2=\frac{(1+\sigma T/2)^2+(\Omega T/2)^2} {(1-\sigma T/2)^2+(\Omega T/2)^2} \]
  • \(\sigma<0\Rightarrow|z|<1\), \(\sigma=0\Rightarrow|z|=1\), \(\sigma>0\Rightarrow|z|>1\). The entire left half plane maps into the unit disc, exactly once.
  • So stability is preserved, and there is no aliasing: the map is one to one, not many to one.
  • On the axis, \(s=j\Omega\) gives \(z=e^{j\omega}\) with
  • \[ \omega=2\tan^{-1}\!\frac{\Omega T}{2},\qquad \boxed{\;\Omega=\frac{2}{T}\tan\frac{\omega}{2}\;} \]

column1: What is frequency warping, what is pre-warping, and why is it necessary
column4:
Digital \(\omega\) against analog \(\Omega T_d\). The curve is \(\omega=2\tan^{-1}(\Omega T_d/2)\): a straight line through the origin at low frequency, flattening to the horizontal asymptotes \(\pm\pi\).
Warping
  • \(\Omega\) runs over all of \((-\infty,\infty)\) but \(\omega\) only over \((-\pi,\pi)\), so the infinite analog axis is compressed into a finite digital one. That compression is the warping.
  • It is almost linear for small \(\omega\) (\(\tan x\approx x\)) and severely non-linear near \(\omega=\pi\).
  • Consequence: a shape defined by more than its band edges, such as a differentiator or an arbitrary magnitude curve, comes out distorted. Bilinear design is only safe for piecewise-constant magnitude responses: low pass, high pass, band pass, band stop.
Pre-warping
  • Because the map bends the axis, designing the analog filter at the stated edges puts the digital edges somewhere else.
  • So push the edges through the same bend first: \(\Omega_p=\frac{2}{T}\tan\frac{\omega_p}{2}\), \(\Omega_s=\frac{2}{T}\tan\frac{\omega_s}{2}\).
  • The warp then undoes the pre-warp exactly, and the critical frequencies land where the specification asked. Everything between them is still bent, which is why only the edges can be guaranteed.
  • Skipping the pre-warp is the single most common lost mark in the chapter.

column1: Compare the impulse invariance method with the bilinear transformation method
column4:
Impulse invarianceBilinear
Basis\(h[n]=h_a(nT)\), a time-domain matchtrapezoidal integration, a frequency-domain map
\(s\to z\)poles only: \(p_k\to e^{p_kT}\)\(s=\dfrac{2}{T}\dfrac{1-z^{-1}}{1+z^{-1}}\) throughout
Frequency map\(\Omega=\omega/T\), linear\(\Omega=\frac{2}{T}\tan\frac{\omega}{2}\), non-linear
Mapping typemany to oneone to one
Aliasingyes, and unavoidablenone

Filter typeslow pass, band pass onlyall four
Non-constant shapescan do a band-limited differentiatorcannot

The one-sentence verdict
  • Bilinear trades shape fidelity for the absence of aliasing; impulse invariance does the reverse.
  • Since almost every filter wanted is piecewise constant, where shape fidelity between the edges is worth nothing, bilinear wins almost always, and 36 of this chapter's 50 questions use it.
  • The exception is a filter whose shape matters across the band. Only impulse invariance can make a band-limited differentiator.
Why \(T\) cancels in a bilinear design verified/added
  • Pre-warping gives \(\Omega_p=\frac{2}{T}\tan\frac{\omega_p}{2}\), so \(\Omega_s/\Omega_p\) is free of \(T\) and so is \(N\).
  • \(\Omega_c\) then carries one factor \(\frac{2}{T}\), so every pole does, so \(H_a(s)\) is a function of \(sT/2\) alone.
  • Substituting \(s=\frac{2}{T}\frac{1-z^{-1}}{1+z^{-1}}\) cancels it. \(H(z)\) is identical for every \(T\).
  • So a paper's "sampling frequency 0.5 Hz" changes nothing in the answer. Use \(T=1\), and say in one line that it cancels to show it was not ignored.
  • This is false for impulse invariance, where \(\Omega=\omega/T\) scales the poles but \(e^{p_kT}\) does not cancel it.
