column1: Why is spectral transformation required, and what are its features and parameters for low pass to high pass conversion
column4:
Why it is required
  • Every design procedure above produces a low pass filter. High pass, band pass and band stop have to come from somewhere.
  • The analog route (transform \(H_a(s)\) into a high pass, then discretise) works for bilinear but fails for impulse invariance, because a high-pass analog filter is not band-limited and aliases.
  • So do it the other way: discretise the low pass first, then transform inside the \(z\) domain. Aliasing is then impossible, because nothing is sampled.
  • For bilinear designs the two routes give the identical filter; for impulse invariance only the digital route exists. That is the answer to "why required".
What the map must satisfy
  • \(p^{-1}=G(z^{-1})\) must be rational in \(z^{-1}\).
  • It must take the unit circle to the unit circle, and the inside to the inside, so that stability survives.
  • The general form that does both is an all-pass function, \(\prod_k\dfrac{z^{-1}-\alpha_k}{1-\alpha_kz^{-1}}\) with every \(|\alpha_k|<1\).
  • \(N\) all-pass factors give an \(N\)-fold map, which is why the two band cases below need \(z^{-2}\) and the two low-pass-like ones need only \(z^{-1}\).
The four transformations (this is the table they want)
ToSubstitute \(z^{-1}\to\)Parameters
Low pass\(\dfrac{z^{-1}-\alpha}{1-\alpha z^{-1}}\)\(\alpha=\dfrac{\sin\frac{\omega_p-\omega'_p}{2}} {\sin\frac{\omega_p+\omega'_p}{2}}\)
High pass\(-\dfrac{z^{-1}+\alpha}{1+\alpha z^{-1}}\)\(\alpha=-\dfrac{\cos\frac{\omega_p+\omega'_p}{2}} {\cos\frac{\omega_p-\omega'_p}{2}}\)
Band pass\(-\dfrac{z^{-2}-a_1z^{-1}+a_2}{a_2z^{-2}-a_1z^{-1}+1}\)\(a_1=\dfrac{2\alpha k}{k+1}\), \(a_2=\dfrac{k-1}{k+1}\)
Band stop\(\dfrac{z^{-2}-a_1z^{-1}+a_2}{a_2z^{-2}-a_1z^{-1}+1}\)\(a_1=\dfrac{2\alpha}{k+1}\), \(a_2=\dfrac{1-k}{1+k}\)
 For the two band cases \(\alpha=\dfrac{\cos\frac{\omega_u+\omega_L}{2}}{\cos\frac{\omega_u-\omega_L}{2}}\), and \(k=\cot\frac{\omega_u-\omega_L}{2}\tan\frac{\omega_p}{2}\) for band pass, \(\tan\frac{\omega_u-\omega_L}{2}\tan\frac{\omega_p}{2}\) for band stop. \(\omega_p\) is the prototype's edge, \(\omega'_p\) the new one.
Reading the table without mistakes
  • Only the low-pass row keeps the sign; the high-pass row carries a leading minus, and that minus is the whole reason the passband moves to \(\omega=\pi\).
  • The substitution goes into \(H_{lp}(p)\) written in \(p^{-1}\), not in \(p\). Every published prototype already is.
  • Every zero at \(z=-1\) becomes a zero at \(z=+1\), so a high pass built this way has \(H(1)=0\) exactly: it kills DC. Free check on the answer.
  • \(|\alpha|<1\) always. If it comes out bigger, the two edge frequencies have been swapped in the cosine.
  • Both band rows raise the order: an \(N\)th-order low pass becomes a \(2N\)th-order band pass or band stop.

column1: Chapter 6 numericals — which formulas does everything come from?
column4:
47 of the 50 questions are one of three calculations and the other 3 are the spectral transformation, which is also below. Every design paper in the 45 is here: 32 bilinear Butterworth, 4 bilinear Chebyshev, 11 impulse invariance (two of them sharing a statement with a bilinear paper), 3 spectral transformation.
The seven steps, used by every problem in §1, §2 and §3
  1. Get \(\omega_p\), \(\omega_s\) in rad/sample. If the paper gives Hz, use \(\omega=2\pi f/f_s\). If it gives them in \(\pi\) already, do nothing.
  2. Get \(\alpha_p\), \(\alpha_s\) in positive dB. From a gain, \(\alpha=-20\log_{10}|H|\). From a ripple \(\delta_p\), the edge gain is \(1-\delta_p\) first. A deviation already in dB is used as printed.
  3. Translate to the analog domain, by the rule of the method: bilinear \(\Omega=\frac{2}{T}\tan\frac{\omega}{2}\) (pre-warp), impulse invariance \(\Omega=\omega/T\).
  4. Order \(N=\left\lceil\dfrac{\log\left[(10^{0.1\alpha_s}-1)/(10^{0.1\alpha_p}-1)\right]} {2\log(\Omega_s/\Omega_p)}\right\rceil\), and cut-off \(\Omega_c=\Omega_p/(10^{0.1\alpha_p}-1)^{1/2N}\).
  5. Poles \(s_k=\Omega_c e^{\,j\pi(N+2k+1)/2N}\), \(k=0\dots N-1\), then \(H_a(s)=\Omega_c^N\big/\prod_k(s-s_k)\), written as real quadratic sections.
  6. Map back: substitute \(s=\frac{2}{T}\frac{1-z^{-1}}{1+z^{-1}}\), or expand in partial fractions and use \(\frac{1}{s-p_k}\to\frac{1}{1-e^{p_kT}z^{-1}}\).
  7. Check \(|H(e^{j\omega_p})|\) and \(|H(e^{j\omega_s})|\) against the specification. Two substitutions, and they catch almost every slip.
Checks that cost nothing
  1. \(H(z)\) from a bilinear design has all its zeros at \(z=-1\), so its numerator is \(K(1+z^{-1})^N\) and its coefficients are \(K\) times the binomials \(1,N,\binom{N}{2},\dots\) Anything else is an algebra error.
  2. \(|H(e^{j0})|=1\) exactly for a Butterworth design, either method. Set \(z=1\), i.e. add up the coefficients: \(\sum b_k/\sum a_k=1\).
  3. \(|H(e^{j\omega_p})|\) must come out at exactly \(10^{-\alpha_p/20}\), because \(\Omega_c\) was chosen to make the passband exact.
  4. Every pole must satisfy \(|z|<1\), and they come in conjugate pairs, so all the printed coefficients are real.
The three shortcuts worth taking in the exam
  1. Set \(T=1\) in any bilinear design and say why. The \(2/T\) from the pre-warp and the \(2/T\) from the substitution cancel, so \(H(z)\) does not depend on \(T\) (§6.5 of the theory). Nine papers give a sampling frequency that changes nothing.
  2. Do not expand \(\prod(s-s_k)\) into a single polynomial unless asked. Leave \(H_a(s)\) as a product of quadratics; the bilinear substitution then runs one quadratic at a time and the arithmetic stays small.
  3. For \(N=2\) use the tabulated normalised form \(H_a(s)=\frac{1}{s^2+\sqrt2\,s+1}\) with \(s\to s/\Omega_c\); for \(N=3\), \(\frac{1}{(s+1)(s^2+s+1)}\). Both are just the pole formula pre-computed.

column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2079 Bhadra · 2071 Chaitra · 2069 Chaitra · [11+4]
Design a digital Butterworth low pass filter using the bilinear transformation method for \(W_p=0.25\pi\) rad, \(W_s=0.55\pi\) rad, \(\delta_p=0.11\), \(\delta_s=0.21\), sampling frequency 0.5 Hz. Then convert the obtained digital low-pass filter to a high-pass filter with new pass band frequency \(W'_p=0.45\pi\) using the digital domain transformation.
column4:
Step 1: the specification in dB
  • \(\delta_p=0.11\) is a deviation, so the passband edge gain is \(1-0.11=0.89\). \(\delta_s=0.21\) is already a gain.
  • \[ \alpha_p=-20\log_{10}0.89=\mathbf{1.0122}\ \text{dB},\qquad \alpha_s=-20\log_{10}0.21=\mathbf{13.5556}\ \text{dB} \]
  • Sampling frequency \(0.5\) Hz means \(T=2\) s. It will cancel, so take \(T=1\) and note it. (Working it through with \(T=2\) gives the identical \(H(z)\); only the intermediate \(\Omega\) values change, by a factor of 2.)
Step 2: pre-warp the band edges
  • \[ \Omega_p=2\tan\frac{0.25\pi}{2}=2\tan(22.5^\circ)=\mathbf{0.828427},\qquad \Omega_s=2\tan\frac{0.55\pi}{2}=2\tan(49.5^\circ)=\mathbf{2.341699} \]
  • This is the step that is skipped, and skipping it puts the finished band edges in the wrong place.
Step 3: order and cut-off
  • \[ 10^{0.1\alpha_p}-1=10^{0.10122}-1=0.262467,\qquad 10^{0.1\alpha_s}-1=10^{1.35556}-1=21.675737 \]
  • \[ N\ \ge\ \frac{\log_{10}(21.675737/0.262467)}{2\log_{10}(2.341699/0.828427)} =\frac{\log_{10}82.5847}{2\log_{10}2.82668} =\frac{1.91690}{2(0.45128)}=2.1239 \]
  • \[ \boxed{N=3} \qquad\text{(round \emph{up}, always)} \]
  • \[ \Omega_c=\frac{\Omega_p}{(10^{0.1\alpha_p}-1)^{1/2N}} =\frac{0.828427}{(0.262467)^{1/6}}=\frac{0.828427}{0.800164} =\mathbf{1.035321} \]
Step 4: the poles, and \(H_a(s)\)
  • \(N=3\), so three left-half-plane poles at radius \(\Omega_c\), spaced \(\pi/3\), at angles \(\pi\frac{3+2k+1}{6}\) for \(k=0,1,2\), i.e. \(120^\circ\), \(180^\circ\), \(240^\circ\):
\(k\)Angle\(s_k=\Omega_c e^{j\theta}\)Factor
0\(120^\circ\)\(-0.517661+j0.896615\)
2\(240^\circ\)\(-0.517661-j0.896615\)[0pt][0pt] \(s^2+1.035321\,s+1.071891\)
1\(180^\circ\)\(-1.035321\)\(s+1.035321\)
  • The conjugate pair multiplies to a real quadratic: sum of roots \(-1.035321\), and product \(=\Omega_c^2=1.071891\). For a Butterworth filter every quadratic section has constant term \(\Omega_c^2\), which is a free check.
  • \[ H_a(s)=\frac{\Omega_c^3}{(s+1.035321)(s^2+1.035321\,s+1.071891)} =\frac{1.109751}{(s+1.035321)(s^2+1.035321\,s+1.071891)} \]
Step 5: the bilinear substitution
  • Put \(s=2\dfrac{1-z^{-1}}{1+z^{-1}}\) into each factor, multiplying numerator and denominator of the whole expression by \((1+z^{-1})^3\):
  • \[ s+1.035321\ \longrightarrow\ \frac{2(1-z^{-1})+1.035321(1+z^{-1})}{1+z^{-1}} =\frac{3.035321-0.964679z^{-1}}{1+z^{-1}} \]
  • \[ s^2+1.035321s+1.071891\ \longrightarrow\ \frac{4(1-z^{-1})^2+2.070642(1-z^{-2})+1.071891(1+z^{-1})^2} {(1+z^{-1})^2} \]
  • \[ =\frac{7.142534-5.856219z^{-1}+3.001248z^{-2}}{(1+z^{-1})^2} \]
  • Multiply the two denominators:
  • \[ 21.679886-24.665755z^{-1}+14.759120z^{-2}-2.895239z^{-3} \]
  • Divide through by the constant term \(21.679886\), and the \((1+z^{-1})^3\) left over on top carries \(\Omega_c^3\), giving \(K=1.109751/21.679886=0.051188\):
  • \[ \boxed{\,H(z)=\frac{0.051188\,(1+z^{-1})^3} {1-1.137725z^{-1}+0.680775z^{-2}-0.133545z^{-3}}\,} \]
  • \[ =\frac{0.051188+0.153564z^{-1}+0.153564z^{-2}+0.051188z^{-3}} {1-1.137725z^{-1}+0.680775z^{-2}-0.133545z^{-3}} \]
  • The numerator coefficients are \(0.051188\times(1,3,3,1)\). If they are not the binomials, the substitution went wrong.
Step 6: check, before writing anything else
  • At \(z=1\) every \(z^{-1}\) becomes 1, so \(H(1)\) is just the sum of the numerator coefficients over the sum of the denominator's:
  • \[ H(1)=\frac{0.051188(1+3+3+1)}{1-1.137725+0.680775-0.133545} =\frac{0.409504}{0.409505}=\mathbf{1.0000} \] ✓Two additions, and they catch a wrong \(K\) instantly.
  • \(|H(e^{j0.25\pi})|=\mathbf{0.8900}\), which is \(1-\delta_p\) exactly, as the choice of \(\Omega_c\) guaranteed. ✓
  • \(|H(e^{j0.55\pi})|=\mathbf{0.0861}\le0.21\). ✓Comfortably over-satisfied, which is what rounding \(N\) up from 2.12 to 3 bought.
Step 7: the low pass to high pass conversion (the 4 marks)
  • Prototype edge \(\omega_p=0.25\pi\), new edge \(\omega'_p=0.45\pi\):
  • \[ \alpha=-\frac{\cos\frac{\omega_p+\omega'_p}{2}} {\cos\frac{\omega_p-\omega'_p}{2}} =-\frac{\cos(0.35\pi)}{\cos(0.10\pi)} =-\frac{0.45399}{0.95106}=\mathbf{-0.47735} \]
  • Substitute \(z^{-1}\to-\dfrac{z^{-1}+\alpha}{1+\alpha z^{-1}} =-\dfrac{z^{-1}-0.47735}{1-0.47735z^{-1}}\) into \(H(z)\) above:
  • \[ \boxed{\,H_{hp}(z)=\frac{0.276238\,(1-z^{-1})^3} {1-0.683740z^{-1}+0.457627z^{-2}-0.068533z^{-3}}\,} \]
  • \[ =\frac{0.276238-0.828713z^{-1}+0.828713z^{-2}-0.276238z^{-3}} {1-0.683740z^{-1}+0.457627z^{-2}-0.068533z^{-3}} \]
  • Checks: \(|H_{hp}(e^{j0})|=\mathbf{0}\) exactly, because every zero moved from \(z=-1\) to \(z=+1\); and \(|H_{hp}(e^{j0.45\pi})|=\mathbf{0.8900}\), the same \(1-\delta_p\) the prototype had at its own edge. Both checks are free and both are worth writing down.
Every other bilinear Butterworth paper

defective as printed
  • With \(f_s=256\) Hz the Nyquist frequency is 128 Hz. The stopband edge of 170 Hz is above it, so it does not exist as a digital frequency: \(\omega_s=2\pi(170)/256=1.3281\pi>\pi\).

73 Ch 11+4
  • \(0.707\) is \(1/\sqrt2\), so the passband edge is the 3 dB point and \(\Omega_c=\Omega_p\) with no formula at all:
  • \[ \Omega_p=2\tan\frac{\pi}{4}=\mathbf{2},\qquad \Omega_s=2\tan\frac{3\pi}{8}=4.82843,\qquad \Omega_c=\Omega_p=2 \]
  • \(\alpha_p=3.0103\) dB, \(\alpha_s=13.9794\) dB, \(N=1.8026\Rightarrow\boxed{N=2}\).
  • \[ H_a(s)=\frac{\Omega_c^2}{s^2+\sqrt2\,\Omega_c s+\Omega_c^2} =\frac{4}{s^2+2\sqrt2\,s+4} \]
  • Substituting \(s=2\frac{1-z^{-1}}{1+z^{-1}}\) the whole thing stays exact:
  • \[ H(z)=\frac{4(1+z^{-1})^2}{(8+4\sqrt2)+(8-4\sqrt2)z^{-2}} =\boxed{\frac{\tfrac{1}{2+\sqrt2}(1+z^{-1})^2} {1+\tfrac{2-\sqrt2}{2+\sqrt2}z^{-2}}} =\frac{0.292893(1+z^{-1})^2}{1+0.171573z^{-2}} \]

QUESTION AS PRINTED 2072 Magh · [11]
Design a low pass discrete time Chebyshev filter by applying bilinear transformation for \(0.707\le|H(e^{jw})|\le1\) for \(|w|\le0.2\pi\) and \(|H(e^{jw})|\le0.1\) for \(0.5\pi\le|w|\le\pi\).
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2075 Bhadra · [10]
Design an analog filter using Chebyshev approximation with maximum passband attenuation 5 dB at 20 rad/sec and stopband attenuation 20 dB at 50 rad/sec; then, taking a sampling frequency of 0.5 Hz, convert the obtained analog filter to digital using the bilinear transformation method.
column4:
Steps 1, 2, 6 and 7 are identical to §1. Only steps 3 to 5 change: a different order formula, \(\Omega_c=\Omega_p\) with no formula, and poles on an ellipse instead of a circle.
Step 1 to 3: spec, pre-warp, ripple factor
  • \(\alpha_p=-20\log_{10}0.707=3.0116\) dB, \(\alpha_s=-20\log_{10}0.1=20\) dB.
  • \(\Omega_p=2\tan(0.1\pi)=\mathbf{0.64984}\), \(\Omega_s=2\tan(0.25\pi)=\mathbf{2}\) exactly.
  • \[ \varepsilon=\sqrt{10^{0.1\alpha_p}-1}=\sqrt{10^{0.30116}-1} =\mathbf{1.00030}\approx1 \]
  • \(\varepsilon=1\) because \(0.707\) is the 3 dB point, the same coincidence 73 Ch exploits in §1.3.
  • \(\Omega_c=\Omega_p=0.64984\). A Chebyshev filter ripples right up to the passband edge, so there is no separate cut-off to compute.
Step 4: order, by the \(\cosh^{-1}\) formula
  • \[ N\ \ge\ \frac{\cosh^{-1}\sqrt{(10^{2}-1)/(10^{0.30116}-1)}} {\cosh^{-1}(2/0.64984)} =\frac{\cosh^{-1}(9.94687)}{\cosh^{-1}(3.07769)}=1.6694 \]
  • \[ \boxed{N=2} \]
  • Use \(\cosh^{-1}x=\ln\!\left(x+\sqrt{x^2-1}\right)\) if the calculator lacks the key: \(\ln(19.8433)=2.98787\) and \(\ln(5.9884)=1.78982\).
  • Compare: a Butterworth filter on this same spec needs \(N=3\). That one saved order is the whole argument for Chebyshev.
Step 5: the pole ellipse
  • \[ \alpha=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}+\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}} =1.0003+1.4145=\mathbf{2.41370} \]
  • \[ a=\tfrac12\!\left(\alpha^{1/2}-\alpha^{-1/2}\right)=\mathbf{0.45497}, \qquad b=\tfrac12\!\left(\alpha^{1/2}+\alpha^{-1/2}\right)=\mathbf{1.09864} \]
  • Semi-axes: \(a\Omega_c=0.29566\) (real direction), \(b\Omega_c=0.71394\) (imaginary direction). Taller than wide, always.
  • \(N=2\), so \(\theta_k=\frac{(2k+1)\pi}{4}=45^\circ,135^\circ\):
  • \[ s_k=-a\Omega_c\sin\theta_k+j\,b\Omega_c\cos\theta_k =\mathbf{-0.20906\pm j0.50483} \]
  • \[ H_a(s)=\frac{K}{s^2+0.418125s+0.298560},\qquad K=\frac{|s_k|^2}{\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}} =\frac{0.298560}{1.41443}=\mathbf{0.211082} \]
  • The \(\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}\) divisor is because \(N\) is even. Omit it and the passband sits a factor of \(1.414\) too high everywhere.
Step 6 and 7: map back and check
  • \[ \boxed{\,H(z)=\frac{0.041108\,(1+z^{-1})^2} {1-1.441705z^{-1}+0.674282z^{-2}}\,} \]
  • \(|H(e^{j0.2\pi})|=\mathbf{0.70700}\), exactly the specified \(0.707\). ✓
  • \(|H(e^{j0.5\pi})|=\mathbf{0.05563}\le0.1\). ✓
  • \(|H(e^{j0})|=\mathbf{0.70700}\), not 1. The passband oscillates between \(0.707\) and \(1\) and, with \(N\) even, it starts at the bottom of the ripple. This is correct and looks wrong: say so in the answer.

  • \[ \alpha=-\frac{\cos\frac{\omega_c+\omega'_c}{2}} {\cos\frac{\omega_c-\omega'_c}{2}} =-\frac{\cos(0.3071\pi)}{\cos(0.0496\pi)} =-\frac{0.569595}{0.987880}=\mathbf{-0.57658} \]
  • \(|\alpha|<1\) ✓, so the map is stable.
  • Substitute \(z^{-1}\to-\dfrac{z^{-1}+\alpha}{1+\alpha z^{-1}} =-\dfrac{z^{-1}-0.57658}{1-0.57658z^{-1}}\), multiplying top and bottom by \((1-0.57658z^{-1})^2\) to clear the fractions:
  • \[ \boxed{\,H_{hp}(z)=\frac{0.48106-0.94325z^{-1}+0.38393z^{-2}} {1-0.68240z^{-1}+0.12585z^{-2}}\,} \]
  • Check: \(|H_{hp}(e^{j0.3567\pi})|=\mathbf{0.70789}\), the same value the low pass had at its own cut-off. That is exactly what the transformation promises, and it is the one line that proves the answer.
  • Note the numerator's signs alternate where the prototype's did not. A high pass built this way pushes the zeros towards \(z=+1\).
80 Ba, 70 Asa 42
Both are bookwork, answered in §6.6 of the theory: why the transformation is required (impulse invariance cannot make a high pass; doing it in the \(z\) domain avoids aliasing entirely), the all-pass form the map must take, and the LP \(\to\) HP row of the table with its \(\alpha\).

column1: Chapter 7 — Discrete Fourier Transform and FFT: how is it examined?
column4:
7 hrs  \(\cdot\) 99 questions across the 45 papers  \(\cdot\) worth about 14 of 80 marks  \(\cdot\) 3 syllabus sub-topics  \(\cdot\) the heaviest chapter in the subject.
Read this first:
  • Three questions, and only three, in 44 of the 45 papers:
    • Compute an \(N\)-point DFT by DIT or DIF TOP 43, 340 marks. Almost always 8-point, almost always "draw the butterfly".
    • Circular convolution TOP 39, 253 marks, in three disguises that are all the same calculation (§7.5).
    • Bookwork on the DFT TOP 17, 52 marks: why DFT, why FFT, the properties, zero padding.
  • The FFT is not a new transform. It is the DFT, computed by a rearrangement that costs \(\tfrac{N}{2}\log_2N\) multiplications instead of \(N^2\). Anyone who says "the FFT of \(x[n]\)" means its DFT.
  • DIT and DIF give identical answers. They differ only in where the bit-reversal sits and where the twiddle factor is applied. If a paper does not say which, either is a full-marks answer.
  • Everything rests on two identities, and nothing else:
  • \[ W_N=e^{-j2\pi/N},\qquad W_N^{\,k+N/2}=-W_N^{\,k},\qquad W_N^{\,k+N}=W_N^{\,k} \] The first halves the work at every stage; the second is what makes the recursion close.
  • A sequence shorter than \(N\) is zero padded. Eleven papers print six or seven values for an 8-point transform. That is not a misprint to fix, it is the zero-padding they ask you to define elsewhere in the same paper.

column1: Why do we need the DFT / FFT although we have the DTFT? Differentiate between the DFT and the DTFT
column4:
Why the DTFT is not enough
  • The DTFT \(X(e^{j\omega})=\sum_n x[n]e^{-j\omega n}\) is a continuous function of \(\omega\).
  • A computer cannot store a continuous function, and it cannot sum an infinite series. Neither end of the DTFT is computable.
  • The DFT fixes both at once: finite sequence in, finite set of samples out.
  • \[ X[k]=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]W_N^{\,nk},\qquad x[n]=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X[k]W_N^{-nk} \]
  • The DFT is the DTFT sampled at \(N\) equally spaced points, \(\omega_k=2\pi k/N\). Nothing more.
  • The price: the DFT implicitly treats \(x[n]\) as one period of a periodic sequence. Every oddity in this chapter, circular shift, circular convolution, wrap-around, follows from that one fact.
DFT against DTFT, as a table
DTFTDFT
Inputany length, even infinitefinite, \(N\) points
Outputcontinuous in \(\omega\)discrete, \(N\) points
Periodic in\(\omega\), period \(2\pi\)\(k\), period \(N\)
Computablenoyes
Assumesnothing\(x[n]\) is periodic with period \(N\)
Convolutionlinearcircular
And why the FFT
  • The DFT as defined costs \(N^2\) complex multiplications. The FFT is an algorithm for the same numbers at \(\tfrac{N}{2}\log_2N\).
  • For \(N=8\): \(64\) against \(12\). For \(N=1024\): \(1\,048\,576\) against \(5120\), a speed-up of 204.8. Quote a number; it is worth a mark.

column1: How does the FFT reduce computational complexity compared with direct computation of the DFT?
column4:
The argument, in four lines
  1. Direct DFT: \(N\) outputs, each a sum of \(N\) products. \(N^2\) complex multiplications and \(N(N-1)\) additions.
  2. Split \(x[n]\) into two half-length sequences. Two \(\tfrac{N}{2}\)-point DFTs cost \(2(\tfrac{N}{2})^2=\tfrac{N^2}{2}\), half the work, plus \(\tfrac{N}{2}\) twiddle multiplications to recombine.
  3. Repeat the split. \(N=2^m\) allows it \(m=\log_2N\) times, until only 2-point DFTs remain, and a 2-point DFT needs no multiplication at all (\(W_2^0=1\)).
  4. Each of the \(\log_2N\) stages has \(\tfrac{N}{2}\) butterflies and each butterfly costs one multiplication:
\[ \boxed{\ \tfrac{N}{2}\log_2N \ \text{multiplications},\quad N\log_2N \ \text{additions}\ } \]
The numbers to quote
\(N\)Direct \(N^2\)FFT \(\frac N2\log_2N\)Speed-up
\(8\)\(64\)\(12\)\(5.33\)
\(32\)\(1024\)\(80\)\(12.8\)
\(256\)\(65\,536\)\(1024\)\(64\)
\(1024\)\(1\,048\,576\)\(5120\)\(204.8\)
  • The saving grows with \(N\), which is the point: it is \(2N/\log_2N\), not a constant factor.
  • Radix-2 needs \(N\) a power of 2. If it is not, zero pad up to one. That is the second reason zero padding exists.
  • The two properties being exploited are periodicity \(W_N^{k+N}=W_N^k\) and symmetry \(W_N^{k+N/2}=-W_N^k\). Name them: they are usually worth a mark each.

column1: State and prove the circular convolution property of the DFT; write about the multiplication and convolution properties
column4:
The property, and its proof
  • Statement. If \(x_3[n]=x_1[n]\circledast x_2[n]\), the circular convolution, then
  • \[ X_3[k]=X_1[k]\,X_2[k] \] Circular convolution in time is multiplication in frequency.
  • Proof. Write the circular convolution and transform it:
  • \[ X_3[k]=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\Big(\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}x_1[m]\, x_2[((n-m))_N]\Big)W_N^{\,nk} \]
  • Swap the sums and put \(\ell=n-m\), so \(n=\ell+m\) and \(W_N^{nk}=W_N^{mk}W_N^{\ell k}\):
  • \[ =\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}x_1[m]W_N^{\,mk} \sum_{\ell=0}^{N-1}x_2[((\ell))_N]W_N^{\,\ell k} =X_1[k]X_2[k] \]
  • The modulo-\(N\) index is what makes the inner sum come out as \(X_2[k]\) exactly, with no leftover terms. That is the whole proof, and the step worth pointing at.
  • The dual (multiplication property): multiplying in time is circular convolution divided by \(N\) in frequency, \(x_1[n]x_2[n]\longleftrightarrow\frac1N X_1[k]\circledast X_2[k]\). Do not forget the \(1/N\).

  • Row 4 is the circular shift: a shift in time is a phase in frequency and nothing else. The magnitude spectrum does not move.
  • Row 3 is duality, and it is the whole of the 67 Mng question in §7.3.
  • The last row is the free check on every answer in this chapter: a real sequence has a conjugate-symmetric spectrum, so \(X[N-k]=X^*[k]\). Compute half the values and mirror the rest.

column1: Define zero padding, and Parseval's theorem
column4:
Zero padding
  • Appending zeros to a sequence before taking its DFT, to reach a chosen length \(N\).
  • Three reasons, and papers accept any of them:
    • to reach a power of 2 so a radix-2 FFT can run;
    • to make \(N\ge L+M-1\) so a circular convolution equals the linear one (§7.5, and this is the reason the question sits beside those problems);
    • to interpolate the spectrum: more samples of the same underlying DTFT.
  • Zero padding does NOT add information and does NOT improve resolution. It samples the same DTFT more finely. Saying otherwise loses the mark.
Parseval's theorem
  • Energy is the same computed either side of the transform:
  • \[ \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|x[n]|^2=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}|X[k]|^2 \]
  • Note the \(1/N\), which is on the frequency side, matching the IDFT.
  • Useful as an arithmetic check: compute \(\sum|x[n]|^2\) from the given sequence in two seconds, then confirm the \(X[k]\) you just worked out.
Linear against circular convolution (75 Ch asks for it directly)
  • Linear: indices run freely, result has length \(L+M-1\), and it is what a real LTI system does.
  • Circular: indices are taken \(\bmod\ N\), result has length \(N\), and it is what multiplying two DFTs gives you.
  • They agree exactly when \(N\ge L+M-1\), and otherwise the circular one is the linear one wrapped round and added to itself.

column1: Using the duality property, how can a forward DFT routine be used to compute the IDFT?
column4:
The conjugate trick, which is the expected answer
  1. Start from the IDFT and conjugate both sides:
  2. \[ x[n]=\frac1N\sum_k X[k]W_N^{-nk} \ \Longrightarrow\ x^*[n]=\frac1N\sum_k X^*[k]W_N^{\,nk} \]
  3. The right-hand sum is a forward DFT of \(X^*[k]\). So:
  4. \[ \boxed{\,x[n]=\frac1N\Big(\mathrm{DFT}\big\{X^*[k]\big\}\Big)^{*}\,} \]
  5. Three steps: conjugate the input, run the same FFT, conjugate the output and divide by \(N\).
  6. No second routine is needed, which is the point of the question: the same butterfly hardware computes both directions.
The duality route, if the paper insists
  • Duality says \(X[n]\xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{DFT}\ }Nx[((-k))_N]\).
  • So feeding the spectrum \(X[k]\) into a forward DFT returns the original sequence, scaled by \(N\) and index reversed modulo \(N\):
  • \[ x[n]=\frac1N\,\mathrm{DFT}\big\{X[k]\big\}\Big|_{\,k\to-n \bmod N} \]
  • Index reversal modulo \(N\) leaves entry \(0\) alone and reverses the rest, so \(\{a,b,c,d\}\to\{a,d,c,b\}\). That single sentence is what the 8 marks are for.
  • Both routes are correct. The conjugate one is easier to defend and is what 72 Ash's worked answer needs (§2 of the numericals).

column1: How do you use the DIT-FFT algorithm to compute the 8-point DFT of a sequence? Explain with the flow graph
column4:
Decimation in time, derived
  • Split the sum by even and odd \(n\):
  • \[ X[k]=\sum_{r}x[2r]W_N^{\,2rk}+\sum_{r}x[2r+1]W_N^{\,(2r+1)k} \]
  • \(W_N^{2}=W_{N/2}\), so both sums are \(\tfrac N2\)-point DFTs:
  • \[ \boxed{\,X[k]=G[k]+W_N^{\,k}H[k]\,} \] with \(G\) from the even samples and \(H\) from the odd ones.
  • The other half comes free from the symmetry:
  • \[ X[k+\tfrac N2]=G[k]-W_N^{\,k}H[k] \]
  • One multiplication serves two outputs. That pair is the butterfly, and it is the entire saving.
  • Recurse \(\log_2N\) times. Splitting by even and odd repeatedly leaves the input in bit-reversed order; the output comes out natural.
The butterfly
Left, the butterfly as first drawn: two twiddles. Right, the same butterfly after \(W_N^{\,r+N/2}=W_N^{\,r}W_N^{\,N/2}=-W_N^{\,r}\) is used, so one multiplication and a sign. Always draw the right-hand form.
  • Every stage is \(\tfrac N2\) of these; there are \(\log_2N\) stages.
  • The \(-1\) on the lower branch is not decoration. Omitting it is the single most common way to lose the marks on a flow graph.
The 8-point DIT flow graph (draw this one)
Input bit-reversed \(\{x[0],x[4],x[2],x[6],x[1],x[5],x[3],x[7]\}\), output natural. Three stages. Twiddles \(W_N^0\) in stage 1; \(W_N^0,W_N^2\) in stage 2; \(W_N^0,W_N^1,W_N^2,W_N^3\) in stage 3. The twiddle count doubles each stage and the butterfly span doubles with it.

column1: Draw the flow graph for the 8-point decimation in frequency algorithm
column4:
Decimation in frequency, derived
  • This time split the input into first and second halves, and the output into even and odd \(k\):
  • \[ g[n]=x[n]+x[n+\tfrac N2],\qquad h[n]=\big(x[n]-x[n+\tfrac N2]\big)W_N^{\,n} \]
  • \[ X[2r]=\mathrm{DFT}_{N/2}\{g[n]\},\qquad X[2r+1]=\mathrm{DFT}_{N/2}\{h[n]\} \]
  • The twiddle multiplies the DIFFERENCE, after the subtraction. In DIT it multiplies before the add. That is the only real difference between the two.
  • Recurse \(\log_2N\) times. Input stays natural; output comes out bit-reversed and has to be unscrambled.
DIT against DIF, the whole comparison
DITDIF
Splitsinput, even/odd \(n\)output, even/odd \(k\)
Input orderbit-reversednatural
Output ordernaturalbit-reversed
Twiddlebefore the addafter the subtract
Stages\(\log_2N\)\(\log_2N\)
Multiplies\(\frac N2\log_2N\)\(\frac N2\log_2N\)
Answeridentical
Bit reversal, which is all either algorithm scrambles
  • The same permutation serves both: \(0,4,2,6,1,5,3,7\) for \(N=8\). It is its own inverse, so there is only one order to memorise.
  • Get it by writing the index in binary and reading it backwards: \(3=011\to110=6\), \(1=001\to100=4\).
  • Exactly one end is scrambled, never both and never neither. DIT scrambles the input, DIF the output.
  • For \(N=4\) it is \(0,2,1,3\); for \(N=16\), \(0,8,4,12,2,10,6,14,1,9,5,13,3,11,7,15\).
  • The scrambling is not overhead you can avoid. It is what lets every butterfly write its result back over its own inputs, so the whole transform runs in one array with no scratch space.
The 8-point DIF flow graph (the other one to be able to draw)
Input natural, output bit-reversed: \(X[0],X[4],X[2],X[6],X[1],X[5],X[3],X[7]\) read down the right edge. The dashed boxes show the recursion, the \(N/2=4\)-point DFTs inside the whole transform and the \(N/4=2\)-point DFTs inside those. The twiddles run \(W_N^0\) to \(W_N^3\) in stage 1 and halve their range at each stage, the mirror image of DIT, where they start at \(W_N^0\) alone and double.

column1: Compute the circular convolution of two sequences
column4:
In one line: circular convolution is ordinary convolution with the index taken modulo \(N\), so the tail that would have run off the end wraps round and adds onto the front instead. Everything below is that sentence applied.
The three disguises
  1. "Compute the circular convolution of \(x_1\) and \(x_2\)." Direct.
  2. "Find \(x_3[n]\) if \(X_3[k]=X_1[k]X_2[k]\)." By the property in §7.2 this IS the circular convolution, so do the same arithmetic and do not compute a single DFT.
  3. "Find the linear convolution using circular convolution." Zero pad both to \(N\ge L+M-1\), then the same arithmetic again.
Recognising that (2) needs no transform is worth several minutes in the exam. The long route, three DFTs and an IDFT, earns the same marks and takes four times as long. Say in one line that you are using the property, then convolve.
The matrix method, which is the fastest by hand
  • Write the circulant of one sequence: first column is \(x_2\), and each next column is the previous rotated down by one.
  • \[ y[n]=\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}x_1[m]\,x_2[((n-m))_N] \]
  • Multiply by \(x_1\) as a column vector. Each row of the product is one output sample, so the whole answer falls out of one \(N\times N\) table.
  • Check: \(\sum y[n]=\big(\sum x_1\big)\big(\sum x_2\big)\), always. It is \(Y[0]=X_1[0]X_2[0]\) in disguise, it costs two additions, and it catches almost every slip.
Choosing \(N\)
  • If the paper names \(N\), use it, and pad both sequences up to it.
  • If not, \(N=\max(L,M)\) for a circular answer, and \(N=L+M-1\) for a linear one.
  • \(N\) smaller than \(L+M-1\) wraps, and the wrap is not an error: it is the correct circular answer to the question that was asked.
  • \(N\) larger than \(L+M-1\) only appends zeros to the result. Harmless, and sometimes needed to reach a power of 2.
The concentric-circle picture
  • The same arithmetic, drawn: \(x_1\) clockwise on an inner circle, \(x_2\) anticlockwise on an outer one, multiply the aligned pairs and sum, then rotate one circle a step for the next output.
  • Use the matrix instead. The circles are slower, easier to misalign, and no paper in the 45 demands them.

column1: Chapter 7 numericals — which formulas does everything come from?
column4:
82 of the 99 questions are two calculations: an \(N\)-point DFT by DIT or DIF (43 questions, 340 marks) and a circular convolution (39 questions, 253 marks). The other 17 are bookwork, answered in the theory chapter. Every computational paper in the 45 is below.
The DIT recipe
  1. Pad \(x[n]\) with zeros up to \(N\), a power of 2. Eleven papers print six or seven values for an 8-point transform; that is the zero padding, not a misprint.
  2. Reorder the input into bit-reversed order. For \(N=8\) that is \(x[0],x[4],x[2],x[6],x[1],x[5],x[3],x[7]\).
  3. Stage 1: \(N/2\) butterflies on adjacent pairs, twiddle \(W_N^0=1\), so it is pure add and subtract.
  4. Stage 2: butterflies spanning 2, twiddles \(W_N^0\) and \(W_N^{2}\).
  5. Stage 3: butterflies spanning 4, twiddles \(W_N^0\dots W_N^{3}\).
  6. Read the output in natural order: it is \(X[0]\) to \(X[N-1]\).
The DIF recipe, which is the same thing backwards
  1. Pad to \(N\) as before, but leave the input in natural order.
  2. Stage 1: butterflies spanning \(N/2\), twiddle applied to the difference, twiddles \(W_N^0\dots W_N^{3}\).
  3. Stage 2: span \(N/4\), twiddles \(W_N^0\) and \(W_N^{2}\).
  4. Stage 3: span 1, twiddle \(W_N^0\), pure add and subtract.
  5. Unscramble the output: what comes out in position \(i\) is \(X[\,\)bitrev\((i)]\).
The twiddle factors, which is all the arithmetic there is
\(W_8^k\)ExactDecimal
\(W_8^0\)\(1\)\(1\)
\(W_8^1\)\(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1-j)\)\(0.7071-j0.7071\)
\(W_8^2\)\(-j\)\(-j\)
\(W_8^3\)\(-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1+j)\)\(-0.7071-j0.7071\)
And \(W_4^k\) is \(1,-j,-1,+j\). Beyond \(k=3\) use \(W_8^{k+4}=-W_8^{k}\); there are only four numbers to know.
Checks that cost nothing
  1. \(X[0]=\sum x[n]\). One addition, and it catches a wrong first stage.
  2. \(X[N-k]=X^*[k]\) for real \(x[n]\). Compute \(X[1]\) to \(X[N/2]\) and mirror the rest, which halves the work and is not a shortcut the examiner can object to.
  3. \(X[N/2]=\sum(-1)^n x[n]\), the alternating sum.
  4. Parseval: \(\sum|x[n]|^2=\frac1N\sum|X[k]|^2\).
  5. For a convolution, \(\sum y[n]=(\sum x_1)(\sum x_2)\).

column1: 1.3  72 Ash: the IDFT through a forward FFT
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2072 Ashwin · [2+6]
Use the FFT algorithm to compute the IDFT of the sequence \(X(k)=\{6,\ -2+2j,\ -2,\ -2-2j\}\).
column4:
• Use \(x[n]=\frac1N\big(\mathrm{DFT}\{X^*[k]\}\big)^*\) from §7.3.
  • Conjugate: \(X^*(k)=\{6,\ -2-2j,\ -2,\ -2+2j\}\).
  • Forward 4-point DFT of that, by DIT: bit-reversed input \(\{6,-2,-2-2j,-2+2j\}\); stage 1 gives \(\{4,8,-4,-4j\}\); stage 2 with \(W_4^1=-j\) gives \(\{0,\ 4,\ 8,\ 12\}\).
  • Conjugate and divide by \(N=4\):
  • \[ \boxed{x[n]=\tfrac14\{0,4,8,12\}^{*}=\{0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3\}} \]
  • Check forwards: \(\sum x[n]=6=X(0)\). ✓ And \(x[n]\) came out real, as it must, because \(X(k)\) was conjugate symmetric (\(X(3)=X^*(1)\)).

column1: 2.2  Linear convolution through circular convolution
column3:
QUESTION AS PRINTED 2074 Chaitra · [1+5]
What is zero padding? Find the linear convolution of \(x=\{1,1,1,1\}\) and \(h=\{2,3\}\) using circular convolution.
column4:
• \(L=4\), \(M=2\), so the linear result has \(L+M-1=\mathbf{5}\) samples. Zero pad both to length 5: \(x=\{1,1,1,1,0\}\), \(h=\{2,3,0,0,0\}\).
  • The \(5\times5\) circulant of \(h\) against \(x\) gives
  • \[ \boxed{y[n]=\{2,\ 5,\ 5,\ 5,\ 3\}} \]
  • Check: \(\sum y=20=(\sum x)(\sum h)=4\times5\). ✓
  • Why the padding matters, in one demonstration. Convolving the same two sequences circularly at \(N=4\) instead gives \(\{5,5,5,5\}\). The 5th sample, \(3\), had nowhere to go, so it wrapped onto \(y[0]\): \(2+3=5\). That is the time-domain aliasing the whole question is about, and it is the answer to the "what is zero padding" part.
